Jataka.title: The Pāḷi Jātaka Stories (from the first 50)
Jataka.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from the Pāḷi Jātaka Stories (the first 50) together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Jataka.intro: This is a collection of 32 Jātaka tales, ancient Buddhist stories detailing the previous lives of the Buddha that impart moral lessons. They are selected from the first 50 stories in the Pāḷi Jātaka collection. The narratives typically follow a consistent structure: a “story of the present” involving the Buddha’s contemporary disciples, followed by a “story of the past” where the Bodhisatta appears in a different form, such as a merchant or a king of the deer. Key themes throughout the texts include the importance of prudence, caution, and compassion in overcoming worldly dangers and spiritual obstacles. For instance, one tale contrasts a wise caravan leader with a foolish one to emphasize the value of truth over deception. Another story highlights how renunciation and contentment bring a sense of security that royal power cannot provide. The records serve therefore as a guide for practitioners to navigate the path to enlightenment by avoiding the traps laid by the senses and strictly following the Dhamma.
Jataka.keywords: Bodhisattva, Perfections, Biography, India, Parables, Folklore, EBT, Pāḷi

001-The-Waterless-Desert.htm.title: 01 The Waterless Desert
001-The-Waterless-Desert.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Waterless Desert from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
001-The-Waterless-Desert.htm.intro: In Benares, Kāsi, a wise Bodhisatta and a foolish merchant led separate caravans across a Waterless Desert. Tricked by a Yakkha pretending rain was ahead, the fool discarded his water, leading his men to be devoured. The Bodhisatta recognized the demon’s trickery, preserved his water, and safely navigated the wilderness. He salvaged the first caravan’s abandoned goods, returning home with great wealth and all his men.

002-The-Well-of-Perseverance.htm.title: 02 The Well of Perseverance
002-The-Well-of-Perseverance.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Well of Perseverance from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
002-The-Well-of-Perseverance.htm.intro: In Benares, under King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, the Bodhisatta led a caravan across a scorching sandy wilderness. When their pilot fell asleep, they lost their way and exhausted their water. While others despaired, the Bodhisatta’s persistent effort led him to find water sixty cubits beneath a rock. By breaking the stone, they were saved, demonstrating that untiring effort eventually brings success and inner peace.

003-The-Golden-Bowl.htm.title: 03 The Golden Bowl
003-The-Golden-Bowl.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Golden Bowl from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
003-The-Golden-Bowl.htm.intro: In the kingdom of Seri, the Bodhisatta and a greedy merchant sold wares in the city of Andhapura. A poor family offered a dirty bowl, unaware it was real gold. The greedy hawker, called Serivā, lied about its value to cheat them, but the honest Bodhisatta recognized its true worth and paid fairly. Consumed by rage and intense sorrow, the greedy merchant perished, marking Devadatta’s first grudge against him.

004-The-Dead-Mouse.htm.title: 04 The Dead Mouse
004-The-Dead-Mouse.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Dead Mouse from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
004-The-Dead-Mouse.htm.intro: In Benares, Kāsi, the Lord High Treasurer Cullakaseṭṭhi noted with a dead mouse he could start a business. A poor young man overheard and sold it for a farthing. Through clever trades involving molasses, water, and firewood, he amassed wealth. After buying a ship’s cargo and earning two hundred thousand pieces, he shared half with Cullakaseṭṭhi. Impressed, the Treasurer married him to his own daughter, making the industrious youth his sole successor.

005-The-Measure-of-Rice.htm.title: 05 The Measure of Rice
005-The-Measure-of-Rice.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Measure of Rice from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
005-The-Measure-of-Rice.htm.intro: In Benares, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi replaced his honest valuer, the Bodhisatta, with a foolish man to preserve royal wealth. This new valuer absurdly priced five hundred horses at just one measure of rice. Advised by the Bodhisatta, the horse-dealer bribed the fool to value that rice before the court. He claimed it was worth all Bārāṇasī, exposing his incompetence and the king’s greed to public laughter and deep ridicule.

006-The-Water-Rakkhasa.htm.title: 06 The Water Rakkhasa
006-The-Water-Rakkhasa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Water Rakkhasa from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
006-The-Water-Rakkhasa.htm.intro: Prince Mahiṁsāsa and his brothers, Candakumāra and Sūriyakumāra, fled to the Himālayas to escape their stepmother’s schemes. At a pool, a Water Rakkhasa captured the younger princes for failing to define the true Deva-nature. Mahiṁsāsa, the Bodhisatta, confronted the monster. He explained that true Deva-nature belongs to those endowed with conscience, concern, and virtue. Consequently, the Bodhisatta shared this sacred wisdom with the monster to secure his trapped brothers’ freedom.

009-The-Kings-Grey-Hair.htm.title: 09 The King’s Grey Hair
009-The-Kings-Grey-Hair.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The King’s Grey Hair from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
009-The-Kings-Grey-Hair.htm.intro: King Makhādeva of Mithilā lived for millennia before spotting a single grey hair. Viewing it as a divine messenger warning of impermanence and death, he immediately abdicated to his son and became an ascetic. Spending millennia cultivating divine virtues in a mango grove, he reached the Brahma Realm. Reborn later as King Nimi, he and his lineage repeated this same path of righteous rule and spiritual renunciation.

010-Bliss-of-Renunciation.htm.title: 10 The Bliss of Renunciation
010-Bliss-of-Renunciation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Bliss of Renunciation from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
010-Bliss-of-Renunciation.htm.intro: The Bodhisatta, a wealthy Brahmin ascetic in the Himālayas, stayed in Benares within the royal gardens. His oldest disciple, a former king, visited and exulted, “Oh, happiness!” (sukhaṁ) ignoring the current King. The Bodhisatta explained that this bliss surpassed royal pomp, arising from renunciation and Absorption. This Dhamma lesson on the monk’s life appeased the King. The Bodhisatta was eventually reborn in the high Realm of Brahma.

011-The-Wisdom-of-Lakkhana.htm.title: 11 The Wisdom of Lakkhaṇa
011-The-Wisdom-of-Lakkhana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Wisdom of Lakkhaṇa from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
011-The-Wisdom-of-Lakkhana.htm.intro: An old stag king appoints his two sons, wise Lakkhaṇa and foolish Kāḷa, to lead five hundred deer each to the mountains to avoid harvest-time traps. Kāḷa travels recklessly during daylight, leading his entire herd to destruction by hunters. Conversely, Lakkhaṇa moves only at night, avoiding human settlements and preserving his entire herd. Lakkhaṇa returns safely with all five hundred deer, while Kāḷa returns utterly alone.

012-The-Golden-Deer.htm.title: 12 The Golden Deer
012-The-Golden-Deer.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Golden Deer from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
012-The-Golden-Deer.htm.intro: Born as the golden deer King Nigrodha, the Bodhisatta lived alongside rival leader Sākha. When a king trapped their herds in his park for hunting, Nigrodha instituted daily turns for slaughter to prevent needless injuries. When a pregnant doe was refused help by Sākha, Nigrodha offered his own life instead. Moved by this compassion, the king granted immunity to Nigrodha, the doe, and ultimately all living creatures. After Nigrodha taught the king righteousness, the doe urged her fawn to follow only Nigrodha, whose moral leadership eventually guided the deer to respect human crops forever.

014-The-Wind-Deer.htm.title: 14 The Wind Deer
014-The-Wind-Deer.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Wind Deer from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
014-The-Wind-Deer.htm.intro: In Benares, gardener Sañjaya discovered a timid Wind-Deer (Vātamiga) in the king’s gardens. Seeking to capture it, Sañjaya smeared grass with honey, effectively exploiting the creature’s "lust of taste". After gaining its confidence, he lured the deer directly into the palace. King Brahmadatta observed the trapped animal, teaching that nothing in the world is viler than sensory craving, which can so easily enslave even the most wild, fearful living beings.

018-The-Sacrificial-Goat.htm.title: 18 The Sacrificial Goat
018-The-Sacrificial-Goat.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Sacrificial Goat from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
018-The-Sacrificial-Goat.htm.intro: A brahmin prepares a sacrificial goat for sacrifice. The goat laughs, knowing its five-hundredth birth of decapitation for killing a goat is finally ending, but weeps for the brahmin’s own future penalty. Despite the brahmin’s promised protection, a lightning bolt-struck rock beheads the creature. The Bodhisatta appears, teaching the Dhamma: Those understanding the intense suffering caused by killing living beings would never slay another.

022-The-Teaching-of-the-Dog.htm.title: 22 The Teaching of the Dog
022-The-Teaching-of-the-Dog.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Teaching of the Dog from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
022-The-Teaching-of-the-Dog.htm.intro: The Bodhisatta, living as a dog, saves his kin from the great King Brahmadatta’s unjust slaughter. After the King’s carriage leather is gnawed, the Bodhisatta identifies the palace’s own thoroughbred dogs as the true culprits. He proves their guilt by inducing vomiting with buttermilk and kusa grass. Moved by this profound wisdom, the King finally embraces the Dhamma, ensuring lifelong safety, food, and righteousness for all living creatures.

023-The-Noble-Warhorse.htm.title: 23 The Noble Warhorse
023-The-Noble-Warhorse.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Noble Warhorse from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
023-The-Noble-Warhorse.htm.intro: Reborn as a noble warhorse, the Bodhisatta was tasked with helping a brave knight defeat seven invading kings surrounding Benares. After successfully capturing six kings, the horse was severely wounded. Seeing his rider prepare an inferior horse for the final battle, the Bodhisatta insisted on being re-armored, charging in to capture the seventh king. Before dying, he advised the king to show mercy, maintain righteousness, and reward the knight generously.

026-The-State-Elephant.htm.title: 26 The State Elephant
026-The-State-Elephant.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The State Elephant from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
026-The-State-Elephant.htm.intro: As a wise minister, the Bodhisatta investigates the king’s once-gentle state elephant, Mahilāmukha, who suddenly turns violent and begins killing his handlers. Recognizing no physical illness, the Bodhisatta discovers the elephant had overheard nightly conversations of burglars plotting murder and violence, mistakenly adopting their advice. By replacing the thieves with virtuous sages to speak of mercy and loving-kindness, the elephant quickly reforms, restoring his gentle nature and earning the Bodhisatta great royal honors.

027-Elephant-and-Dog.htm.title: 27 The Elephant and the Dog
027-Elephant-and-Dog.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Elephant and the Dog from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
027-Elephant-and-Dog.htm.intro: In ancient Benares, a state elephant and a stray dog became inseparable friends, eating and playing together daily. When a villager took the dog away, the heartbroken elephant refused all food. The wise Bodhisatta, acting as the king’s minister, identified the elephant’s profound grief. Following his advice, the king proclaimed a penalty, forcing the dog’s release. The pair joyfully reunited, and the minister received great honours for his keen understanding.

028-Nandivisala.htm.title: 28 The Bull Nandivisāla
028-Nandivisala.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Bull Nandivisāla from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
028-Nandivisala.htm.intro: In Taxila, a brahmin raised the Bodhisatta as the bull Nandivisāla. To repay his kindness, the bull suggested a wager to pull one hundred loaded carts. When the brahmin called him a rascal, the bull refused to move, causing a loss. After the brahmin switched to pleasant speech, calling him a fine fellow, the bull successfully pulled the massive load. This proves kind words bring success, unlike harsh, hurtful speech.

029-Grannys-Blackie.htm.title: 29 Granny’s Blackie
029-Grannys-Blackie.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Granny’s Blackie from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
029-Grannys-Blackie.htm.intro: The Bodhisatta, born as a black bull named Ayyikā Kāḷaka, was raised lovingly by a poor woman. To ease her poverty, he agreed to pull five hundred wagons across a rough ford for one thousand coins. When the merchant underpaid him, the bull blocked the path until he received the full amount. Exhausted, he brought the wealth to his "mother," who cared for him before they both eventually passed away.

030-Deadly-Food.htm.title: 30 Deadly Food
030-Deadly-Food.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Deadly Food from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
030-Deadly-Food.htm.intro: Mahālohita and his brother Cullalohita are hardworking oxen who eat only sorry straw. Cullalohita envies Muṇika, a pig being fattened on rice for a daughter’s wedding feast. Mahālohita warns that the pig eats food of death. When guests arrive, Muṇika is slaughtered and cooked into curry. The brothers finally realize their simple grass and chaff are superior because such fare ensures a long, harm-free, and secure life for them both.

032-The-Peacocks-Dance.htm.title: 32 The Peacock’s Dance
032-The-Peacocks-Dance.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Peacock’s Dance from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
032-The-Peacocks-Dance.htm.intro: Golden King Swan granted his daughter her choice of a husband from among all the birds. She chose the Peacock for his exquisite plumage. Overjoyed, the Peacock proudly began to dance, unabashedly exposing himself. Disgusted by his utter lack of modesty and self-restraint, King Swan withdrew the offer and gave his daughter to a refined courtier instead, leaving the shameless Peacock empty-handed.

033-The-Quails-and-the-Net.htm.title: 33 The Quails and the Net
033-The-Quails-and-the-Net.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Quails and the Net from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
033-The-Quails-and-the-Net.htm.intro: A clever Bodhisatta quail saved his flock from a hunter by teaching them to cooperate: when caught in a net, they flapped in unison, lifted the net, and escaped onto a thorn bush. However, after an argument broke out over who stepped on whom, unity collapsed. Quarrelsome and divided, they failed to act together during the next catch, allowing the hunter to capture and sell the entire flock.

034-The-Amorous-Fish.htm.title: 34 The Amorous Fish
034-The-Amorous-Fish.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Amorous Fish from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
034-The-Amorous-Fish.htm.intro: In Benares, an amorous fish is caught while following his wife. Facing death, he laments not the fire, but that his lady might think: “Aññaṁ so ratiyā gato”—he went for joy to another. The Bodhisatta, understanding animal speech, hears this. To save him from a rebirth in hell caused by passion, the wise priest secures his release from the fishermen. He warns the fish and returns him to the river.

037-The-Senior-Partridge.htm.title: 37 The Senior Partridge
037-The-Senior-Partridge.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Senior Partridge from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
037-The-Senior-Partridge.htm.intro: On the slopes of the Himālayas, a partridge, monkey, and elephant sought to establish order by determining who was oldest. The elephant remembered the banyan tree as a bush, while the monkey recalled it as tiny. The partridge proved seniority by revealing he planted the tree from a seed. Following his counsel and the Precepts, they attained rebirth in heaven, illustrating why monks must honour elders as skilled in Dhamma.

046-The-Folly-of-the-Monkeys.htm.title: 46 The Folly of the Monkeys
046-The-Folly-of-the-Monkeys.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Folly of the Monkeys from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
046-The-Folly-of-the-Monkeys.htm.intro: In Benares, during a festive holiday, a gardener asks resident monkeys to water the king’s pleasure gardens. The monkey king, wishing to conserve water, instructs his tribe to uproot every young tree to inspect its roots, watering them according to their size. A wise man observes this destruction, noting that the ignorant, despite good intentions, cause only harm. He concludes that the unintelligent always ruins what is good and beneficial.

039-Nanda-and-the-Hoard.htm.title: 39 Nanda and the Buried Hoard
039-Nanda-and-the-Hoard.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Nanda and the Buried Hoard from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
039-Nanda-and-the-Hoard.htm.intro: An old householder in Benares buried treasure with his slave, Nanda, to secure his young son’s future inheritance. After the father died, the son sought the riches. However, whenever Nanda stood directly atop the buried gold, the wealth’s influence made him insolently abuse his master. Seeking counsel, the son visited the wise Bodhisatta. Following his advice, the son ousted Nanda, recovered the hoard, and lived a generously fulfilling life thereafter.

040-The-Fiery-Pit.htm.title: 40 The Fiery Pit
040-The-Fiery-Pit.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Fiery Pit from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
040-The-Fiery-Pit.htm.intro: In Benares, the Bodhisatta, serving as Lord High Treasurer, sought to provide dainty alms to a visiting Paccekabuddha. Seeking to disrupt this meritorious act, Māra created a deep, fiery pit filled with red-hot acacia-charcoal. Undeterred by the panic-stricken crowds, the Bodhisatta bravely stepped into the flames. A magnificent lotus flower miraculously rose to support his feet, enabling completion of his offering. After Māra’s dejected defeat, the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma.

041-The-Unfortunate-Monk.htm.title: 41 The Unfortunate Monk
041-The-Unfortunate-Monk.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Unfortunate Monk from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
041-The-Unfortunate-Monk.htm.intro: In the days of Kassapa, a jealous monk discarded an Arahat’s alms. Reborn in hell and then as the cursed Mittavindaka, he faced endless misfortune and hunger. After visiting celestial palaces of Devadhītā and being hurled across the sea by a Yakkhini, he was nearly executed for theft. Finally, the Bodhisatta rescued him, explaining that his extreme suffering resulted from failing to heed wise advice throughout his long, arduous wanderings.

043-The-Monk-and-the-Viper.htm.title: 43 The Monk and the Viper
043-The-Monk-and-the-Viper.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Monk and the Viper from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
043-The-Monk-and-the-Viper.htm.intro: In Benares, the Bodhisatta led five hundred ascetics in the kingdom of Kāsi. One monk adopted a poisonous viper named Veḷuka, treating it like a child. Despite the Bodhisatta’s warning that the snake would kill him, the monk refused to part with his pet. Later, after being left hungry for days, the viper bit and killed the monk. The Bodhisatta taught that those ignoring wise advice are destroyed like him.

044-The-Son-and-the-Mosquito.htm.title: 44 The Foolish Son and the Mosquito
044-The-Son-and-the-Mosquito.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Foolish Son and the Mosquito from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
044-The-Son-and-the-Mosquito.htm.intro: In a Kāsi village, a bald carpenter asked his son to kill a stinging mosquito. The foolish son used a sharp axe, splitting his father’s head in twain. The Bodhisatta, witnessing the tragedy, remarked that a wise enemy is better than a friend lacking wisdom. This story illustrates how a fool’s help is dangerous, as senseless actions can lead to unintended and fatal results for the people who are involved.

048-The-Rain-of-Ruin.htm.title: 48 The Rain of Ruin
048-The-Rain-of-Ruin.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rain of Ruin from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
048-The-Rain-of-Ruin.htm.intro: Ignoring the Bodhisatta’s warning, a Brahmin uses the Vedabbha charm to rain treasure for his captors. This sudden wealth triggers a cycle of carnage. A second robber band kills the Brahmin and slaughters the first group. Deadly internal strife leaves only two survivors, who kill each other through sword and poison. The Bodhisatta finds the bodies and concludes that seeking atthaṁ through misguided means leads to total destruction for all.

049-The-Lucky-Star.htm.title: 49 The Lucky Star
049-The-Lucky-Star.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Lucky Star from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
049-The-Lucky-Star.htm.intro: In Benares, townsfolk scheduled a wedding but stayed home when a spiteful ascetic falsely claimed the stars were unpropitious. Consequently, the country folk married the girl to someone else. When the townsfolk later arrived and tried to claim the bride, they were rejected. A wise man observed that while waiting on lucky stars, opportunity passes the fool by; “Attho atthassa nakkhattaṁ”—the benefit is benefit’s lucky star.

050-The-Kings-Stratagem.htm.title: 50 The King’s Stratagem
050-The-Kings-Stratagem.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The King’s Stratagem from the Pāḷi Jātaka stories together with further information.
050-The-Kings-Stratagem.htm.intro: Prince Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta, observed his subjects performing bloody animal sacrifices to a Devatā. Determined to end this slaughter without violence, he feigned devotion to a banyan tree. Upon becoming king, he proclaimed a vow to sacrifice a thousand unrighteous citizens who broke the Five Precepts. Terrified of execution, the people immediately abandoned their wicked ways. Through this clever stratagem, the righteous king successfully established peace and saved many lives.

Pannasa.title: Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories
Pannasa.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Pannasa.intro: This collection presents fifty birth-stories from the Paññāsa Jātaka, a compilation of stories popular in Southeast Asian Buddhism, probably written in Lannā. Each story recounts a past life of the Bodhisatta—the future Buddha—illustrating virtues like generosity, patience, truthfulness, and renunciation. Kings give away their kingdoms, queens sacrifice their lives, animals display extraordinary compassion, and Sakka, king of the gods, frequently tests the Bodhisatta’s resolve. Through these vivid narratives, the Buddha teaches his disciples about karma, the fruits of merit, and the long path to enlightenment. The collection concludes with teachings on the merit of writing scriptures, making and repairing Buddha-images, and maintaining precepts, showing how ordinary acts lead to awakening.
Pannasa.keywords: Bodhisattva, Perfections, Biography, India, Southeast Asia, Parables, Folklore, Medieval, Pāḷi

01-King-Aditta.htm.title: 01 King Āditta
01-King-Aditta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Āditta from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
01-King-Aditta.htm.intro: In this birth-story, King Āditta of Joti, a future Buddha, is tested by Sakka, king of devas. Disguised first as an old brahman, Sakka receives and discards the king’s meal of rice. Returning as a young brahman, Sakka requests the king’s beloved wife, Queen Saṅkhā. The king selflessly gives her away. Impressed by their perfect generosity, Sakka reveals his identity, returns the queen, and foretells the king’s eventual spiritual awakening.

02-Tulakapandita.htm.title: 02 The Wise Tulakapaṇḍita
02-Tulakapandita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Wise Tulakapaṇḍita from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
02-Tulakapandita.htm.intro: In a past life, the Bodhisatta, Tulakapaṇḍita, sought to save thirty-three falsely accused monks sentenced to death by King Cinna. Using his family’s gold and bartering his wife and son, he ransomed thirty-two of them. To save the final novice, Tulakapaṇḍita offered his own life. Fortunately, his father arrived in time, ransoming him with gold. The monks became arahants, the king reformed, and the evil advisor fell into hell.

03-Sammajiva.htm.title: 03 The Poor Boy Sammājīva
03-Sammajiva.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Poor Boy Sammājīva from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
03-Sammajiva.htm.intro: In this Jātaka tale, the Bodhisatta, named Sammājīva, diligently supports his widowed mother. After she dies from a poisonous snakebite, Sakka, disguised as a brahman, offers a healing mantra in exchange for a human heart. Sammājīva selflessly cuts out his own heart to revive her and dies. Devastated, his mother performs a powerful act of truth, prompting Sakka to restore her beloved son’s life. Both are eventually reborn in heaven.

04-Arindama.htm.title: 04 King Arindama
04-Arindama.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Arindama from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
04-Arindama.htm.intro: King Arindama of Suci, renowned for his extreme generosity, willingly surrenders his kingdom to the king of devas, Sakka, who is disguised as a brahman. Proceeding on foot, Arindama sells both his queen and himself into slavery to pay a debt. When their newborn son dies, the queen wanders to Arindama’s gate. By a solemn Act of Truth, Arindama revives the boy, prompting Sakka to restore their kingdom.

05-Sumbhamitta.htm.title: 05 King Sumbhamitta
05-Sumbhamitta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Sumbhamitta from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
05-Sumbhamitta.htm.intro: Fleeing his brother Asumbhamitta’s rebellion to avoid bloodshed, King Sumbhamitta of Campā exiled himself to the forest with Queen Kesinī and their two young sons. While crossing a deep river, the sons were lost and rescued by fishermen, while Kesinī was separated and taken by a boatman. Sumbhamitta subsequently became king of Takkasilā, where he was joyfully reunited with his entire family, while his unrighteous brother suffered in Niraya hell.

06-Samuddaghosa.htm.title: 06 Prince Samuddaghosa
06-Samuddaghosa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Samuddaghosa from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
06-Samuddaghosa.htm.intro: Prince Samuddaghosa (the Bodhisatta) marries the beautiful Princess Bandhumati. Gifted a magical flying sword by a grateful, injured sorcerer they cured, they travel to wondrous lands. However, a thief steals the sword, and a violent storm shipwrecks and separates the couple at sea. The queen builds an alms-hall carved with their life story to search for him. Reunited after Sakka’s intervention, they return home to rule both kingdoms righteously.

07-Cagadana.htm.title: 07 The Poor Boy Cāgadāna
07-Cagadana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Poor Boy Cāgadāna from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
07-Cagadana.htm.intro: In a past life, the Bodhisatta was born as Cāgadāna, a poor but generous youth who supported his parents. When he encountered a robbed Paccekabuddha in the forest, he selflessly surrendered his only cloaks, clothing himself in leaves. This supreme act of giving moved deities like Sakka, who showered him with celestial garments, jewels, and immense wealth. Sharing his riches, Cāgadāna inspired others to practice generosity, leading to heavenly rebirths.

08-Dhammikapandita.htm.title: 08 King Dhammikapaṇḍita
08-Dhammikapandita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Dhammikapaṇḍita from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
08-Dhammikapandita.htm.intro: King Dhammikapaṇḍita of Bārāṇasī distributed immense charity to his people, causing the earth to quake. Sakka, king of devas, escorted the generous king to the heavenly realm. Declining a gifted celestial mansion, the king returned to the human world to actively earn his own merit through continued generosity and morality. His subsequent teachings inspired his subjects to perform good deeds, leading to their eventual rebirth in the beautiful celestial world.

09-Siridhara.htm.title: 09 The Merchant Siridhara
09-Siridhara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Merchant Siridhara from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
09-Siridhara.htm.intro: While staying at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the past life of the great merchant Siridhara. Siridhara offered his sumptuous meal to a paccekabuddha and made an aspiration to attain future Buddhahood. Consequently, his house miraculously turned to gold and he received divine wealth, which he shared generously with the public. After teaching King Brahmadatta and his citizens about the supreme benefits of giving, everyone was reborn in the heavenly realms.

10-Sankhapatta.htm.title: 10 King Saṅkhapatta
10-Sankhapatta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Saṅkhapatta from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
10-Sankhapatta.htm.intro: Prince Saṅkhapatta, the Bodhisatta, traveled to marry Princess Ratanavatī. When a storm wrecked his ship, his selfless generosity led him to give passengers his survival planks, swimming ashore alone. A greedy brahman he rescued later gouged out the sleeping prince’s eyes to steal a ring. Saved by foresters, Saṅkhapatta reunited with Ratanavatī. Through solemn acts of truth, both his eyes and his blinded attacker’s sight were miraculously and fully restored.

11-Sudhana.htm.title: 11 Prince Sudhana
11-Sudhana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Sudhana from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
11-Sudhana.htm.intro: Prince Sudhana falls in love with and marries the captured kinnari princess Manohara. While Sudhana is away battling adversaries, a jealous adviser plots to sacrifice her, forcing her to flee back to her celestial kingdom. Heartbroken, the prince embarks on a perilous seven-year quest. Guided by her left-behind ring and magical herbs, he overcomes deadly obstacles, passes her father’s trials, and is finally and happily reunited with his beloved princess.

12-Narajiva.htm.title: 12 Narajīva
12-Narajiva.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Narajīva from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
12-Narajiva.htm.intro: In a past life, the Bodhisatta, Narajīva, inspired a pious householder to offer sacred kaṭhina cloth to Buddha Padumuttara, earning a prophecy of his future Buddhahood as Gotama. The immense karmic merits of this generous act, alongside their past friendships, shaped the subsequent rebirths of Narajīva and his companions. This profound Jātaka story beautifully illustrates how deeds of generosity and moral choices bear powerful, enduring fruits across multiple lifetimes.

13-Suvannakumara.htm.title: 13 Suvaṇṇakumāra
13-Suvannakumara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Suvaṇṇakumāra from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
13-Suvannakumara.htm.intro: King Brahmadatta orders his pregnant concubine executed, but the executioner secretly spares her. She gives birth to Suvaṇṇakumāra, who is the Bodhisatta. Years later, a deity threatens the king’s life with ten complex questions. The wise young prince answers them all perfectly, saving his father. The deity then reveals the prince’s true royal identity. The king happily crowns Suvaṇṇakumāra, who rules righteously and is later reborn as Siddhattha, who would become the Buddha.

14-Surupa.htm.title: 14 King Surūpa
14-Surupa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Surūpa from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
14-Surupa.htm.intro: Seeking the glorious Dhamma, virtuous King Surūpa offers his wealth to find a teacher. To test his devotion, Sakka, king of devas, appears as a terrifying yakkha demanding flesh. The king sacrifices his beloved wife, young son, and finally his own body to feed the monster in exchange for sacred verses. Moved by this supreme sacrifice, Sakka reveals his true identity, restores the family, and prophesies the king’s future Buddhahood.

15-Kambala.htm.title: 15 King Kambala
15-Kambala.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Kambala from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
15-Kambala.htm.intro: The Buddha recounts how, in a past life under Buddha Saraṇaṅkara, he was a householder’s son who gifted kaṭhina-cloth to achieve future enlightenment. Hearing of this supreme gift, King Kambala also presented kaṭhina-cloth yearly, learning of its extraordinary karmic rewards—which far surpass all other offerings in bringing wealth, heavenly happiness, and ultimate liberation. Today, the Buddha identifies King Kambala as Sāriputta and himself as that householder’s son.

16-Cowherds-Hut.htm.title: 16 The Cowherd’s Hut
16-Cowherds-Hut.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Cowherd’s Hut from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
16-Cowherds-Hut.htm.intro: The Buddha relates how a cowherd’s simple act of building a roadside hut earned him rebirth in a beautiful, heavenly palace. He then recounts a past life as King Dhammarāja, who constructed four city-gate huts, distributed immense daily charity, and was invited by Sakka to visit the deva-world. Inspired by heavenly bliss, the king and his subjects redoubled their meritorious deeds, ultimately securing rebirth in heaven through their outstanding generosity.

17-Siricudamani.htm.title: 17 King Siricudāmaṇi
17-Siricudamani.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Siricudāmaṇi from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
17-Siricudamani.htm.intro: King Siricudamani of Bārānasī, a generous ruler, desired to donate parts of his own body for supreme enlightenment. Sakka, king of the devas, tested his resolve by appearing as a half-bodied brahman requesting the king’s other half. Despite his family’s immense grief, the king resolutely allowed two yakkhas to saw him in half. Moved by this ultimate sacrifice, Sakka healed him. The king was later reborn as the supreme Buddha.

18-The-Eight-Requisites.htm.title: 18 The Eight Requisites
18-The-Eight-Requisites.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Eight Requisites from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
18-The-Eight-Requisites.htm.intro: The Buddha explains that Prince Nandakumāra and his followers instantly received monastic robes and bowls due to past merit. In a past life as the rich brahman Surucira, the Bodhisatta invited Buddha Sumaṅgala and his massive retinue for alms. Assisted by the king of devas, Sakka, who miraculously built a magnificent pavilion, Surucira donated the eight requisites to the monks. Consequently, Sumaṅgala prophesied Surucira’s future Buddhahood as Gotama Buddha himself.

19-Sirivipulakitti.htm.title: 19 King Sirivipulakitti
19-Sirivipulakitti.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Sirivipulakitti from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
19-Sirivipulakitti.htm.intro: King Yasakitti of Campā and Queen Sirimatī fled to the forest when an evil king invaded. Their son, the Bodhisatta Sirivipulakitti, was born in exile after Yasakitti was betrayed and imprisoned. As a youth, Sirivipulakitti offered his life to free his father. Surviving multiple execution attempts through his miraculous power, he was rescued by a nāga king, crowned ruler of Campā, and reunited with his father, though his mother perished.

20-Sattadhanu.htm.title: 20 Prince Sattadhanu
20-Sattadhanu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Sattadhanu from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
20-Sattadhanu.htm.intro: Prince Sattadhanu, the Bodhisatta, is born alongside a magical flying horse, Maṇikakkha. He wins Princess Cirappabhā’s hand after proving his superior archery skills. On their journey home, a yakkha captures his horse, and a violent shipwreck separates the couple. Cirappabhā builds a hall illustrated with their story to find him. After escaping a yakkhinī and retrieving Maṇikakkha, Sattadhanu locates the hall, reunites with his wife, and teaches the yakkha morality.

21-Candakumara.htm.title: 21 Candakumāra
21-Candakumara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting XXX from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
21-Candakumara.htm.intro: Born as Candakumāra, the Bodhisatta sailed to Suvaṇṇabhumi, using his wealth to buy and release captured animals, earning immense merit. When his ship foundered, the ocean goddess Maṇimekhalā rescued him, carrying him safely to land. There, a royal carriage chose him as the new king. He ruled righteously with Princess Sibbali, receiving miraculous gifts from grateful animals and the god Sakka, before finally ascending to heaven as a future Buddha.

22-Sadhita.htm.title: 22 King Sādhita
22-Sadhita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Sādhita from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
22-Sadhita.htm.intro: Reigning in Mithilā, King Sādhita, who was the Bodhisatta, realized his prosperity came from past generosity. He built six alms halls, distributing immense wealth daily. Moved by his boundless giving, Sakka, king of devas, descended to praise him, predicting Sādhita’s future Buddhahood. Sakka then showered the entire city with miraculous rains of wealth, which Sādhita gladly distributed. Sādhita ruled righteously and, upon passing, was reborn in the Tusita deva world.

23-Ratanapajjota.htm.title: 23 Prince Ratanapajjota
23-Ratanapajjota.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Ratanapajjota from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
23-Ratanapajjota.htm.intro: In the past, King Mahāratha and Queen Siriratanagabbhā of Meghavatī were separated by a great flood. The pregnant queen floated to Mount Caṇḍa, giving birth to the Bodhisatta, Ratanapajjota. At age five, the young boy sacrificed his own heart’s flesh to the yakkha Bāḷhahaka to save his mother. He was miraculously healed by Sakka. Later, Ratanapajjota ruled, renounced the world, and was reborn in the Brahmaloka, identified as the future Buddha.

24-Two-Headed-Swan.htm.title: 24 The Two-Headed Swan
24-Two-Headed-Swan.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Two-Headed Swan from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
24-Two-Headed-Swan.htm.intro: In the past, a devoted husband and wife wished to remain united. Consequently, they were reborn as a single golden swan with two heads on Mount Himavanta. Captured and presented to King Dhammika of Bārāṇasī, a cunning minister sowed distrust between the swan’s heads by whispering to only one. Consumed by jealousy and suspicion, the heads fought and tore their single body apart, demonstrating how easily anger can destroy unity.

25-Viriyapandita.htm.title: 25 Viriyapaṇḍita
25-Viriyapandita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Viriyapaṇḍita from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
25-Viriyapandita.htm.intro: King Mahāratha sends a miraculous Buddha image to King Pañcāla, converting the unbelieving ruler. To gild a new sandalwood Buddha image, the poor Bodhisatta Viriyapaṇḍita sells his wife Sujātā and son Revata to purchase gold. When the gold proves insufficient, Viriyapaṇḍita sacrifices his own flesh, which the god Sakka transforms into gold to complete the image. Impressed, Sakka heals him; King Pañcāla reunites Viriyapaṇḍita with his family and bestows wealth.

26-Vipularaja.htm.title: 26 King Vipula
26-Vipularaja.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Vipula from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
26-Vipularaja.htm.intro: In Sudhammavatī, the righteous King Vipula established six charity halls to fulfill the Perfection of Charity. Aspiring for Buddhahood, he vowed to grant any request. Testing his virtue, Sakka, king of gods, disguised as a Brāhmaṇa and requested Queen Candā, Prince Vijala, and the entire kingdom. King Vipula joyfully surrendered each. Astonished by this supreme selflessness, Sakka revealed his divine identity, praised the Bodhisatta, and restored his family and realm.

27-Mahapaduma.htm.title: 27 Prince Mahāpaduma
27-Mahapaduma.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Mahāpaduma from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
27-Mahapaduma.htm.intro: When Queen Sumekhalā dies from a poisonous snakebite in the forest, her son, Prince Mahāpaduma, sacrifices his own heart to save her. Sakka, disguised as a Brahman, uses ambrosia to revive the queen, but the devoted prince collapses and dies. Overcome with sorrow, Queen Sumekhalā performs a resolution of truth, prompting Sakka to resurrect Mahāpaduma. Together, they live righteously in the forest hermitage until achieving rebirth in a heavenly realm.

28-Mahasurasena.htm.title: 28 King Mahāsūrasena
28-Mahasurasena.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Mahāsūrasena from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
28-Mahasurasena.htm.intro: King Mahāsūrasena of Bārāṇasī, seeking supreme enlightenment through internal charity, wished to give his own body. To fulfill his noble aspiration, Sakka appeared disguised as a headless youth and requested the king’s head. Unwavering in his pursuit of Buddhahood, Mahāsūrasena cut off his head and presented it. Moved by this ultimate sacrifice, Sakka revealed himself, restored the righteous king to life, and praised his perfect generosity before returning to heaven.

29-Brahmaghosa.htm.title: 29 King Brahmaghosa
29-Brahmaghosa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Brahmaghosa from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
29-Brahmaghosa.htm.intro: Righteous King Brahmaghosa of Kusumapura and Queen Nandā piously served Lord Padumuttara Buddha and his Saṅgha. To test the king’s virtue, Sakka descended with Mātali, disguised as a terrifying, hungry dog and keeper. When Sakka advocated unrighteousness, the Bodhisatta fearlessly rejected his false words and defended the Dhamma. Delighted, Sakka revealed his celestial form, praised the king’s boundless merit, and prophesied his ultimate attainment of future Buddhahood.

30-White-Mouse.htm.title: 30 The White Mouse
30-White-Mouse.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The White Mouse from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
30-White-Mouse.htm.intro: In the White Mouse (Setamūsika) Jātaka, the Bodhisatta is born as a mouse who keeps the five precepts. His virtue brings prosperity to Sudhammapālika, but he is stolen and then given to King Brahmadatta. Later, Sakka tests him by requesting his flesh. The mouse joyfully offers his life, and a lotus saves him.

31-Ariyachatta.htm.title: 31 Ariyachatta
31-Ariyachatta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ariyachatta from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
31-Ariyachatta.htm.intro: King Dhammasoṇa tests his subjects’ faith by ordering them to abandon the Three Jewels. The Bodhisatta, born as Ariyachatta, who name means Noble Student, refuses despite threats of death. Moved by his unwavering devotion, the king honours him as crown prince. The Buddha reveals Ariyachatta was himself in a past life.

32-Subhadda.htm.title: 32 King Subhadda
32-Subhadda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Subhadda from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
32-Subhadda.htm.intro: The Bodhisatta Subhadda faithfully takes refuge in the Three Jewels despite poverty and his wife’s scorn. Sakka grants him a one-day boon; Subhadda becomes king of Bārāṇasī and distributes all wealth in charity. When his merit wanes, the gods transfer their own merit, extending his reign for 500 years.

33-Bahalaputta.htm.title: 33 The Calf Bahalaputta
33-Bahalaputta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting 33 The Calf Bahalaputta from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
33-Bahalaputta.htm.intro: A cow named Bahalā promises a tiger she will return after feeding her calf, Bahalaputta. The Bodhisatta calf offers his own body instead. Moved by their truthfulness, forbearance, and gratitude, the tiger spares them. Sakka praises these three virtues and brings all three to Tāvatiṁsa heaven.

34-Four-Deaf-People.htm.title: 34 Four Deaf People
34-Four-Deaf-People.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Four Deaf People from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
34-Four-Deaf-People.htm.intro: Four deaf family members constantly misunderstand each other, causing quarrels. The non-deaf son seeks King Brahmadatta, who reveals they were deaf in past lives for chatting irreverently during a sermon. The king teaches that respectful listening to the Dhamma brings wisdom, while disrespect brings deafness and misfortune.

35-Gift-of-Lamps.htm.title: 35 A Gift of Lamps
35-Gift-of-Lamps.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting 35 A Gift of Lamps from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
35-Gift-of-Lamps.htm.intro: A princess offers sesame oil to Elder Tipitakadhara for lamp-worship, aspiring to Buddhahood. The Buddha Former Dīpaṅkara explains she lacks the eight prerequisites, including male gender, but prophesies she will receive confirmation from the future Buddha Dīpaṅkara. That princess is reborn as Gotama Buddha.

36-Velama.htm.title: 36 Brahmin Velāma
36-Velama.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Brahmin Velāma from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
36-Velama.htm.intro: The Bodhisatta, born as the Brahmin Velāma, establishes immense charity for seven years, giving countless treasures to all Jambudīpa. Yet he finds no worthy recipients—not even one who keeps the precepts. The Buddha teaches Anāthapiṇḍika that giving to a single noble disciple far exceeds those vast gifts.

37-Vattanguli.htm.title: 37 King Vaṭṭaṅguli
37-Vattanguli.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Vaṭṭaṅguli from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
37-Vattanguli.htm.intro: King Pasenadi asks the Buddha for permission to make his image. The Buddha recounts a past life as King Vaṭṭaṅguli, who repaired a broken Buddha-image finger. This merit brought him great power, wealth, and eventual Buddhahood. The Buddha explains the vast benefits of making Buddha-images, and Pasenadi creates a sandalwood image.

38-Sirasakumara.htm.title: 38 Prince Sirasā
38-Sirasakumara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Sirasā from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
38-Sirasakumara.htm.intro: Devadatta’s enmity toward the Buddha prompts this tale. King Paṭhama’s son, Sirasākumāra, is born miraculously and later floated down the Ganges with his mother due to a wicked Brahman’s advice. Saved by a loyal army chief, the boy reveals he is a Buddha-sprout, teaches Dhamma, and returns to Tāvatiṁsa heaven, reborn as a god.

39-Sonananda.htm.title: 39 Prince Soṇananda
39-Sonananda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Soṇananda from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
39-Sonananda.htm.intro: King Surabhata’s son, the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇakumāra, proves his merit by walking on the ocean and receiving a white elephant from a goddess. When King Bhaṭosura of Sīhala demands the elephant, Suvaṇṇakumāra conquers him with five magic arrows from Sakka. Bhaṭosura submits, and Suvaṇṇakumāra returns to Bārāṇasī, ruling righteously and establishing charity halls.

40-Suvannakumara.htm.title: 40 Prince Suvaṇṇakumāra
40-Suvannakumara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Suvaṇṇakumāra from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
40-Suvannakumara.htm.intro: King Surabhata’s son, the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇakumāra, proves his merit by walking on the ocean and receiving a white elephant from a goddess. When King Bhaṭosura of Sīhala demands the elephant, Suvaṇṇakumāra conquers him with five magic arrows from Sakka. Bhaṭosura submits, and Suvaṇṇakumāra returns to Bārāṇasī, ruling righteously and establishing charity halls.

41-Brahmakumara.htm.title: 41 Prince Brahmakumāra
41-Brahmakumara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Brahmakumāra from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
41-Brahmakumara.htm.intro: The Bodhisatta, born poor, clears an overgrown shrine and offers lamp-worship, resolving to become a Buddha. Reborn as Brahmakumāra, son of King Brahmadatta, he is consecrated by one hundred kings. The text praises the fruits of clearing shrines and offering lamps—long life, wisdom, wealth, and eventual Nibbāna. The Buddha identifies himself as Brahmakumāra.

42-Sucika.htm.title: 42 The Ascetic Sucika
42-Sucika.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Ascetic Sucika from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
42-Sucika.htm.intro: A crow captures a giant worm, who poses four riddles. Unable to answer, the crow carries him to the Buddha, who answers correctly: Nibbāna is greatest, mind is fastest, water is sharpest, and the Buddha is strongest. The worm is spared. The Buddha then reveals a past life as the ascetic Sūcika, who similarly answered riddles and saved a moth from an eagle.

43-Writing.htm.title: 43 The Merit of Writing
43-Writing.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Merit of Writing from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
43-Writing.htm.intro: Sāriputta asks about the merit of writing down the Tipiṭaka. The Buddha explains that in the time of the former Buddha Gotama, he was a minister who wrote and had others write the scriptures to preserve them for five thousand years. He then enjoyed celestial rewards and ruled as a universal monarch. The Buddha praises the act of writing scriptures, which brings happiness and prevents rebirth in lower realms.

44-Vaddhana.htm.title: 44 The Merchant Vaddhana
44-Vaddhana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Merchant Vaddhana from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
44-Vaddhana.htm.intro: King Pasenadi asks about the merit of making Buddha-images. The Buddha recounts how the merchant Vaddhana, seeing a broken Buddha-image in an abandoned monastery, repaired its finger, offered lamps and banners, and worshipped it. Sakka praised his merit and showered jewels. The Buddha explains that making Buddha-images brings beauty, wealth, long life, and eventual Nibbāna.

45-Ungratefulness.htm.title: 45 Ungratefulness
45-Ungratefulness.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ungratefulness together with further information.
45-Ungratefulness.htm.intro: A crow makes a poor fisherman king by hiding him in a chest and claiming he returned from the dead. The king prospers but forgets his promise to feed the crow, who then carries him back to his fishing spot. The Buddha teaches that ungrateful people are censured and reborn in hell, while the grateful prosper. Devadatta is identified as the ungrateful king.

46-Dukamma.htm.title: 46 Prince Dukamma
46-Dukamma.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Dukamma from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
46-Dukamma.htm.intro: Dukamma tests his father’s advice by marrying a thrice-widowed woman and befriending a thrice-renounced man. His wife betrays him for gold, and his friend abandons him. Gatekeepers tell stories of rash actions causing remorse, delaying his execution. He proves his innocence, refuses a kingdom, and later becomes king of Takkasilā. The Buddha teaches that bad company brings ruin.

47-Quarrelsomeness.htm.title: 47 Quarrelsomeness
47-Quarrelsomeness.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Quarrelsomeness from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
47-Quarrelsomeness.htm.intro: A crow joins a colony of birds, claiming to keep precepts, but eats their chicks while their parents gather food. The birds discover his deceit and attack him. The Bodhisatta, born as a sārika bird, admonishes the crow and teaches that the wicked and good cannot mix. The Buddha identifies Devadatta as the crow and himself as the sārika.

48-Siddhisara.htm.title: 48 Prince Siddhisāra
48-Siddhisara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Prince Siddhisāra from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
48-Siddhisara.htm.intro: Prince Siddhisāra and his friend Puññasāra are banished. A tree deity helps them find a golden deer; Siddhisāra eats the right eye to become a cakkavatti, Puññasāra the left to emit jewels when laughing. Siddhisāra becomes king of Mithilā; Puññasāra gains a princess but is poisoned by her father. A deity revives him, and he reunites with Siddhisāra, eventually becoming cakkavatti.

49-Precepts.htm.title: 49 Maintaining the Precepts
49-Precepts.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Maintaining the Precepts from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
49-Precepts.htm.intro: A layman keeps precepts in a forest; deities, pleased, bring him two thousand cartloads of wealth. The Buddha recounts how, in a past life, the Bodhisatta refused to kill birds for a prince, was thrown into a crocodile-infested river, but was protected by his precepts. A golden palace arose, and he converted the king and prince, then renounced the world. Precepts bring wealth and protection.

50-Mahasudassana.htm.title: 50 King Mahāsudassana
50-Mahasudassana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Mahāsudassana from Fifty Lannā Jātaka Stories together with further information.
50-Mahasudassana.htm.intro: King Ajita gives the Saṅgha a wish-fulfilling tree. The Buddha recounts how, in the time of Kassapa Buddha, the Bodhisatta gave a leaf-hut and requisites to a monk. As a result, he became the cakkavatti king Sudassana, endowed with seven jewels, 84,000 cities, and a lifespan of 330,000 years. The Buddha identifies himself as Sudassana, teaching that gifts to the Saṅgha yield great fruit.

Jatakamala.title: Jātakamāla, The Garland of Birth Stories
Jatakamala.summary:
Illustrated Stories from the Jātakamāla, The Garland of Birth Stories, which relates many exemplary lives of the Bodhisattva.
Source of the Stories
Jatakamala.intro: The Jātakamālā, or Garland of Birth-Stories, is a classic work of Sanskrit Buddhist literature attributed to the poet Āryaśūra. It contains thirty-four stories that illustrate the Buddha’s previous incarnations as he cultivated the Ten Perfections. The stories, such as the famous account of a prince sacrificing his body to a starving tigress, serve as moral parables to inspire faith, compassion, and selflessness. The collection functions as a religious and educational tool, emphasizing the law of Karma and the boundless mercy of the Bodhisattva on his path to enlightenment. The law of Karma is the core metaphysical framework that connects the Jātaka stories, serving as the unbroken chain of cause and effect that binds all existences together and operates under the firm conviction that nothing is ever lost in the universe, which exists as one massive moral system.
Jatakamala.keywords: Bodhisattva, Perfections, Biography, India, Parables, Folklore, Sanskrit
