01-Tigress.htm.title: 1. The Story of the Tigress (Dāna)
01-Tigress.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Tigress (Dāna) together with further information.
01-Tigress.htm.intro: The Bodhisattva, living as a high-born ascetic, encounters a starving tigress about to devour her own cubs. Overcome by extreme compassion, he realizes his body is transient and offers it as food, sacrificing himself to save the animals and illustrating the perfection of generosity.

02-Sibi.htm.title: 2. The Story of the King of the Śibis (Dāna)
02-Sibi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the King of the Śibis (Dāna) together with further information.
02-Sibi.htm.intro: King Sibi, known for his boundless charity, is tested by Śakra (disguised as a blind Brahmin). The King offers his own eyes to restore the beggar’s sight. Despite the pain, his resolve remains unshaken, proving that his love for all beings outweighs his own well-being.

03-Gruel.htm.title: 3. The Story of the Small Portion of Gruel (Dāna)
03-Gruel.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Small Portion of Gruel (Dāna) together with further information.
03-Gruel.htm.intro: In a past life as a king, the Bodhisattva reflects on a previous humble existence where he offered a meager portion of gruel to holy men with a pure heart. This story emphasizes that the merit of an offering depends on the intention, not the size.

04-Guild.htm.title: 4. The Story of the Head of A Guild (Dāna)
04-Guild.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Head of A Guild (Dāna) together with further information.
04-Guild.htm.intro: As a wealthy merchant, the Bodhisattva is tested by Māra, who creates a pit of fire to prevent him from giving food to a mendicant. The merchant fearlessly steps into the flames, which turn into a lotus, demonstrating that virtue overcomes all obstacles.

05-Avisahya.htm.title: 5. The Story of Aviṣahya, the Head of a Guild (Dāna)
05-Avisahya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Aviṣahya, the Head of a Guild (Dāna) together with further information.
05-Avisahya.htm.intro: Living as the merchant Aviṣahya, the Bodhisattva’s wealth is magically taken away by Śakra to test his charity. Even when reduced to gathering grass for a living, he continues to give away what little he has, proving that true generosity is independent of wealth.

06-Hare.htm.title: 6. The Story of the Hare (Dāna)
06-Hare.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Hare (Dāna) together with further information.
06-Hare.htm.intro: The Bodhisattva, born as a hare, instructs his friends on the importance of charity. When Śakra appears as a hungry traveler, the hare, having no food to give, jumps into a fire to offer his own body as a meal, earning eternal honor.

07-Agastya.htm.title: 7. The Story of Agastya (Dāna)
07-Agastya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Agastya (Dāna) together with further information.
07-Agastya.htm.intro: Living as the ascetic Agastya on a remote island, the Bodhisattva is repeatedly tested by Śakra, who asks for his meager food. Agastya gives joyfully every time, showing that even those in solitude can practice the highest forms of selflessness and detachment.

08-Maitribala.htm.title: 8. The Story of Maitrībala (Dāna)
08-Maitribala.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Maitrībala (Dāna) together with further information.
08-Maitribala.htm.intro: King Maitrībala, a paragon of kindness, is approached by five ogres (Yakṣas) seeking food. Since they only consume blood and flesh, the King allows them to drink from his own veins, demonstrating a compassion that seeks to alleviate the suffering of even the most demonic beings.

09-Visvantara.htm.title: 9. The Story of Viśvantara (Dāna)
09-Visvantara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Viśvantara (Dāna) together with further information.
09-Visvantara.htm.intro: Prince Viśvantara vows to give away anything requested. After giving away the kingdom’s auspicious elephant, he is exiled. In the forest, he eventually gives away his children and wife to testers. His ultimate detachment and charity lead to a divine restoration of his family and kingdom.

10-Sacrifice.htm.title: 10. The Story of the Sacrifice (Śīla)
10-Sacrifice.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Sacrifice (Śīla) together with further information.
10-Sacrifice.htm.intro: A king is advised by priests to perform a massive animal sacrifice to end a drought. The Bodhisattva, as the king, instead proposes a sacrifice of virtuous conduct and charity, teaching his subjects that true protection comes from morality rather than the slaughter of innocents.

11-Sakra.htm.title: 11. The Story of Śakra (Karuṇā)
11-Sakra.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Śakra (Karuṇā) together with further information.
11-Sakra.htm.intro: In a life as Śakra, King of the Gods, the Bodhisattva is engaged in a war with demons. While retreating, he orders his chariot to turn back—risking capture—just to avoid crushing a nest of eagles. His compassion impresses his enemies and secures his victory.

12-Brahman.htm.title: 12. The Story of the Brāhman (Hrī)
12-Brahman.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Brāhman (Hrī) together with further information.
12-Brahman.htm.intro: A teacher tests his students’ integrity by asking them to steal food to alleviate his poverty. All agree except the Bodhisattva, who argues that there is no such thing as a secret crime because one’s own conscience is always watching, upholding the virtue of honesty.

13-Unmadayanti.htm.title: 13. The Story of Unmādayantī (Dhairya)
13-Unmadayanti.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Unmādayantī (Dhairya) together with further information.
13-Unmadayanti.htm.intro: A king becomes infatuated with Unmadayanti, the beautiful wife of his minister. Despite his intense desire, the king refuses to take her, prioritizing Dharma and the protection of his subjects’ trust over his personal passion, showcasing the strength of self-control and royal duty.

14-Suparaga.htm.title: 14. The Story of Supāraga (Satya)
14-Suparaga.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Supāraga (Satya) together with further information.
14-Suparaga.htm.intro: As an elderly, blind navigator, Supāraga is asked to guide a ship through perilous, mythical seas. When the ship faces destruction, he performs an Act of Truth, invoking his lifelong commitment to virtue, which miraculously brings the vessel and its crew safely back to shore.

15-Fish.htm.title: 15. The Story of the Fish (Satya)
15-Fish.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Fish (Satya) together with further information.
15-Fish.htm.intro: Born as a king of fish during a severe drought, the Bodhisattva sees his kin dying as the lake dries up. He performs an Act of Truth based on his purity, calling for rain. The heavens respond with a deluge, saving the aquatic creatures from death.

16-Quail.htm.title: 16. The Story of the Quail’s Young (Satya)
16-Quail.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Quail’s Young (Satya) together with further information.
16-Quail.htm.intro: A forest fire threatens a young quail (the Bodhisattva), who is too small to fly. He addresses the fire with a declaration of truth regarding his innate virtue. The fire miraculously bypasses his nest, demonstrating the protective power of truth and innocence.

17-Jar.htm.title: 17. The Story of the Jar (Vāra)
17-Jar.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Jar (Vāra) together with further information.
17-Jar.htm.intro: Śakra disguises himself as a Brahmin carrying a jar of liquor to warn a king about the evils of alcohol. He describes the madness and ruin caused by drinking so effectively that the king vows to abstain, illustrating the importance of sobriety and moral leadership.

18-Childless.htm.title: 18. The Story of the Childless One (Praviveka)
18-Childless.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Childless One (Praviveka) together with further information.
18-Childless.htm.intro: A wealthy man, realizing the hollowness of worldly life, renounces his riches to live as an ascetic. Even when his former wealth is offered back, he remains steadfast, proving that the peace found in renunciation is far superior to the anxieties of material possession.

19-Lotus-Stalks.htm.title: 19. The Story of the Lotus-Stalks (Praviveka)
19-Lotus-Stalks.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Lotus-Stalks (Praviveka) together with further information.
19-Lotus-Stalks.htm.intro: A group of ascetics is tested by Śakra, who steals their lotus stalks to see if they will succumb to anger or suspicion. The Bodhisattva maintains his composure and teaches that a true seeker of peace must remain undisturbed by the loss of trifles.

20-Treasurer.htm.title: 20. The Story of the Treasurer (Hrī)
20-Treasurer.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Treasurer (Hrī) together with further information.
20-Treasurer.htm.intro: As a royal treasurer, the Bodhisattva faces a dilemma when his mother-in-law attempts to sow discord between him and his wife. He handles the situation with such wisdom and patience that he preserves the family harmony while upholding his commitment to truth and integrity.

21-Cuddabodhi.htm.title: 21. The Story of Cuḍḍabodhi (Kṣānti)
21-Cuddabodhi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Cuḍḍabodhi (Kṣānti) together with further information.
21-Cuddabodhi.htm.intro: Cuḍḍabodhi, an ascetic, remains unmoved when a king insults him and attempts to seize his beautiful wife (who is also an ascetic). His total lack of anger in the face of provocation demonstrates the perfection of patience and the mastery of the mind over selfish instincts.

22-Swans.htm.title: 22. The Story of the Holy Swans (Maitrī)
22-Swans.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Holy Swans (Maitrī) together with further information.
22-Swans.htm.intro: The Bodhisattva, born as a wise swan king, is captured in a hunter’s snare. His loyal commander refuses to leave his side. Their mutual devotion and the king’s wisdom so move the hunter that he releases them, illustrating the power of loyalty and virtue.

23-Mahabodhi.htm.title: 23. The Story of Mahābodhi (Kṣānti)
23-Mahabodhi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Mahābodhi (Kṣānti) together with further information.
23-Mahabodhi.htm.intro: As a wandering ascetic, Mahābodhi is unfairly treated by a king influenced by corrupt ministers. Instead of seeking revenge, he uses his wisdom to expose the ministers’ fallacies and restore the king to the path of righteousness, showing that wisdom should be used for guidance.

24-Great-Ape.htm.title: 24. The Story of the Great Ape (Anukampā)
24-Great-Ape.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Great Ape (Anukampā) together with further information.
24-Great-Ape.htm.intro: The Bodhisattva, as a large ape, saves a man who has fallen into a deep pit. Despite the man later trying to kill the ape for food, the Bodhisattva forgives him and ensures he finds his way home, epitomizing unconditional mercy and forgiveness.

25-Sarabha.htm.title: 25. The Story of the Śarabha (Anukampā)
25-Sarabha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Śarabha (Anukampā) together with further information.
25-Sarabha.htm.intro: As a Śarabha (a mythical deer), the Bodhisattva is hunted by a king. When the king falls into a chasm during the chase, the Śarabha rescues his pursuer instead of escaping. This act of kindness humbles the king, teaching him to value all life.

26-Ruru.htm.title: 26. The Story of the Ruru-Deer (Dayā)
26-Ruru.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Ruru-Deer (Dayā) together with further information.
26-Ruru.htm.intro: A beautiful golden deer rescues a drowning man, asking only that his location remain secret. The man betrays him for a reward, but the deer’s nobility in the face of betrayal moves the king to protect all animals, proving that virtue is its own reward.

27-Great-Monkey.htm.title: 27. The Story of the Great Monkey (Anuvartinā)
27-Great-Monkey.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Great Monkey (Anuvartinā) together with further information.
27-Great-Monkey.htm.intro: As a leader of monkeys, the Bodhisattva uses his own body as a bridge to save his tribe from a king’s archers. His self-sacrifice for his followers so impresses the king that he adopts a more compassionate rule over his own people.

28-Ksantivadin.htm.title: 28. The Story of Kṣāntivādin (Kṣānti)
28-Ksantivadin.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Kṣāntivādin (Kṣānti) together with further information.
28-Ksantivadin.htm.intro: An ascetic named Preacher of Forbearance is brutally mutilated by a jealous king. Throughout the torture, the ascetic feels no anger, only pity for the king’s ignorance. This story is the ultimate example of Kṣānti (patience) and the refusal to harbor ill will.

29-Brahmaloka.htm.title: 29. The Story of the Inhabitant of the Brahmaloka (Anukampā)
29-Brahmaloka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Inhabitant of the Brahmaloka (Anukampā) together with further information.
29-Brahmaloka.htm.intro: A king is led astray by nihilistic views, believing there is no afterlife or fruit of action. The Bodhisattva descends from the Brahma-world to debate the king, using logic and divine authority to restore his faith in morality and the law of Karma.

30-Elephant.htm.title: 30. The Story of the Elephant (Karuṇā)
30-Elephant.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Elephant (Karuṇā) together with further information.
30-Elephant.htm.intro: Born as a benevolent elephant, the Bodhisattva encounters a group of starving men lost in the desert. To save them, he flings himself off a cliff so they can eat his flesh and use his intestines as bags for water, exemplifying extreme self-sacrifice.

31-Sutasoma.htm.title: 31. The Story of Sutasoma (Satsaṁga)
31-Sutasoma.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Sutasoma (Satsaṁga) together with further information.
31-Sutasoma.htm.intro: Prince Sutasoma is captured by a man-eating king. Having promised to return after settling a debt, Sutasoma voluntarily goes back into captivity. His unwavering commitment to truth eventually reforms the man-eater, demonstrating that honesty has the power to transform even the most wicked hearts.

32-Ayogrha.htm.title: 32. The Story of Ayogṛha (Saṁvega)
32-Ayogrha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Ayogṛha (Saṁvega) together with further information.
32-Ayogrha.htm.intro: A prince, born after his mother’s previous children died, is raised in an iron house for protection. Realizing that death is inevitable regardless of physical barriers, he renounces his kingdom to seek spiritual liberation, emphasizing the urgency of spiritual practice over worldly security.

33-Buffalo.htm.title: 33. The Story of the Buffalo (Kṣānti)
33-Buffalo.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Buffalo (Kṣānti) together with further information.
33-Buffalo.htm.intro: The Bodhisattva, as a buffalo, patiently endures the constant harassment of a mischievous monkey. When asked why he tolerates such behavior, he explains that practicing patience on the weak is the true test of character, teaching a lesson in humility and restraint.

34-Woodpecker.htm.title: 34. The Story of the Woodpecker (Kṣānti)
34-Woodpecker.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of the Woodpecker (Kṣānti) together with further information.
34-Woodpecker.htm.intro: A woodpecker saves a lion by removing a bone stuck in its throat. Later, when the woodpecker is hungry, the lion refuses to help him. The woodpecker chooses not to seek revenge, showing that the virtuous do good because it is right, not for reciprocity.

After-Awakening.title: From the Awakening to the Chief Disciples
After-Awakening.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters From the Buddha’s Awakening to the Chief Disciples together with further information.
Source of the Stories
After-Awakening.intro: This story from the Great Chapter (Vinaya Mahāvagga) chronicles the foundational period of the Buddha’s ministry, beginning with his attainment of enlightenment at the Bodhi tree. The narrative follows his initial hesitation to teach, the subsequent delivery of the First Sermon on the Four Noble Truths, and the early growth of his monastic community. Key episodes describe the conversion of prominent figures, including the merchant Yasa, the Magadhan King Bimbisāra, and the chief disciples Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Through these encounters, the text illustrates the systematic spread of the Dhamma across ancient India and the establishing of the first Buddhist parks. The collection also documents the public reaction to these conversions, ranging from royal support and divine celebration to local social concern over the rapid expansion of the new spiritual order.
After-Awakening.keywords: Buddha, Biography, Great Disciples, Dharma, Kings, Śāsana, India, EBT, Pāḷi

01-03-After-Awakening.htm.title: 01-03 The Three Trees
01-03-After-Awakening.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting After Awakening together with further information.
01-03-After-Awakening.htm.intro: Following his Awakening at Uruvelā, the Buddha spends consecutive weeks sitting in deep meditation under different trees to experience liberation. Under the Bodhi tree, he contemplates the profound sequence of conditional origination in forward and reverse order. He later encounters a proud, grumbling Brahmin and redefines true Brahminhood as being free from blemish. Finally, Mucalinda, the Nāga king, shelters the meditating Buddha from a severe, week-long rainstorm.

04-Tapussa-Bhallika.htm.title: 04 Tapussa and Bhallika
04-Tapussa-Bhallika.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Tapussa and Bhallika together with further information.
04-Tapussa-Bhallika.htm.intro: While the Buddha is experiencing the happiness of liberation, two traveling merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, are directed to him by a deity. They offer the Buddha milk-rice and honey-balls. After the Four Great Kings provide stone bowls for the Buddha to accept the food, the merchants declare their faith. By taking refuge in the Buddha and the Dhamma, they become the world’s very first two-refuge lay disciples.

05-Brahmas-Request.htm.title: 05 Brahma’s Request
05-Brahmas-Request.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Brahma’s Request together with further information.
05-Brahmas-Request.htm.intro: The Buddha hesitates to teach the Dhamma, reflecting that humanity, deeply mired in desire and attachment, will find conditional origination and Nibbāna too profound to comprehend. Realizing the world will perish without these teachings, Brahmā Sahampati descends from the heavens. He formally requests the Buddha to teach, pointing out that some individuals have little dust in their eyes and will understand. The Buddha compassionately agrees.

06-08-First-Teachings.htm.title: 06-08 The First Teachings
06-08-First-Teachings.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The First Teachings together with further information.
06-08-First-Teachings.htm.intro: The Buddha travels to the Deer Park in Isipatana to share his realization. Along the way, he encounters Upaka the ascetic, who walks away skeptical. At Isipatana, the group of five ascetics initially receive him coldly but are soon won over by his presence. The Buddha delivers his first discourse, setting the Dhamma wheel rolling by teaching the Middle Way, avoiding extremes, and explaining the Four Noble Truths.

10-11-Further-Attainments.htm.title: 10-11 Further Attainments
10-11-Further-Attainments.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Further Attainments together with further information.
10-11-Further-Attainments.htm.intro: Following the first discourse, the group of five monks receive further instructions and attain deep insights into the Dhamma. The Buddha then delivers his second major teaching, focusing on the characteristic of non-self. He systematically analyzes the five aggregates—body, feeling, perception, mental processes, and consciousness—showing they are impermanent, unsatisfactory, and devoid of a permanent self. Upon hearing this, all five monks attain complete liberation, becoming Arahants.

12-Yasas-Going-Forth.htm.title: 12 Yasa’s Going Forth
12-Yasas-Going-Forth.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Yasa’s Going Forth together with further information.
12-Yasas-Going-Forth.htm.intro: Yasa, a wealthy young man living a life of immense luxury, grows deeply disillusioned with his sensory pleasures after waking up to see his sleeping female musicians in disarray. Distressed, he flees his home in the night and wanders to the Deer Park. There, he meets the Buddha, who comforts him, delivers a progressive discourse on generosity and morality, and guides Yasa to realize the Dhamma and enter monastic life.

13-14-Yasas-Parents.htm.title: 13-14 Yasa’s Parents
13-14-Yasas-Parents.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Yasa’s Parents together with further information.
13-14-Yasas-Parents.htm.intro: Yasa’s father tracks his son’s footprints to the Buddha. The Buddha uses psychic power to conceal Yasa temporarily while he teaches the father. The discourse leads the father to become the first three-refuge lay disciple. Meanwhile, Yasa, listening in, attains full liberation. When revealed, Yasa receives full ordination. Later, the Buddha visits Yasa’s mother and former wife, who also attain insight and become dedicated lay disciples.

15-16-Yasas-Friends.htm.title: 15-16 Yasa’s Friends
15-16-Yasas-Friends.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Yasa’s Friends together with further information.
15-16-Yasas-Friends.htm.intro: Word of Yasa’s sudden ordination spreads rapidly through his social circles, surprising his peers. First, four of his closest wealthy friends from prominent families visit him and the Buddha. Upon receiving the Buddha’s progressive teachings, they join the Sangha and achieve full liberation. Soon after, fifty more householder friends from the countryside follow their example, receive ordination, and likewise become Arahants, expanding the early community of liberated monastics.

20-Good-Group-of-Friends.htm.title: 20 The Good Group of Friends
20-Good-Group-of-Friends.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Good Group of Friends together with further information.
20-Good-Group-of-Friends.htm.intro: While resting in a forest grove on his way to Uruvelā, the Buddha encounters a company of thirty wealthy young men, known as the Good Group, who are out enjoying themselves. One courtesan had stolen their belongings and fled. When they ask the Buddha if he has seen her, he reorients their focus, asking whether it is better to seek a missing woman or to seek themselves.

21-35-Miracles.htm.title: 21-35 The Miracles at Gayā
21-35-Miracles.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Miracles at Gayā together with further information.
21-35-Miracles.htm.intro: To convert Uruvelā Kassapa, a proud matted-hair ascetic, and his massive following, the Buddha performs a remarkable series of fifteen distinct categories of miracles. He tames a fierce, venomous dragon-king in a fire-room, reads minds, commands cosmic entities like Sakka and Brahmā, splits wood supernaturally, and controls the elements by walking on dry ground amid a raging flood. These displays systematically dismantle Kassapa’s spiritual pride and stubbornness.

36-38-Kassapa-Brothers.htm.title: 36-38 The Kassapa Brothers’ Ordination
36-38-Kassapa-Brothers.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Kassapa Brothers’ Ordination together with further information.
36-38-Kassapa-Brothers.htm.intro: Overwhelmed by the Buddha’s vast array of miracles, Uruvelā Kassapa finally concedes that he is not fully liberated and submits to the Buddha. He and his five hundred followers cast their ritual ascetic hair and fire apparatus into the river and receive ordination. Prompted by this sudden mass conversion, Kassapa’s two brothers, Nadī and Gayā Kassapa, along with their remaining five hundred followers, quickly follow suit and join the Sangha.

39-40-King-Bimbisara.htm.title: 39-40 King Bimbisara and Veḷuvana
39-40-King-Bimbisara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting King Bimbisara and Veḷuvana together with further information.
39-40-King-Bimbisara.htm.intro: The Buddha travels to Rājagaha with his newly converted thousand-monk entourage. King Bimbisāra of Magadha arrives with a vast multitude to meet him. To clarify who is the master, Kassapa publicly bows to the Buddha. After the Buddha teaches, King Bimbisāra attains the Dhamma, fulfills his lifelong aspirations, and generously donates the serene Bamboo Wood pleasure park, establishing the very first monastic residential property for the Sangha.

41-42-Sariputta-and-Others.htm.title: 41-42 Sāriputta, Moggallāna and Others
41-42-Sariputta-and-Others.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting 41-42 Sāriputta, Moggallāna and Others together with further information.
41-42-Sariputta-and-Others.htm.intro: The wanderer Sāriputta hears a concise verse about causation from the monk Assaji and instantly attains the Dhamma. He shares it with his close friend Moggallāna, who achieves the same realization. Together with their two hundred and fifty followers, they ordain under the Buddha. As many other prominent young men of good families join the order, the public grows anxious, fearing the Buddha is making families childless and destroying lineages.

The-Great-Emancipation.title: The Great Emancipation
The-Great-Emancipation.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters concerning the Buddha’s Great Emancipation (Parinibbāna) together with further information.
Source of the Stories
The-Great-Emancipation.intro: These storybooks chronicle the final months and teachings of the Buddha as he traveled toward his eventual passing in Kusinārā. The text highlights his interactions with various followers, including the wealthy courtesan Ambapālī, his faithful attendant Ānanda, and his final convert, Subhadda. Central to these accounts are the Buddha’s instructions on mindfulness and the importance of self-reliance, urging his disciples to seek refuge in the Teaching rather than in any individual leader. Despite facing a severe, life-threatening illness after a meal provided by Cunda the Smith, the Buddha remains composed and compassionate, ensuring that his host feels no guilt for the accidental affliction. The narrative concludes by detailing the miraculous events surrounding his passing and the establishment of sacred pilgrimage sites intended to inspire future generations of practitioners.
The-Great-Emancipation.keywords: Buddha, Biography, Great Disciples, Dharma, Kings, Śāsana, India, EBT, Pāḷi

40. The Last Instructions of the Realised One

15-The-Courtesan-Ambapali.htm.title: 15. The Courtesan Ambapāli
15-The-Courtesan-Ambapali.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Courtesan Ambapāli together with further information.
15-The-Courtesan-Ambapali.htm.intro: The Buddha arrives in Vesali and stays in Ambapāli’s mango grove. Hearing of his arrival, the wealthy courtesan invites him and the Saṅgha for a meal. Though the local Licchavi princes attempt to buy the invitation from her for a vast sum, she refuses, prioritising the merit of serving the Buddha. After the meal, she donates her pleasure park to the Saṅgha. The Buddha accepts, emphasising that virtue and wisdom are the highest fruits.

16-The-Fortunate-Ones-Sickness.htm.title: 16. The Fortunate One’s Sickness
16-The-Fortunate-Ones-Sickness.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Fortunate One’s Sickness together with further information.
16-The-Fortunate-Ones-Sickness.htm.intro: While staying at Beluva during the rainy season, the Buddha falls gravely ill with sharp, life-threatening pains. Realising it is not yet time for his final passing without addressing the Saṅgha, he suppresses the illness through sheer willpower. Upon recovering, he tells Ānanda that he has taught everything openly and that the monks should live as their own islands, with the Dhamma as their refuge.

17-Anandas-Failure.htm.title: 17. Ānanda’s Failure
17-Anandas-Failure.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ānanda’s Failure together with further information.
17-Anandas-Failure.htm.intro: At the Capala Shrine, the Buddha hints three times to Ānanda that a Tathāgata has the power to remain for an entire aeon if requested. However, Ānanda’s mind is clouded by Māra, and he fails to make the request. Consequently, the Buddha sends Ānanda away. This failure is a pivotal moment in the narrative, signifying that the window for the Buddha to extend his physical life has closed due to the lack of a formal invitation.

18-The-Relinquishment-of-the-Life-Proces.title: 18. The Relinquishment of the Life Process
18-The-Relinquishment-of-the-Life-Proces.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Relinquishment of the Life Process together with further information.
18-The-Relinquishment-of-the-Life-Proces.intro: After Ānanda departs, Māra approaches the Buddha and urges him to enter Parinibbāna. The Buddha agrees, stating that his mission is complete and his disciples are well-trained. He formally relinquishes his will to live, an act that causes a great earthquake and thunder. When Ānanda later realises his mistake and begs the Buddha to stay, the Buddha refuses, explaining that the time for such a request has passed and all things must end.

29-The-Last-Meal.htm.title: 29. The Last Meal
29-The-Last-Meal.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Last Meal together with further information.
29-The-Last-Meal.htm.intro: The Buddha travels to Pāvā and stays in the mango grove of Cunda the Smith. Cunda prepares a special meal called sukaramaddava. The Buddha eats it but instructs Cunda to bury the remainder, as no one else could digest it. Soon after, the Buddha suffers from bloody dysentery and intense pain. Despite his physical agony, he remains mindful and composed, beginning the final walk toward Kusinārā, demonstrating his mastery over physical suffering.

30-Bringing-Drinking-Water.htm.title: 30. Bringing Drinking Water
30-Bringing-Drinking-Water.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Bringing Drinking Water together with further information.
30-Bringing-Drinking-Water.htm.intro: Exhausted and thirsty on the road to Kusinara, the Buddha asks Ānanda for water from a nearby stream. Ānanda hesitates because five hundred wagons had just crossed, leaving the water muddy and fouled. However, at the Buddha’s third request, Ānanda approaches the stream and finds it miraculously clear and pure. This event highlights the Buddha’s spiritual power and his deteriorating physical state, requiring frequent rest as he nears his final destination.

31-The-Story-Concerning-Pukkusa-Mallaput.title: 31. The Story Concerning Pukkusa Mallaputta
31-The-Story-Concerning-Pukkusa-Mallaput.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story Concerning Pukkusa Mallaputta together with further information.
31-The-Story-Concerning-Pukkusa-Mallaput.intro: A disciple of Āḷāra Kālāma named Pukkusa meets the Buddha and is impressed by his profound serenity. The Buddha recounts a time he remained in deep meditation during a violent thunderstorm that killed two farmers and four oxen nearby, completely oblivious to the noise. Inspired, Pukkusa goes for refuge and offers the Buddha two robes of golden cloth. When draped, the Buddha’s skin glows so radiantly it outshines the gold, signaling his imminent passing.

32-Cundas-Great-Gain.htm.title: 32. Cunda’s Great Gain
32-Cundas-Great-Gain.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Cunda’s Great Gain together with further information.
32-Cundas-Great-Gain.htm.intro: Sensing that Cunda might feel guilty that his meal caused the Buddha’s illness, the Buddha instructs Ānanda to reassure him. He explains that two offerings of food are of equal and supreme merit: the meal eaten before Awakening and the meal eaten before Parinibbāna. By validating Cunda’s gift, the Buddha ensures the smith receives honor rather than blame, teaching that the intention behind the gift is what creates lasting merit and happiness.

33-Worshipping-the-Realised-One.htm.title: 33. Worshipping the Realised One
33-Worshipping-the-Realised-One.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Worshipping the Realised One together with further information.
33-Worshipping-the-Realised-One.htm.intro: Arriving at the Sāl Wood of Kusinārā, the Buddha lies down between twin Sāl trees, which bloom out of season, showering him with blossoms. Divine music and sandalwood powder fall from the sky in worship. However, the Buddha tells Ānanda that such external displays are not the highest worship. Instead, the person who practices the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma and lives with integrity truly honors, respects, and reveres the Tathāgata.

34-The-Visit-of-the-Divinities.htm.title: 34. The Visit of the Divinities
34-The-Visit-of-the-Divinities.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Visit of the Divinities together with further information.
34-The-Visit-of-the-Divinities.htm.intro: The Buddha informs Ānanda that countless divinities from ten world-systems have gathered to witness his final passing. He notes that while some deities are weeping and tearing their hair in grief, those who are free from passion remain composed, reflecting on the truth that all conditioned things are impermanent. This chapter contrasts worldly sorrow with the equanimity of the awakened, emphasizing the core teaching on the inevitability of change and death.

35-The-Four-Places-that-Produce-Enthusia.title: 35. The Four Places that Produce Enthusiasm
35-The-Four-Places-that-Produce-Enthusia.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Four Places that Produce Enthusiasm together with further information.
35-The-Four-Places-that-Produce-Enthusia.intro: The Buddha identifies four locations that will inspire devotion in followers after his passing: his birthplace (Lumbini), the place of his Awakening (Bodh Gaya), where he first turned the Wheel of Dhamma (Sarnath), and the site of his final passing (Kusinārā). He explains that those who die while making a pilgrimage to these shrines with a confident heart will be reborn in a heavenly world, establishing a tradition of physical connection to the Dhamma.

36-Anandas-Marvellous-Qualities.htm.title: 36. Ānanda’s Marvellous Qualities
36-Anandas-Marvellous-Qualities.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ānanda’s Marvellous Qualities together with further information.
36-Anandas-Marvellous-Qualities.htm.intro: Overcome with grief, Ānanda leans against a doorpost and weeps. The Buddha calls for him, offering comfort by reminding him of the law of impermanence. He then praises Ānanda before the assembly, highlighting his four wonderful qualities: his popularity, his skill in teaching, his remarkable memory, and his ability to know the right time for people to meet the Buddha. He encourages Ānanda to strive diligently, predicting he will soon reach Awakening.

37-Kusinaras-History.htm.title: 37. Kusinārā’s History
37-Kusinaras-History.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Kusinārā’s History together with further information.
37-Kusinaras-History.htm.intro: Ānanda suggests the Buddha should not pass away in a small, wattle-and-daub town like Kusinārā, suggesting grander cities like Rājagaha or Sāvatthī instead. The Buddha corrects him, revealing that Kusinārā was once the magnificent capital city, Kusavati, ruled by the Great King of Glory, Mahā Sudassana. This teaching serves to humble the pride associated with grand cities and emphasises that even the most glorious civilizations are subject to the inevitable law of decay.

38-The-Mallas-Worship-the-Fortunate-One..title: 38. The Mallas Worship the Fortunate One
38-The-Mallas-Worship-the-Fortunate-One..summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Mallas Worship the Fortunate One together with further information.
38-The-Mallas-Worship-the-Fortunate-One..intro: The Mallas, the local ruling clan, gather to pay their final respects. To ensure everyone has the opportunity to see him before he passes, the Buddha has Ānanda organize them by family groups rather than individually. This systematic approach allows thousands to pay homage in a single watch of the night. The scene depicts the deep communal respect held for the Buddha and the somber atmosphere as an entire community prepares for his departure.

39-Subhadda-the-Last-Direct-Disciple.htm.title: 39. Subhadda, the Last Direct Disciple
39-Subhadda-the-Last-Direct-Disciple.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Subhadda, the Last Direct Disciple together with further information.
39-Subhadda-the-Last-Direct-Disciple.htm.intro: An ascetic named Subhadda seeks an audience, but Ānanda repeatedly refuses him to avoid disturbing the dying Buddha. Overhearing this, the Buddha insists on seeing him. Subhadda asks about the validity of other teachers, but the Buddha focuses on the Noble Eightfold Path, stating that where this path is found, true renunciants exist. Subhadda is deeply moved, goes for refuge, and becomes the Buddha’s last direct convert and disciple before his passing.

40-The-Last-Instructions-of-the-Realised.title: 40. The Last Instructions of the Realised One
40-The-Last-Instructions-of-the-Realised.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Last Instructions of the Realised One together with further information.
40-The-Last-Instructions-of-the-Realised.intro: The Buddha gives his final guidance to the Saṅgha. He tells them that after he is gone, the Dhamma and the Discipline (Vinaya) shall be their teacher. He allows for the abolishment of minor rules and instructs on how to handle the monk Channa. Finally, he asks the monks three times if they have any doubts or questions. When they remain silent, he utters his final words: “All conditioned things are subject to decay; strive on with diligence.”

41-The-Final-Emancipation.htm.title: 41. The Final Emancipation
41-The-Final-Emancipation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Final Emancipation together with further information.
41-The-Final-Emancipation.htm.intro: The Buddha enters a series of deep meditative absorptions, moving through the four jhānas and the formless attainments. Emerging from the state of cessation, he descends back to the first jhāna and then ascends again to the fourth. Upon emerging from the fourth jhāna, he immediately passes away into Parinibbāna. His death is marked by a massive earthquake and terrifying thunder, signifying the end of the life of the Great Teacher of gods and men.

42-The-Preparation-of-the-Body.htm.title: 42. The Preparation of the Body
42-The-Preparation-of-the-Body.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Preparation of the Body together with further information.
42-The-Preparation-of-the-Body.htm.intro: Following the Buddha's passing, the Mallas of Kusinārā spend seven days honoring the body with music, dance, and garlands. In accordance with the Buddha’s previous instructions to Ānanda, they treat his remains like those of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). The body is wrapped in layers of new cloth and wool, placed in an iron oil-vessel, and prepared for cremation on a magnificent pyre, reflecting the highest level of worldly honor.

43-The-Story-Concerning-Mahakassapa.htm.title: 43. The Story Concerning Mahākassapa
43-The-Story-Concerning-Mahakassapa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story Concerning Mahākassapa together with further information.
43-The-Story-Concerning-Mahakassapa.htm.intro: The funeral pyre refuses to ignite despite the Mallas’ efforts. The venerable Anuruddha explains that the deities are waiting for Mahākassapa, who is traveling to Kusinārā with five hundred monks. Upon arrival, Mahākassapa pays his respects at the Buddha’s feet. Only after he and the monks have finished their salutations does the pyre spontaneously burst into flames. This event underscores the spiritual seniority and importance of Mahākassapa within the Saṅgha.

44-The-Distribution-of-the-Relics.htm.title: 44. The Distribution of the Relics
44-The-Distribution-of-the-Relics.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Distribution of the Relics together with further information.
44-The-Distribution-of-the-Relics.htm.intro: After the cremation, several kings and clans demand the Buddha’s relics, leading to a potential conflict. A Brahmin named Doṇa intervenes, reminding them of the Buddha’s teachings on peace. He divides the remains into eight equal portions for the various claimants, who then build stūpas over them in their respective lands. This distribution ensures that the Buddha’s physical remains serve as a focus for devotion and practice across the region.

Vinaya-Stories.title: Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka
Vinaya-Stories.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Vinaya-Stories.intro: These stories recount the Buddha’s teaching and the early history of the monastic community. It opens with the Buddha at Verañjā, converting the brahmin Verañja and recounting his enlightenment. It then details the circumstances leading to the first four major monastic rules (pārājika). Further sections describe how many of the other rules came to be laid down, including the ordination of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and the establishment of the nuns’ order, and also the First Council at Rājagaha where the teachings were recited, and the Second Council at Vesālī a century later, which rejected ten lax practices.
Vinaya-Stories.keywords: Buddha, Biography, India, Disciples, Discipline, Folklore, EBT, Pāḷi

00-Veranja.htm.title: The Famine at Verañjā
00-Veranja.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Famine at Verañjā from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
00-Veranja.htm.intro: The brahmin Verañja challenges the Buddha regarding respect and monastic discipline. The Buddha refutes each criticism, defining true spiritual qualities and explaining his spiritual seniority through the egg-shell metaphor. Despite facing a harsh famine during the vassa at Verañjā, the Buddha declines Mahāmoggallāna’s psychic interventions. Addressing Sāriputta, he explains that rules and Pātimokkha recitation are established only when corrupting conditions manifest in the Saṅgha.

01-Intercourse.htm.title: 01 The Rule about Intercourse
01-Intercourse.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rule about Intercourse from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
01-Intercourse.htm.intro: Sudinna, a merchant’s son, starves himself until his parents permit his ordination. During a famine, he visits his family in Vesālī to secure alms for monks. Urged by his mother to produce an heir, Sudinna engages in sexual intercourse with his former wife, conceiving Bījaka. Overcome with remorse, he confesses. The Buddha sharply rebukes his conduct, leading to the formulation of the first parājika training rule against sexual intercourse.

02-Theft.htm.title: 02 The Rule about Theft
02-Theft.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rule about Theft from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
02-Theft.htm.intro: Dhaniya builds a clay hut after his grass huts are destroyed, but the Buddha orders it demolished to avoid harming living beings during firing. Dhaniya then tricks an accountant into giving him royal emergency timber by misinterpreting King Bimbisāra’s general decree on forest resources. Upon discovery, Bimbisāra spares Dhaniya due to his monastic status. Prompted by public outrage, the Buddha consults a former judge regarding theft thresholds and establishes the second parājika rule prohibiting theft.

03-Killing.htm.title: 03 The Rule about Killing
03-Killing.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rule about Killing from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
03-Killing.htm.intro: Following the Buddha’s teachings on foulness, monks experience extreme disgust toward their bodies and begin taking their own lives, killing each other, or hiring Migalaṇḍika to execute them. After emerging from seclusion, the Buddha notices the diminished community and teaches mindfulness of breathing as a balanced meditation practice. He then rebukes the monks’ actions and establishes the third parājika rule prohibiting the intentional taking of human life.

04-False-Claims.htm.title: 04 The Rule about False Claims
04-False-Claims.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rule about False Claims from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
04-False-Claims.htm.intro: During a famine, monks along the Vaggumudā River agree to falsely praise each other’s spiritual attainments to local laypeople to secure abundant almsfood. While other monks suffer from starvation, these monks thrive on stolen offerings. Upon uncovering their deception, the Buddha severely rebukes them, identifies false claimants of spiritual attainments as the supreme thieves in the world, and establishes the fourth parājika rule prohibiting false claims of super-human achievements.

05-Uposatha.htm.title: 05 The Uposatha and the Pātimokkha
05-Uposatha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Uposatha and the Pātimokkha from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
05-Uposatha.htm.intro: King Bimbisāra suggests assembling on lunar observance days, prompting the Buddha to allow gatherings and teaching. To prevent silent assemblies, the Buddha authorizes teaching the Dhamma and establishes the biweekly Pātimokkha recitation as the formal legal Observance (Uposatha). Monks must declare purity or confess offenses during this assembly. The practice is restricted to once per fortnight within a single unified residence.

06-Rains.htm.title: 06 The Rains Retreat
06-Rains.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rains Retreat from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
06-Rains.htm.intro: Public complaints arose because monks wandered during the rainy season, trampling young grass and harming small living beings, unlike other ascetics and nesting birds who remained sedentary. In response, the Buddha authorized the rains retreat (Vassa) during the rainy season and established two entry periods: the day after the full moon of Āsāḷhī (early) or one month after it (late). He made entering the retreat mandatory, forbade intentionally bypassing a residence to avoid it, and made it an offense to go on a journey during the three-month period.

07-Invitation.htm.title: 07 The Invitation for Correction
07-Invitation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Invitation for Correction from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
07-Invitation.htm.intro: To prevent disagreement during their rains retreat, monks took a vow of silence. The Buddha criticized this practice as uncomfortable, comparable to living like livestock or sectarians, and prohibited it. To promote harmony, he established the Invitation (Pavāraṇā) ceremony, requiring monks completing the retreat to invite mutual admonishment based on what was seen, heard, or suspected, and allowed monks to sit on seats after inviting admonishment.

08-Allowances.htm.title: 08 Allowances Outside the Middle Lands
08-Allowances.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Allowances Outside the Middle Lands from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
08-Allowances.htm.intro: In remote Avanti, Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa faces long delays before Venerable Mahākaccāna assembles ten monks for his ordination. Soṇa then travels to Sāvatthī, where he recites the Section of the Eights (Aṭṭhakavagga) before the Buddha. On Mahākaccāna’s behalf, Soṇa requests and receives five allowances for border regions, including ordination by only five monks, multi-soled sandals, frequent bathing, leather sandals and flexible robe rules.

09-Luxury.htm.title: 09 The Rules Against Luxury
09-Luxury.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rules Against Luxury from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
09-Luxury.htm.intro: Venerable Pilindavaccha cleans a cave, leading King Bimbisāra to offer five hundred monastery attendants once permitted by the Buddha. Later, Pilindavaccha turns a grass pad into a golden garland for a poor girl. When Bimbisāra imprisons her family for suspected theft, Pilindavaccha transforms the palace into gold to secure their release. Devotees offer five medicines, but excessive storing by disciples leads the Buddha to limit storage to seven days.

10-Meat.htm.title: 10 The Rules about Meat-Eating
10-Meat.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rules about Meat-Eating from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
10-Meat.htm.intro: Suppiyā cuts flesh from her thigh for a sick monk. After healing her the Buddha bans human flesh and unexamined meat. He also prohibits eating elephant, horse, dog, snake, and wild animal meats. Later, General Sīha converts and serves meat to the sangha, prompting Jain criticism. The Buddha then bans meat known, seen, or suspected to be killed for monks, allowing only three-fold pure meat.

11-Sacrifices.htm.title: 11 The Correct Sacrifices
11-Sacrifices.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Correct Sacrifices from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
11-Sacrifices.htm.intro: When the Buddha arrives in Āpaṇa, the matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya offers allowable fruit and plant beverages, which ancient sages permitted. The Buddha accepts and allows monks to consume various fruit, leaf, flower, and sugarcane juices. Keṇiya then invites the Buddha and his 1,250 monks to a meal. Afterwards, the Buddha praises the Community as the foremost recipient of offerings for those seeking merit.

12-Kathina.htm.title: 12 The Kaṭhina Celebration
12-Kathina.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Kaṭhina Celebration from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
12-Kathina.htm.intro: Thirty monks traveling to Sāvatthī for a retreat are delayed in Sāketa by rains. Arriving afterward with drenched robes, they meet the Buddha, who establishes the kaṭhina ceremony. Monks who spread the kaṭhina receive five privileges, including traveling without full robes. The Buddha details proper formal motions, strict manufacturing requirements for suitable cloth, valid spreading procedures within the boundary, and eight grounds for withdrawing privileges.

13-Jivaka.htm.title: 13 The Physician Jīvaka
13-Jivaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Physician Jīvaka from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
13-Jivaka.htm.intro: Abandoned at birth, Jīvaka studies medicine at Takkasilā and becomes a renowned physician. He earns wealth curing a merchant’s wife’s headache and performs successful brain surgery on a merchant. After secretly administering repulsive ghee to cure King Pajjota’s jaundice, Jīvaka flees his wrath. Later, he treats the Buddha’s illness with a gentle, lily-infused purgative and hot baths.

14-Robes.htm.title: 14 The Rules about Robes
14-Robes.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rules about Robes from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
14-Robes.htm.intro: Monks collecting rag-robes from cemeteries must share them with absent or late companions. To resolve distribution and storage issues, the Buddha permits appointing dedicated, unbiased monks as robe-accepters and robe-keepers. Noticing monks carrying excessive garments, he tests winter temperatures and limits a monk’s allowance to three robes, banning extra sets beyond ten unassigned days. Finally, he approves patching worn robes and customizing cloth layers based on material wear.

15-Visakha.htm.title: 15 Visākhā and Her Boons
15-Visakha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Visākhā and Her Boons from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
15-Visakha.htm.intro: Visākhā invites the Buddha and his monks for a meal during a heavy rainstorm. When her slave misinterprets monks bathing in the rain as naked ascetics, Visākhā realizes the need for proper attire. After miraculously arriving dry to eat, the Buddha grants Visākhā eight lifelong boons, allowing her to provide rain cloths, various meals, medicines, gruel, and bathing cloths for nuns to support the Sangha.

16-Sick.htm.title: 16 Tending to the Sick
16-Sick.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Tending to the Sick from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
16-Sick.htm.intro: Finding a sick monk lying uncared-for in his own excrement, the Buddha and Ānanda personally bathe and tend to him. The Buddha subsequently mandates that monastics must care for one another, declaring that serving the sick is equivalent to serving him. He outlines duty hierarchies for attendants and defines the five traits that make a patient easy or difficult to treat, and a caregiver fit or unfit.

17-Reconciliation.htm.title: 17 Reconciliation
17-Reconciliation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Reconciliation from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
17-Reconciliation.htm.intro: A resident monk named Kassapagotta welcomes visiting monks with great hospitality. Later, they accuse him of an offence and suspend him. He travels to the Buddha, who rules the suspension invalid. The visiting monks, filled with remorse, confess their transgression, and the Buddha praises the value of acknowledging and making amends for one’s faults.

18-Kosambi.htm.title: 18 The Rift at Kosambī
18-Kosambi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rift at Kosambī from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
18-Kosambi.htm.intro: A dispute arises over whether a monk’s action was an offence. Monks suspend him, but he gains supporters, causing a schism. The Buddha warns against suspension that divides the community and urges reconciliation. The monks ignore his counsel. The Buddha departs alone, reciting verses on how enmity is only appeased by non-enmity and the value of solitary practice.

19-Dighavu.htm.title: 19 The Story of Dīghāvu
19-Dighavu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story of Dīghāvu from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
19-Dighavu.htm.intro: King Brahmadatta seizes King Dīghīti’s kingdom and executes him. Dīghīti’s son, Dīghāvu, becomes the king’s servant, plotting revenge. When they are alone, Dīghāvu draws his sword three times but recalls his father’s dying words: enmities are appeased by non-enmity. He spares the king. Brahmadatta, moved by his forbearance, restores everything and gives him his daughter.

20-Bamboo-Park.htm.title: 20 Harmony in the Bamboo Park
20-Bamboo-Park.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Harmony in the Bamboo Park from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
20-Bamboo-Park.htm.intro: The Buddha visits three monks—Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimila—who dwell in the Eastern Bamboo Grove. They explain that they live in harmony, setting aside their own minds to act according to one another’s minds. They are diligent, sharing duties, and never break into speech over tasks. The Buddha approves of their exemplary communal living.

21-Palileyyaka.htm.title: 21 The Palileyyaka Elephant
21-Palileyyaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Palileyyaka Elephant from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
21-Palileyyaka.htm.intro: After failing to settle the Kosambī dispute, the Buddha goes alone to the forest. A great bull elephant, weary of his herd, also seeks solitude there. The two dwell together peacefully, each understanding the other’s mind. The Buddha notes their shared delight in solitary forest life. He later returns to Sāvatthī, where lay followers refuse to support the quarrelsome monks, forcing them to reconcile.

22-Banishment.htm.title: 22 The Act of Banishment
22-Banishment.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Act of Banishment from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
22-Banishment.htm.intro: Monks named Assaji and Punabbasuka reside at Kīṭāgiri, engaging in frivolous misconduct—gardening, wearing garlands, dancing, gambling, and associating with women. A visiting monk reports this to the Buddha. The Buddha rebukes them, lists their many offences, and instructs Sāriputta and Moggallāna to perform the act of banishment, forbidding them from dwelling there.

23-Reconciliation.htm.title: 23 Reconciliation with a Householder
23-Reconciliation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Reconciliation with a Householder from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
23-Reconciliation.htm.intro: The monk Sudhammo jealously resents that the householder Citta invited elder monks without consulting him. He visits Citta’s house, jeers at him, and departs for Sāvatthī to report the matter. The Buddha rebukes Sudhammo for scoffing at a faithful supporter and instructs the Community to perform a legal act of reconciliation, requiring him to ask forgiveness from Citta.

24-Suspension.htm.title: 24 Suspension of Channa
24-Suspension.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Suspension of Channa from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
24-Suspension.htm.intro: The monk Channa commits an offence but refuses to make amends. Monks report this to the Buddha, who questions Channa and rebukes him. The Buddha then instructs the Community to perform a legal act of suspension on Channa for not making amends—non-eating with the Community. He directs that this be announced from residence to residence.

25-Views.htm.title: 25 Wrong Views
25-Views.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Wrong Views from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
25-Views.htm.intro: The monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-killer, holds a wrong view: that sense pleasures, declared as obstructions by the Buddha, are not actually sufficient to obstruct one indulging in them. Monks try to dissuade him, but he clings to his view. The Buddha rebukes him and instructs the Community to suspend him for not giving up the evil view.

26-Innocence.htm.title: 26 Proclaiming Innocence
26-Innocence.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Proclaiming Innocence from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
26-Innocence.htm.intro: The Venerable Dabba, an arahant, is authorized to assign lodgings and meals. Jealous monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, who receive poor lodgings and food, bribe the nun Mettiyā to accuse Dabba of sexual misconduct. Dabba declares his innocence, even in dreams. The Buddha removes the nun and investigates. The monks confess to inciting her. The Buddha gives Dabba a verdict of innocence.

27-Supernormal-Powers.htm.title: 27 The Use of Supernormal Powers
27-Supernormal-Powers.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Use of Supernormal Powers from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
27-Supernormal-Powers.htm.intro: A millionaire offers a costly sandalwood bowl to anyone with supernormal powers. Heretical teachers fail to take it. Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, an arahant, flies up and takes it, causing a commotion. The Buddha rebukes him for displaying supernormal powers to laypeople for a miserable bowl, comparing it to a woman exposing herself for a small coin. He rules that such displays are an offence.

28-Overturning-the-Bowl.htm.title: 28 Overturning the Bowl
28-Overturning-the-Bowl.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Overturning the Bowl from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
28-Overturning-the-Bowl.htm.intro: Vaḍḍha the Licchavi, incited by the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, falsely accuses Dabba the Mallian of violating his wife. The Buddha gives Dabba a verdict of innocence and orders the Community to overturn the bowl for Vaḍḍha, meaning no communion with him. Vaḍḍha faints, repents, and the Buddha restores him after he shows remorse.

29-Dwellings.htm.title: 29 The Rules about Dwellings
29-Dwellings.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Rules about Dwellings from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
29-Dwellings.htm.intro: Monks initially live in forests, tree roots, and open air. A millionaire of Rājagaha, impressed by their deportment, wishes to build dwellings. The Buddha allows five kinds of rock cells. The millionaire builds sixty dwellings in one day and donates them to the Saṅgha of the four directions. The Buddha gives thanks, praising the gift of dwellings as the highest gift, leading to Nibbāna.

30-Anathapindika.htm.title: 30 Anāthapiṇḍika and Jetavana
30-Anathapindika.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Anāthapiṇḍika and Jetavana from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
30-Anathapindika.htm.intro: Anāthapiṇḍika, a wealthy merchant, hears the word “Buddha” and is filled with faith. He rises in the night, spirits open the gate, and darkness turns to light. He meets the Buddha, who teaches him the Dhamma. He attains stream-entry and invites the Buddha to Sāvatthī. He purchases Jeta’s Grove for ten million gold coins and builds a monastery there.

31-Seniority.htm.title: 31 The Importance of Seniority
31-Seniority.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Importance of Seniority from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
31-Seniority.htm.intro: The pupils of the six monks take the best seats and lodgings, leaving Sāriputta without a place to sleep. The Buddha, learning of this, teaches a past life story: a partridge, monkey, and elephant lived together. They asked who was eldest, and the partridge’s ancient memory revealed he was oldest. The animals honored him and kept the precepts. The Buddha rules that respect should be paid according to seniority.

32-Schism.htm.title: 32 Devadatta and Schism in the Sangha
32-Schism.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Devadatta and Schism in the Sangha from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
32-Schism.htm.intro: Devadatta, corrupted by gain and honor, desires to lead the Community. He gains Prince Ajātasattu’s favor and asks for five ascetic practices. The Buddha refuses. Devadatta then incites Ajātasattu to kill his father and sends assassins after the Buddha. The Buddha converts the assassins and tames the elephant Nāḷāgiri. Devadatta creates a schism, taking five hundred monks, but Sāriputta and Moggallāna bring them back.

33-Pindapata.htm.title: 33 The Duties on Piṇḍapāta
33-Pindapata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Duties on Piṇḍapāta from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
33-Pindapata.htm.intro: Alms-gathering monks were going for alms improperly dressed and behaving carelessly, causing a monk to be falsely accused of violating a woman. The Buddha rebukes the monks and lays down detailed rules for alms-gathering monks: how to dress, enter a village, stand at a dwelling, accept almsfood, and return. The rules govern proper deportment and respectful conduct while collecting alms.

34-Pupils-Duties.htm.title: 34 Pupils’ Duties to Preceptors
34-Pupils-Duties.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Pupils’ Duties to Preceptors from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
34-Pupils-Duties.htm.intro: Co-resident pupils fail to behave properly toward their preceptors. The Buddha rebukes them and lays down detailed duties: providing toothbrush, water, seat, and gruel in the morning; assisting with robes and bowl; accompanying them to the village; preparing seats and water on return; washing and storing bowls and robes; attending them in sickness; and caring for them throughout life.

35-Preceptors-Duties.htm.title: 35 Preceptors’ Duties to Pupils
35-Preceptors-Duties.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Preceptors’ Duties to Pupils from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
35-Preceptors-Duties.htm.intro: Preceptors fail to behave properly toward their co-resident pupils. The Buddha lays down the preceptor’s duties: supporting pupils with recitation, questioning, exhortation, and instruction; providing bowls, robes, and requisites if they lack them; caring for them when sick; and attending to their needs in the same detailed manner that pupils care for preceptors.

36-Patimokkha.htm.title: 36 The Recital of the Pātimokkha
36-Patimokkha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Recital of the Pātimokkha from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
36-Patimokkha.htm.intro: On the Observance day, the Buddha three times refuses to recite the Pātimokkha because the assembly is not pure. Moggallāna discovers an impure monk and removes him. The Buddha declares he will no longer perform the Observance or recite the Pātimokkha, and that those with offences must not hear it. The six monks set aside the Pātimokkha of pure monks, and the Buddha rules this is an offence.

37-Bhikkhuni-Ordination.htm.title: 37 Bhikkhunī Ordination
37-Bhikkhuni-Ordination.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Bhikkhunī Ordination from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
37-Bhikkhuni-Ordination.htm.intro: Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the Buddha’s foster mother, requests ordination for women and is refused three times. She and many Sakyan women shave their heads and walk to Vesālī, standing tearfully outside. Ānanda intercedes, asking if women can attain the fruits of the path. The Buddha agrees, establishing the eight rules of respect as full ordination. Later the rules for the ordination of women are explained.

38-First-Council.htm.title: 38 Events Surrounding the First Council
38-First-Council.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Events Surrounding the First Council from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
38-First-Council.htm.intro: After the Buddha’s final Nibbāna, Mahākassapa convenes five hundred arahants at Rājagaha to recite the Teaching and Monastic Discipline, lest false teachings prevail. Upāli recites the Vinaya and Ānanda the Discourses, with Ānanda attaining arahantship just before the council. The elders decide not to abolish the lesser training rules, and Ānanda confesses several wrongdoings. Channa receives the highest penalty, then attains arahantship, and the council concludes.

39-Second-Council.htm.title: 39 Events Surrounding the Second Council
39-Second-Council.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Events Surrounding the Second Council from Stories from the Vinayapiṭaka together with further information.
39-Second-Council.htm.intro: A century after the Buddha’s Nibbāna, Vesālian monks adopt ten lax practices, including accepting gold and silver. The elder Yasa publicly rejects this, is reconciled, and travels to gather support. Seven hundred arahants, led by Revata and Sabbakāmī, convene at Vesālī. They examine each of the ten practices, find them against the Teaching, and reject them. This recitation is called the Recitation of the Seven Hundred.

Way-Beyond.title: The Way to the Beyond
Way-Beyond.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Way-Beyond.intro: The brahmin Bāvari, cursed by a beggar that his head will split in seven days, sends his sixteen students to find the Buddha, who alone knows the meaning of head-splitting. At Sāvatthī, each student asks profound questions about suffering, ignorance, craving, and liberation. The Buddha answers that ignorance envelops the world, craving defiles it, and mindfulness and wisdom free it. He teaches that seeing the world as empty, abandoning craving, and not clinging enables one to cross birth and old age. The students attain awakening, and the text praises these teachings as the path going beyond saṃsāra.
Way-Beyond.keywords: Buddha, Biography, India, Dharma, EBT, Pāḷi

toc.label: Verses in Praise of the Way to the Beyond
Verses on the Recital of the Way to the Beyond

00-Introduction.htm.title: Introductory Verses
00-Introduction.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Introductory Verses from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
00-Introduction.htm.intro: The brahmin Bāvari, having given away his wealth, is threatened by a beggar: his head will split in seven days. Terrified, he learns from a god that only a Buddha knows the meaning of head-splitting. He sends his sixteen students—including Ajita and Piṅgiya—to find the Buddha. They travel to Sāvatthī, where the Buddha answers Ajita’s unspoken question, revealing that ignorance is the head and understanding is its splitter.

01-Ajita.htm.title: 01 Ajita’s Questions
01-Ajita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ajita’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
01-Ajita.htm.intro: Ajita asks what envelops the world, why it lacks clarity, its defilement, and its great fear. The Buddha answers: ignorance envelops it; heedlessness and meanness obscure it; hunger is its defilement; and the great fear is death. He then explains that mindfulness restrains the streams of craving, and wisdom shuts them off. Ajita and his thousand students attain awakening.

02-Tissa-Metteyya.htm.title: 02 Tissa Metteyya’s Questions
02-Tissa-Metteyya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Tissa Metteyya’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
02-Tissa-Metteyya.htm.intro: Tissa Metteyya asks who is satisfied, free from turmoil, wise, undefiled in the middle, a Great Man, and has gone beyond the seamstress (craving). The Buddha answers: the monk who is chaste, free from craving, always mindful, and discerning is emancipated and free from turmoil. He is the wise one, knowing both ends and undefiled in the middle; he is a Great Man who has gone beyond craving.

03-Punnaka.htm.title: 03 Puṇṇaka’s Questions
03-Punnaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Puṇṇaka’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
03-Punnaka.htm.intro: Puṇṇaka asks why seers, nobles, and brahmins offer many sacrifices to the gods. The Buddha answers that they do so yearning for mundane existence, driven by old age and the passion for existence. When Puṇṇaka asks if such sacrificers have crossed over birth and old age, the Buddha says no. Only one who has discerned far and near, is peaceful, and free from yearning has crossed over birth and old age.

04-Mettagu.htm.title: 04 Mettagū’s Questions
04-Mettagu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mettagū’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
04-Mettagu.htm.intro: Mettagū asks about the origin of suffering and how the wise cross the flood. The Buddha explains that suffering arises from attachment and craving; the wise, having understood this, cross the flood by abandoning delight in sense pleasures. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus attain Nibbāna.

05-Dhotaka.htm.title: 05 Dhotaka’s Questions
05-Dhotaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Dhotaka’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
05-Dhotaka.htm.intro: Dhotaka asks the Buddha to free him from doubt and teach him Nibbāna here and now. The Buddha says he cannot liberate everyone from doubt, but Dhotaka should learn from him and cross the flood. When Dhotaka asks where to find safety, the Buddha answers: cultivate mindfulness and equanimity, abandon craving, and realize the cessation of all things.

06-Upasiva.htm.title: 06 Upasīva’s Questions
06-Upasiva.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Upasīva’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
06-Upasiva.htm.intro: Upasīva asks how to cross the flood and reach the goal. The Buddha teaches: contemplate emptiness, be mindful, and abandon craving. When Upasīva asks about the state of one who has attained Nibbāna, the Buddha explains that such a one has no measure, no support, and cannot be described; all phenomena cease.

07-Nanda.htm.title: 07 Nanda’s Questions
07-Nanda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Nanda’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
07-Nanda.htm.intro: Nanda asks about the wise ones who are free from doubt and how they cross the flood. The Buddha answers that the wise abandon craving and conceit, and by understanding the nature of things, they cross the flood. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus attain liberation.

08-Hemaka.htm.title: 08 Hemaka’s Questions
08-Hemaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Hemaka’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
08-Hemaka.htm.intro: Hemaka asks about the nature of the world and how to be free from suffering. The Buddha explains that the world is deluded by ignorance, and the wise abandon craving and conceit. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus attain Nibbāna.

09-Todeyya.htm.title: 09 Todeyya’s Questions
09-Todeyya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Todeyya’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
09-Todeyya.htm.intro: Todeyya asks about the source of suffering and how to be free from it. The Buddha explains that suffering arises from craving and attachment. The wise, understanding this, abandon craving and attain liberation. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus cross the flood.

10-Kappa.htm.title: 10 Kappa’s Questions
10-Kappa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Kappa’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
10-Kappa.htm.intro: Kappa asks about the origin of the world and how to be free from suffering. The Buddha explains that the world is deluded by ignorance, and the wise abandon craving and conceit. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus attain Nibbāna.

11-Jatukanni.htm.title: 11 Jatukaṇṇī’s Questions
11-Jatukanni.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Jatukaṇṇī’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
11-Jatukanni.htm.intro: Jatukaṇṇī asks about the source of suffering and how to be free from it. The Buddha explains that suffering arises from craving and attachment. The wise, understanding this, abandon craving and attain liberation. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus cross the flood.

12-Bhadravuddha.htm.title: 12 Bhadrāvudha’s Questions
12-Bhadravuddha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Bhadrāvudha’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
12-Bhadravuddha.htm.intro: Bhadrāvudha asks about the source of suffering and how to be free from it. The Buddha explains that suffering arises from craving and attachment. The wise, understanding this, abandon craving and attain liberation. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus cross the flood.

13-Udaya.htm.title: 13 Udaya’s Questions
13-Udaya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Udaya’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
13-Udaya.htm.intro: Udaya asks about the source of suffering and how to be free from it. The Buddha explains that suffering arises from craving and attachment. The wise, understanding this, abandon craving and attain liberation. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus cross the flood.

14-Posala.htm.title: 14 Posāla’s Questions
14-Posala.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Posāla’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
14-Posala.htm.intro: Posāla asks about the source of suffering and how to be free from it. The Buddha explains that suffering arises from craving and attachment. The wise, understanding this, abandon craving and attain liberation. He teaches that one should be mindful, not cling to anything, and thus cross the flood.

15-Mogharaja.htm.title: 15 Mogharāja’s Questions
15-Mogharaja.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mogharāja’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
