15-Mogharaja.htm.intro: Mogharāja asks how, looking upon the world, one is not seen by the King of Death. The Buddha answers: look upon the world as empty, always mindful, and abandon the view of self. Thus one goes beyond death. Mogharāja and his students attain awakening.

16-Pingiya.htm.title: 16 Piṅgiya’s Questions
16-Pingiya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Piṅgiya’s Questions from The Way to the Beyond together with further information.
16-Pingiya.htm.intro: Piṅgiya, old and feeble, asks how to give up birth and old age. The Buddha teaches: seeing people struck down by forms and tormented by craving, the heedful one gives up form and craving, and does not come into existence again. Piṅgiya, reassured, declares his confidence in the Buddha and his intent on Nibbāna.

17-Verses-1.htm.title: Verses in Praise of the Way to the Beyond
17-Verses-1.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Verses in Praise of the Way to the Beyond together with further information.
17-Verses-1.htm.intro: This epilogue praises the Buddha and the sixteen students who asked him subtle questions. The Buddha answered each question truly, satisfying the brahmins. Those who practice in conformity with these teachings go beyond old age and death. The path is therefore called The Way to the Beyond.

18-Verses-2.htm.title: Verses on the Recital of the Way to the Beyond
18-Verses-2.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Verses on the Recital of the Way to the Beyond together with further information.
18-Verses-2.htm.intro: Piṅgiya recites the Way to the Beyond, praising the Buddha as the unstained, wise, and free one. Bāvari asks why he dwells apart from the Buddha; Piṅgiya replies that he sees the Buddha in his mind and is always joined to him. The Buddha tells him to release his confidence, and Piṅgiya declares his heart is intent on Nibbāna.

Light-of-Asia.title: The Light of Asia by Edwin Arnold
Light-of-Asia.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Light of Asia by Edwin Arnold together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Light-of-Asia.intro: Illustrations based on The Light of Asia, Edwin Arnold’s epic poem, which for many in the West was their first introduction to Buddhism. The Light of Asia is in the form of a narrative poem, the book describes the life and time of Prince Siddharta Gautama, who became the Buddha, the Awakened One. The book presents his life, character, and philosophy in a series of eight chapters. It is a free adaptation of the the Chinese translation of the Sanskrit Abhiniṣkramaṇasutta and the Lalitavistara Sūtra. The poetry is outstanding in its lyricism and beautiful language.
Light-of-Asia.keywords: Bodhisattva, Buddha, Biography, India, Poetry, Epic

01-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the First
01-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the First, together with further information.
01-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: Book the First details Prince Siddhartha’s miraculous birth and early life. Born to King Suddhodana and Queen Maya, he is prophesied to become a world savior. Though raised in royal luxury, Siddhartha displays profound wisdom and compassion, famously saving a swan from his cousin’s arrow. The chapter concludes with the Prince witnessing the cycle of suffering in nature, leading him to deep meditation on life’s hardships and the pursuit of a remedy.

02-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the Second
02-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the Second, together with further information.
02-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: Prince Siddhartha enters manhood surrounded by luxury in three palaces built to shield him from suffering. To prevent his departure, King Suddhodana arranges a festival where Siddhartha falls in love with Yasodhara. After winning her hand by defeating rivals in archery, swordsmanship, and horsemanship—notably taming a wild stallion—they marry. Siddhartha lives in a "pleasant prison" of delight, unaware of old age, pain, or death.

03-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the Third
03-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the Third, together with further information.
03-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: In Book the Third, Siddhartha ventures outside his secluded palace for the first time. Despite his father's attempts to hide the truth, the Prince encounters an old man, a diseased man, and a corpse. These sights shatter his illusions of eternal youth and joy. Realizing that all living beings are subject to age, sickness, and death, Siddhartha is overwhelmed by compassion and vows to find a way to end universal suffering.

04-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the Fourth
04-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the Fourth, together with further information.
04-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: In Book the Fourth, Yasodhara dreams of omens signaling Siddhartha's departure. Despite her grief, the Prince—driven by a "prodigious love" for all suffering beings—resolves to renounce his royalty. Under a full moon, he leaves his sleeping wife and child, slips past the magically silenced palace guards with his charioteer Channa, and crosses the river Anoma. There, he sheds his princely robes and hair, vowing to find the path to enlightenment.

05-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the Fifth
05-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the Fifth, together with further information.
05-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: In Book the Fifth, Siddhartha lives as an ascetic near Rajagriha, practicing intense meditation and seeking truth. He challenges the extreme self-mortification of fellow hermits, advocating for a balanced path. After comforting a grieving mother (Kisagotami) and saving a lamb from sacrifice, he intervenes at King Bimbisara's court. He preaches against animal sacrifice, emphasizing compassion for all life. Though the King offers his kingdom, Siddhartha continues his quest toward Gaya.

06-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the Sixth
06-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the Sixth, together with further information.
06-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: In Book the Sixth, Siddhartha nears the end of his six-year quest at Uruvela. After nearly dying from extreme fasting, he realizes the Middle Way—balancing austerity and health. He accepts life-restoring milk-rice from Sujata, regaining his strength. Siddhartha then seats himself beneath the Bodhi Tree, vowing not to rise until he attains Enlightenment. Despite the fierce temptations and terrors sent by Mara, he remains unshaken, eventually achieving perfect Awakening.

07-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the Seventh
07-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the Seventh, together with further information.
07-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: In Book the Seventh, word of Siddhartha’s enlightenment reaches Kapilavastu. King Suddhodana and Princess Yasodhara, who have spent seven years in mourning, are overjoyed. The King sends messengers to invite Siddhartha home; though they are converted by his teaching, the Buddha eventually returns. He enters his city as a humble mendicant. After an emotional reunion with Yasodhara and a conversation with his father about his spiritual lineage, the King and many Sakyas embrace his Law.

08-Light-of-Asia.htm.title: Book the Eighth
08-Light-of-Asia.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting the Light of Asia, Book the Eighth, together with further information.
08-Light-of-Asia.htm.intro: In the final book, Siddhartha delivers his great discourse at Kapilavastu. He teaches that neither prayer nor sacrifice brings deliverance, as each person creates their own prison or freedom through Karma. He outlines the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, leading to Nirvana—the end of suffering and rebirth. His father, Yasodhara, and Rahula all embrace the Law, finding peace in the Light of Asia before Siddhartha continues his forty-five-year mission.

Foremost-Monks.title: The Lives of the Foremost Monks
Foremost-Monks.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Lives of the Foremost Monks from The Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Foremost-Monks.intro: The posters illustrate the hagiographies of 41 prominent Bhikkhu disciples of Buddha Gotama, tracing their spiritual journeys across vast eons. Each account follows a consistent structural narrative, beginning with an aspiration in the past made during the era of a previous Buddha, such as Buddha Padumuttara. These individuals performed significant acts of merit and received prophecies confirming they would achieve the title of foremost in specific spiritual qualities. The chronicles then transition to their final existence, describing their noble births, their eventual renunciation of worldly life, and their attainment of Arahatship. Notable figures highlighted include Ven. Koṇḍañña, the first to realize the Four Truths, and Ven. Cūḷa Panthaka, who excelled in creating mind-made bodies despite initial struggles with memorization. Through these stories, the sources emphasize the themes of karmic continuity, the power of focused resolve, and the diverse paths to enlightenment within the Buddhist tradition.
Foremost-Monks.keywords: Buddha, Arahats, Great Disciples, Biography, India, Commentary, Pāḷi

toc.label: 11-12 Vens. Mahā Panthaka and Cūḷa Panthaka

01-Kondanna.htm.title: 1. Ven. Koṇḍañña
01-Kondanna.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Koṇḍañña from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
01-Kondanna.htm.intro: Over 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a wealthy householder made a lavish seven-day offering, aspiring to become the first disciple to comprehend the Four Noble Truths under a future Buddha. Buddha Padumuttara prophesied his fulfillment under Buddha Gotama. After multiple rebirths—including as Mahākāla 91 aeons ago during Buddha Vipassī's era, where he made vast offerings of first-harvest grain—he was born in his final existence as Koṇḍañña, a wealthy Brahmin. Recognizing Prince Siddhattha’s destiny, he became an ascetic and attended on him. Upon hearing the Buddha’s first sermon, Koṇḍañña became the first person to attain Stream-entry. The Buddha declared him foremost in seniority (Rattaññū). Koṇḍañña spent his final twelve years in solitary meditation in the Chaddanta forest before attaining Parinibbāna.

02-03-Sariputta-Moggallana.htm.title: 2-3. Ven. Sāriputta and Ven. Moggallāna
02-03-Sariputta-Moggallana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Sāriputta and Ven. Moggallāna from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
02-03-Sariputta-Moggallana.htm.intro: An immeasurable period and 100,000 aeons ago during the era of Buddha Anomadassī, two wealthy friends, Sarada and Sirivaḍḍhana, sought spiritual liberation. Sarada became a mountain hermit with 74,000 followers. Upon meeting Buddha Anomadassī, Sarada held a floral canopy over him for seven days in deep devotion. Inspired by the chief disciple Nisabha, Sarada aspired to become the right-hand chief disciple of a future Buddha. His friend Sirivaḍḍhana similarly aspired to become the left-hand chief disciple. In their final existence under Buddha Gotama, they were reborn as Upatissa (Sāriputta) and Kolita (Moggallāna). Upon hearing the Dhamma from Ven. Assaji, Upatissa attained Stream-entry and shared it with Kolita. They joined the Saṅgha, became Arahats, and were appointed the Buddha’s two Chief Disciples, foremost in wisdom (Paññā) and psychic powers (Iddhi).

04-Maha-Kassapa.htm.title: 4. Ven. Mahā Kassapa
04-Maha-Kassapa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Mahā Kassapa from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
04-Maha-Kassapa.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago during the era of Buddha Padumuttara, a wealthy householder named Videha observed the Buddha declare a monk foremost in ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). Inspired, he made grand offerings to the Buddha and Saṅgha for seven days and aspired to hold the same title under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment under Buddha Gotama. In his final existence, he was born as Pipphali Kassapa into a wealthy Brahmin family. Renouncing vast wealth, he and his wife Bhaddā Kāpilānī entered the homeless life. Upon meeting Buddha Gotama, Pipphali was ordained and attained Arahatship in just seven days. Highly revered for his strict austerity and solitary practice, the Buddha honored him by exchanging robes with him and declaring him foremost in ascetic practices.

05-Anuruddha.htm.title: 5. Ven. Anuruddha
05-Anuruddha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Anuruddha from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
05-Anuruddha.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago during the era of Buddha Padumuttara, an unnamed householder observed a monk declared foremost in the psychic power of the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu). Inspired, he offered seven days of lavish alms, lit thousands of lamps to cultivate the gift of light, and aspired to hold the same title under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment under Buddha Gotama. In a later life during Buddha Kassapa’s era, he continued offering thousands of oil lamps around a sacred shrine. In his final existence as Prince Anuruddha, cousin of Prince Siddhattha, he entered the Saṅgha and diligently practiced meditation. He attained Arahatship and was declared by Buddha Gotama as foremost in the Divine Eye.

06-Bhaddiya.htm.title: 6. Ven. Bhaddiya
06-Bhaddiya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Bhaddiya from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
06-Bhaddiya.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to be foremost among those of high family. Through many lives, he performed meritorious deeds including donating seats, covers, and lights. In his final life, he was a Sakyan prince who became king but renounced it to ordain. He became an Arahat in his first Rains Retreat, later declared foremost among monastics from noble families.

07-Lakundaka.htm.title: 7. Ven. Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya
07-Lakundaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
07-Lakundaka.htm.intro: He aspired for a sweet voice under Buddha Padumuttara. As the Cittapatta cuckoo, he offered a mango to Buddha Vipassī. Later as a master carpenter, he argued for the reduction in size of a relic shrine, resulting in his being reborn with a small body size. In his final life, though dwarfish, he became an Arahat through Ven. Sāriputta’s teaching and was declared foremost in sweet voice.

08-Pindola.htm.title: 8. Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja
08-Pindola.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
08-Pindola.htm.intro: As a lion, he honoured Buddha Padumuttara with floral seats for seven days. Later reborn as a merchant’s son, he aspired to be foremost in making fearless declarations. In his final life as a Brahmin teacher, he ordained and became an Arahat. He famously brought down a sandalwood bowl by psychic power and was declared foremost among those who roar like lions.

09-Punna.htm.title: 9. Ven. Mantāṇiputta Puṇṇa
09-Punna.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Mantāṇiputta Puṇṇa from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
09-Punna.htm.intro: As ascetic Gotama with 18,000 pupils, he honoured Buddha Padumuttara with floral seats. He aspired to be foremost in teaching Dhamma. In his final life, he was ordained by his uncle Ven. Koṇḍañña and became an Arahat. He taught 500 monks using the ten bases for speech. He was declared foremost among Dhamma teachers.

10-Kaccana.htm.title: 10. Ven. Kaccāyana
10-Kaccana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Kaccāyana from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
10-Kaccana.htm.intro: In Buddha Padumuttara’s time, he aspired to be foremost in elaborating brief teachings. He donated gold bricks to Buddha Kassapa’s shrine, wishing for golden complexion. In his final life as a Brahmin chaplain, he ordained with seven companions and became an Arahat. He was declared foremost in analytically explaining the Buddha’s concise teachings.

11-12-Panthakas.htm.title: 11-12. Ven. Mahā Panthaka and Ven. Cūḷa Panthaka
11-12-Panthakas.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Mahā Panthaka and Ven. Cūḷa Panthaka from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
11-12-Panthakas.htm.intro: Two brothers aspired under Buddha Padumuttara—the elder for formless absorption, the younger for mind-made images and form absorption. The younger one had been a learned monk who jeered a dullard, causing his own dullness in his last lfie. Buddha gave him a cloth to meditate on staining. He became an Arahat with psychic powers.

13-Subhuti.htm.title: 13. Ven. Subhūti
13-Subhuti.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Subhūti from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
13-Subhuti.htm.intro: As ascetic Nanda, he honoured Buddha Padumuttara with floral seats and aspired to twofold honour. In his final life, he built Jetavana monastery and ordained. He taught with Dhamma itself as objective, not referencing persons, and meditated on loving-kindness before alms. He was declared foremost in living free from defilements and worthy of gifts.

14-Khadiravaniya-Revata.htm.title: 14. Ven. Khadiravaniya Revata
14-Khadiravaniya-Revata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Khadiravaniya Revata from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
14-Khadiravaniya-Revata.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago during the era of Buddha Padumuttara, Revata was a boatman operating a ferry at Payāga port. When Buddha Padumuttara arrived with 100,000 monks, Revata built a decorated barge with a white canopy to ferry them across. Inspired upon witnessing a monk declared foremost among forest-dwellers, he offered grand alms for seven days and aspired to hold the same title under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment. In his final existence, Revata was born as the youngest brother of Venerable Sāriputta. Fleeing an arranged marriage after realizing the impermanence of physical beauty, he entered the Saṅgha and chose to live in a harsh acacia forest (khadira). Cultivating deep meditation, he attained Arahatship and was declared by Buddha Gotama as foremost among forest-dwellers (araññaka).

15-Kankha-Revata.htm.title: 15. Ven. Kaṅkhā Revata
15-Kankha-Revata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Kaṅkhā Revata from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
15-Kankha-Revata.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to be foremost in meditation. In his final life, he ordained and became an Arahat. He doubted even permitted things, like molasses with raw ingredients and sprouting beans, earning the name Revata the Doubter. But eventually he was declared foremost among meditating monastics.

16-Sona-Kolivisa.htm.title: 16. Ven. Soṇa Koḷivisa
16-Sona-Kolivisa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Soṇa Koḷivisa from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
16-Sona-Kolivisa.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a wealthy householder observed a monk declared foremost in exerting energy. Inspired, he offered grand seven-day alms and aspired for the same title under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment under Buddha Gotama. In his final existence, he was born into vast wealth with extraordinarily delicate feet that grew soft hair. After ordaining under Buddha Gotama, he practiced walking meditation so relentlessly that his feet bled, yet he failed to attain liberation. The Buddha visited him and taught the famous simile of the lute: just as strings sound best when properly tuned, energy must be balanced with tranquility. Applying this advice, Soṇa attained Arahatship and was declared foremost in energetic exertion.

17-Sona-Kutikanna.htm.title: 17. Ven. Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa
17-Sona-Kutikanna.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
17-Sona-Kutikanna.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a wealthy householder observed a monk declared foremost in clear and pleasant speech. Inspired, he offered grand alms for seven days and aspired to achieve the same distinction under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment. In his final existence, he was born into a wealthy family in Avantī and named Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa. Becoming a lay follower of Venerable Mahākaccāna, he waited three years for full ordination due to the scarcity of monks in Avantī. Sent to pay respects to Buddha Gotama in Sāvatthī, Soṇa recited the sixteen octets of the Aṭṭhakavagga with exceptional skill and clarity. Delighted, the Buddha declared him foremost in sweet, melodious recitation (kalyāṇa-vāk-karaṇa).

18-Sivali.htm.title: 18. Ven. Sīvali
18-Sivali.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Sīvali from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
18-Sivali.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to receive abundant gifts. As a villager, he offered honey and curds to Buddha Vipassī, wishing for great offerings. In his final life, he stayed seven years in his mother’s womb due to past evil deeds. After birth, he ordained and became an Arahat during the shaving of hair and beard. He was declared foremost in receiving material gains.

19-Vakkali.htm.title: 19. Ven. Vakkali
19-Vakkali.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Vakkali from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
19-Vakkali.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to be foremost in devotion. In his final life, he was captivated by the Buddha’s appearance and ordained to gaze at him constantly. The Buddha told him: He who sees the Dhamma sees me. Exiled from the Buddha’s presence, he despaired. The Buddha’s radiant vision and verse brought him to Arahatship. He was declared foremost in devoted faith.

20-21-Rahula-Ratthapala.htm.title: 20-21. Ven. Rāhula and Ven. Raṭṭhapāla
20-21-Rahula-Ratthapala.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Rāhula and Ven. Raṭṭhapāla from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
20-21-Rahula-Ratthapala.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, two wealthy friends practiced immense generosity. One was reborn as the Nāga King Pathavindhara. Seeing Buddha Padumuttara’s novice son Uparevata, he aspired to become the son of a future Buddha. His friend, aspiring to join the Saṅgha after a seven-day hunger strike, received a prophecy to be foremost amongst those with faith. In their final existence, Pathavindhara became Rāhula, Prince Siddhattha’s son, who was ordained as a novice, attained Arahatship, and was declared foremost in training (sikkhākāma). His friend became Raṭṭhapāla, who starved himself for seven days to gain parental consent to ordain, attained Arahatship, and was declared foremost among those who went forth through faith (saddhā-pabbajita).

22-Kundadhana.htm.title: 22. Ven. Kuṇḍadhāna
22-Kundadhana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Kuṇḍadhāna from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
22-Kundadhana.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to be first in drawing lots. In Buddha Kassapa’s time, as a Deva, he caused a schism between two monks by appearing as a woman. For this, he was reborn in lower worlds. In his final life, a woman’s apparition followed him, causing ridicule. Later he became an Arahat and was declared foremost in drawing lots.

23-Vangisa.htm.title: 23. Ven. Vaṅgīsa
23-Vangisa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Vaṅgīsa from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
23-Vangisa.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to quick wit. A Brahmin skilled in reading skulls, he couldn't tell the destiny of an Arahat. The Buddha taught him, and he ordained to learn the Buddha-mantra. Meditating on the body’s 32 parts, he became an Arahat. He composed spontaneous verses praising the Buddha and was declared foremost in poetic wit.

24-Upasena-Vangantaputta.htm.title: 24. Ven. Upasena Vaṅgantaputta
24-Upasena-Vangantaputta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Upasena Vaṅgantaputta from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
24-Upasena-Vangantaputta.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to win high esteem. He ordained and was reprimanded for admitting a disciple too early. Determined to earn praise, he meditated and became an Arahat. He gained 500 disciples through his forest-dwelling example. He was declared foremost in winning a following. He died serenely after a snake bite, showing no change in faculties.

25-Dabba.htm.title: 25. Ven. Dabba
25-Dabba.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Dabba from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
25-Dabba.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to arrange lodgings. In Buddha Kassapa’s time, he meditated on a mountain with six others. Born from a cremation pyre onto dabba grass, he ordained at seven. He became an Arahat during the head-shaving. He served the Saṅgha by allocating lodgings and alms. Slandered unjustly, he passed away in flames. He was later declared foremost in arranging dwellings.

26-Pilinda-Vaccha.htm.title: 26. Ven. Pilinda Vaccha
26-Pilinda-Vaccha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Pilinda Vaccha from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
26-Pilinda-Vaccha.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to be adored by Devas. A former Universal Monarch, he established people in morality, earning the Devas’ gratitude. In his final life, he was an ascetic whose powers failed after the Buddha’s arrival. He ordained, became an Arahat, but habitually called others outcaste, as a result of having 500 Brahmin births. He meant no harm. He was declared foremost in being adored by Devas.

27-Bahiya-Daruciriya.htm.title: 27. Ven. Bāhiya Dārucīriya
27-Bahiya-Daruciriya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Bāhiya Dārucīriya from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
27-Bahiya-Daruciriya.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a householder observed a monk declared foremost in swift realization. Inspired, he made grand seven-day offerings and aspired for the same distinction under a future Buddha, receiving a prophesy of fulfillment. In Buddha Kassapa’s era, he was one of seven monks who climbed a steep mountain to meditate unto Arahatship or until death. In his final existence, he became a shipwrecked merchant named Bāhiya, living in bark robes (Dārucīriya) and wrongly believed to be an Arahat. Admonished by a Deva, he rushed to Buddha Gotama, who delivered a brief teaching on sense perception (“in the seen, only the seen ...”). Bāhiya instantly attained Arahatship—the quickest awakening—and was declared foremost in swift intuition (khippābhiññā). Shortly after, he was tragically gored to death by a cow.

28-Kumara-Kassapa.htm.title: 28. Ven. Kumāra Kassapa
28-Kumara-Kassapa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Kumāra Kassapa from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
28-Kumara-Kassapa.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to be foremost in energetic Dhamma exposition. He meditated on a mountain with six others. Born from a nun’s womb, he was raised by King Pasenadi. Ordained as a novice, he became an Arahat. A Brahma gave him the Ant-hill riddles, which the Buddha explained as the body, defilements, and the path. He was declared foremost in energetic teaching.

29-Maha-Kotthita.htm.title: 29. Ven. Mahā Koṭṭhita
29-Maha-Kotthita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Mahā Koṭṭhita from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
29-Maha-Kotthita.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to the four analytical knowledges. In his final life, born a Brahmin in Sāvatthī, he mastered the Vedas, heard the Buddha’s discourse, and ordained. He meditated and became an Arahat endowed with analytical knowledge: of meanings, Dhamma, language, and inspiration. The Buddha declared him foremost among those possessing the four analytical knowledges.

30-Ananda.htm.title: 30. Ven. Ānanda
30-Ananda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Ānanda from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
30-Ananda.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a prince named Sumana observed a monk declared foremost among attendants. Inspired, he made a grand seven-day offering and aspired for the same position under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment under Buddha Gotama. In his final existence, he was born as Prince Ānanda, cousin to Prince Siddhattha. After ordaining, he was chosen as the Buddha's personal attendant, serving him with utter devotion under eight strict conditions. Ānanda memorized every discourse, earning five supreme titles, including foremost in great learning (bahussuta) and memory (sati). Though attaining Arahatship only after the Buddha's Parinibbāna, he recited all the Suttas at the First Buddhist Council.

31-Uruvela-Kassapa.htm.title: 31. Ven. Uruvelā Kassapa
31-Uruvela-Kassapa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Uruvelā Kassapa from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
31-Uruvela-Kassapa.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to a large following. As Prince Sumana, he served Buddha Phussa. In his final life he was a fire-worshipping ascetic with 500 disciples, he was converted by the Buddha through 3,500 miracles, including taming a Nāga. He and his 1,000 followers ordained and became Arahats. He was declared foremost in having a large following.

32-Kaludayi.htm.title: 32. Ven. Kāḷudāyī
32-Kaludayi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Kāḷudāyī from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
32-Kaludayi.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to arouse devotion in the Buddha’s kin. Born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, he was his childhood playmate. Sent as a royal messenger, he ordained and became an Arahat. He prepared the king’s heart with verses describing the season’s beauty, then invited the Buddha to Kapilavatthu. He was declared foremost in inspiring the Buddha’s relatives.

33-Bakula.htm.title: 33. Ven. Bākula
33-Bakula.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Bākula from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
33-Bakula.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a wealthy householder observed a monk declared foremost in good health and longevity. Inspired, he built a vast monastery, provided medicinal requisites to the Saṅgha for seven days, and aspired for the same distinction under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment. In Buddha Vipassī’s era, he again gained great merit by curing sick monks with herbal medicines. In his final existence, he was born into a rich family and swallowed by a giant fish as an infant, miraculously surviving unharmed due to his vast merit. Ordained by Buddha Gotama at age eighty, he attained Arahatship in seven days. Living to 160 without a single day of illness, he was declared foremost in good health (appābādha).

34-Sobhita.htm.title: 34. Ven. Sobhita
34-Sobhita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Sobhita from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
34-Sobhita.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to remember past lives. In his final life, he ordained and became an Arahat with a keen memory of past existences. He had been reborn in the unconscious form realm for 500 aeons, which he could not recall directly but deduced through wisdom. The Buddha declared him foremost among those who recollect their past lives.

35-Upali.htm.title: 35. Ven. Upāli
35-Upali.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Upāli from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
35-Upali.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to uphold the Vinaya. Born a barber, he ordained with six Sakyan princes. He became an Arahat and the foremost master of the monastic rules. He gave some key rulings: dreams do not count as faults; showing property as instructed is blameless. The Buddha endorsed his judgments. He was declared foremost in upholding the Vinaya discipline.

36-Nandaka.htm.title: 36. Ven. Nandaka
36-Nandaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Nandaka from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
36-Nandaka.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to be foremost in admonishing nuns. In his final life, he became an Arahat with past-life recall. He twice taught the same discourse to 500 nuns—first establishing them in Stream-entry, then making them Arahats. The Buddha praised his teaching as moon-like. He was declared foremost in instructing nuns.

37-Nanda.htm.title: 37. Ven. Nanda
37-Nanda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Nanda from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
37-Nanda.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to guard his sense faculties. In his final life as the Buddha’s cousin, he pined for his wife. The Buddha showed him celestial maidens, promising them if he practised. Mocked as mercenary, he felt remorse, guarded his senses strictly, and became an Arahat. He was declared foremost in sense-restraint.

38-Maha-Kappina.htm.title: 38. Ven. Mahā Kappina
38-Maha-Kappina.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Mahā Kappina from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
38-Maha-Kappina.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a householder observed a monk declared foremost in instructing and exhorting monks. Inspired, he made grand seven-day offerings and aspired for the same title under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment. In a subsequent life during Buddha Kassapa’s era, he led 500 weavers in building a grand monastery for the Saṅgha. In his final existence, he was King Mahā Kappina of Kukkutavatī. Upon hearing traders mention the Three Jewels, he immediately abdicated, leaving his kingdom alongside his 500 ministers to seek the Buddha. Intercepted by Buddha Gotama, Kappina and his retinue attained Arahatship upon hearing the Dhamma. The Buddha later declared him foremost in exhorting the monastics (bhikkhu-ovādaka).

39-Sagata.htm.title: 39. Ven. Sāgata
39-Sagata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Sāgata from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
39-Sagata.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to master the fire-element meditation. In his final life, he tamed a vicious serpent by producing greater flames. Later at Kosambī, he drank alcohol offered by lay supporters and became intoxicated. After recovering, he felt deep remorse, strove diligently, and became an Arahat. He was declared foremost in fire-element mastery.

40-Radha.htm.title: 40. Ven. Rādha
40-Radha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Rādha from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
40-Radha.htm.intro: Under Buddha Padumuttara, he aspired to inspire the Buddha’s teachings. Rejected for ordination due to old age, Ven. Sāriputta remembered his past kindness and admitted him. He became an Arahat through diligent practice. The Buddha praised his amenability to admonition and declared him foremost among those who inspire an amplification of discourses. His story illustrates gratitude’s power.

41-Mogharaja.htm.title: 41. Ven. Mogharāja
41-Mogharaja.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Mogharāja from the Great Chronicles together with further information.
41-Mogharaja.htm.intro: 100,000 aeons ago under Buddha Padumuttara, a wealthy householder observed a monk declared foremost among those who wear coarse or rough robes. Inspired, he made grand seven-day offerings to the Buddha and Saṅgha and aspired for the same title under a future Buddha, receiving a prophecy of fulfillment. In his final existence, he was born into a Brahmin family as Mogharāja. He initially studied as a student of the ascetic Bāvari. Going to Buddha Gotama alongside fifteen other Brahmin youths, Mogharāja asked his famous question regarding how to view the world to escape Death. Upon hearing the Buddha’s verse on observing the world as void (suñña), he instantly attained Arahatship. The Buddha later declared him foremost in wearing coarse robes (lūkha-cīvara-dhara).

Foremost-Nuns.title: The Lives of the Foremost Nuns
Foremost-Nuns.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Lives of the Foremost Nuns together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Foremost-Nuns.intro: These posters chronicle the extraordinary biographies and past-life aspirations of 13 prominent female disciples of the Buddha. Each narrative follows a similar spiritual trajectory, beginning with an ancient vow made before a previous Buddha to achieve a specific area of excellence. The text details the lives of figures such as Mahā Pajāpati Gotamī, the founder of the nuns’ order, and Ven. Khemā, celebrated for her profound wisdom. Other accounts, like those of Kisā Gotamī and Uppalavaṇṇā, emphasize how personal tragedies and karmic shifts eventually led them to spiritual awakening. These records highlight the diverse backgrounds of these women, ranging from royalty to laborers, and their shared dedication to the monastic life. The collection serves to document the foremost titles granted to these nuns for their unique mastery of the Buddhist path.
Foremost-Nuns.keywords: Buddha, Arahats, Great Disciples, Biography, India, Commentary, Pāḷi

01-Maha-Pajapati-Gotami.htm.title: 01 Ven. Mahā Pajāpatī Gotamī
01-Maha-Pajapati-Gotami.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Mahā Pajāpatī Gotamī based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
01-Maha-Pajapati-Gotami.htm.intro: Mahā Pajāpati Gotamī’s spiritual journey began during the era of Buddha Padumuttara, where she aspired to become the foremost senior nun. Across past existences—notably as a head water-carrier and a weaver—she led others in performing meritorious deeds, such as providing shelter and fine robes to Paccekabuddhas. In her final rebirth as a Sakyan princess, she married King Suddhodana and became Buddha Gotama’s stepmother and devoted nurse after Queen Mahā Māyā’s death. Following Suddhodana’s passing, she led 500 Sakyan women on foot to Vesālī to request ordination. Supported by Venerable Ānanda, the Buddha admitted her through the eight principal vows, establishing the female Saṅgha. She subsequently attained Arahatship and was declared foremost among nuns of long standing.

02-Khema.htm.title: 02 Ven. Khemā
02-Khema.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Khemā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
02-Khema.htm.intro: Aspiring to be foremost in wisdom under Buddha Padumuttara, she was reborn as Princess Samaṇī in Buddha Kassapa’s time, she remained chaste, memorized the Mahā-nidāna-sutta, and was later reborn as Queen Khemā. Fearful the Buddha would criticize her beauty, she avoided him until King Bimbisāra’s plan lured her to his monastery. The Buddha used his powers to age a beautiful maiden before her, sparking spiritual urgency. He then taught the very discourse she had memorized in a past life, leading her to Stream-entry. She renounced her queenship, became a nun, and through meditating on a lamp’s flame, she attained full Awakening. Later, she famously taught King Pasenadi that the Buddha does not answer questions about a sentient being after death because he has eradicated all clinging to the aggregates that define such a concept.

03-Uppalavanna.htm.title: 03 Ven. Uppalavaṇṇā
03-Uppalavanna.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Uppalavaṇṇā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
03-Uppalavanna.htm.intro: Aspiring to be foremost in supernormal powers under Buddha Padumuttara, she was reborn through many existences, including as Princess Samaṇaguttā, one of King Kikī’s seven daughters. In one life, as a farmer’s daughter, she offered popcorn and a lotus flower to a Paccekabuddha but wavered, leading to mixed fortunes. She was later born from a lotus as Queen Padumāvatī, whose every step produced a lotus flower. After her 500 sons became Paccekabuddhas and she passed away, she was reborn as a farmhand who offered meals to them. She finally was born in her last life as Uppalavaṇṇā, who, due to her past aspiration and extensive merit, would become the foremost female monastic in supernormal powers under Buddha Gotama.

04-Patacara.htm.title: 04 Ven. Paṭācārā
04-Patacara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Paṭācārā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
04-Patacara.htm.intro: In the time of Buddha Padumuttara, she aspired to be foremost in Vinaya learning. She was later born as Princess Bhikkhunī, the third daughter of King Kikī, and lived a chaste life. In her final life as a rich man’s daughter in Sāvatthī, a series of catastrophes struck: her husband died of a snakebite, her infant was carried off by a hawk, her elder son drowned, and her parents’ house collapsed, killing her entire family. Grief-stricken and naked, she wandered madly until the Buddha calmed her, teaching about the endless tears shed in Saṁsāra. She attained Stream-entry and became a nun. Later, while washing her feet and observing the flow of water, she gained deep insight into impermanence and, with the Buddha’s guidance, became an Arahat, earning her title as foremost in Vinaya knowledge.

05-Dhammadinna.htm.title: 05 Ven. Dhammadinnā
05-Dhammadinna.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Dhammadinnā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
05-Dhammadinna.htm.intro: Born poor in the time of Buddha Padumuttara, she offered her only cake to Ven. Sujāta, which led to her becoming a rich man’s daughter-in-law and aspiring to be foremost in expounding the Dhamma. She was later born as Princess Sudhammā, the sixth daughter of King Kikī. In her final life, she was the wife of Visākha in Rājagaha. When her husband became a Non-Returner and lived chastely, she not only understood but chose to become a nun herself. She swiftly became an Arahat. She then gave a profound Dhamma discourse to her former husband, Visākha, on topics including Nibbāna, which the Buddha later fully endorsed, declaring that he would have answered the same way, thus earning her the title of foremost in teaching the Dhamma.

06-Nanda.htm.title: 06 Ven. Nandā
06-Nanda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Nandā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
06-Nanda.htm.intro: She first aspired to be foremost in absorption under Buddha Padumuttara. Born as the beautiful Sakyan Princess Janapadakalyāṇī in her last life, she avoided the Buddha fearing criticism of her looks. He created a vision of surpassing beauty that humbled her. Hearing verses on the body’s loathsomeness and the Discourse about Victory, she meditated diligently and became an Arahat. The Buddha declared her the foremost nun in enjoying meditative absorption.

07-Sona.htm.title: 07 Ven. Soṇā
07-Sona.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Soṇā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
07-Sona.htm.intro: Her quest for earnest endeavour began with Buddha Padumuttara. Mother of ten ungrateful children, she became a nun in her old age but was ridiculed by her seniors and mocked by her offspring. This spurred her to unrelenting effort—meditating ceaselessly while holding a post or tree at night. The Buddha praised her diligence, and she attained Arahatship, even miraculously heating water without fire. She was declared foremost in earnest effort.

08-Sakula.htm.title: 08 Ven. Sakulā
08-Sakula.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Sakulā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
08-Sakula.htm.intro: She resolved to master the divine eye during Buddha Padumuttara’s time. As Princess Nandā, she was the Buddha’s half-sister. In Buddha Kassapa’s age, she was an ascetic who offered lights at his relic shrine. Reborn in Sāvatthī, she became a lay disciple, then a nun. Diligent in practice, she attained Arahatship and excelled in remembering past existences, earning the foremost title for the divine eye.

09-Bhadda-Kundalakesa.htm.title: 09 Ven. Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā
09-Bhadda-Kundalakesa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
09-Bhadda-Kundalakesa.htm.intro: During Buddha Padumuttara’s time, she aspired to be the quickest to attain Awakening. She was later born as Princess Bhikkhadāyikā, the fourth daughter of King Kikī. In her final life, she was a wealthy man’s daughter in Rājagaha who fell for the notorious robber Sattuka. After she saved him from execution and married him, he tried to murder her for her jewels, but she outwitted him and pushed him off a cliff. Traumatized, she became an ascetic named Kuṇḍalakesā. She became a renowned debater, challenging all comers. At Sāvatthī, she was defeated by a single question from Ven. Sāriputta. She then went to the Buddha, who spoke a single verse, upon hearing which she immediately became an Arahat, fulfilling her aspiration for the quickest insight.

10-Bhadda-Kapilani.htm.title: 10 Ven. Bhaddā Kāpilānī
10-Bhadda-Kapilani.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Bhaddā Kāpilānī based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
10-Bhadda-Kapilani.htm.intro: Born as a rich man’s wife in the time of Buddha Padumuttara, she aspired to be foremost in recalling past lives. In one existence, she committed a fault by throwing away a Paccekabuddha’s alms food out of anger but made amends by offering the finest food, wishing for a radiant complexion. Her life is closely linked to that of her husband, Pippali, who later became Ven. Mahā Kassapa. They both agreed to lead a celibate life together. After her parents died and arranged a lavish funeral pyre, the couple saw the impermanence of wealth and beauty and decided to renounce the world. For five years she lived as a wanderer before both she and her husband became disciples of the Buddha, she as a nun. She thus became the foremost nun in the supernormal power of remembering past existences.

11-Bhadda-Kaccana.htm.title: 11 Ven. Bhaddā Kaccānā
11-Bhadda-Kaccana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Bhaddā Kaccānā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
11-Bhadda-Kaccana.htm.intro: Her aspiration for great supernormal powers began under Buddha Padumuttara. Born as Princess Yasodharā, she married Prince Siddhattha and bore Rāhula. After his awakening, she became a nun with Mahā Pajāpati Gotamī. She attained Arahatship and could recall past lives over an entire incalculable period—a feat matched by only three others. The Buddha declared her foremost in supernormal powers.

12-Kisa-Gotami.htm.title: 12 Ven. Kisā Gotamī
12-Kisa-Gotami.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Kisā Gotamī based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
12-Kisa-Gotami.htm.intro: In the time of Buddha Padumuttara, she aspired to be foremost in wearing coarse robes. She was later born as Princess Dhammā, the fifth daughter of King Kikī. In her final life, born into poverty and thus known as Kisā (lean) Gotamī, she married a rich man’s son. Her status was confirmed when she gave birth to a son, but the child died young. Grief-stricken, she carried the corpse, begging for medicine. The Buddha instructed her to find mustard seed from a house where no one had ever died. Her search revealed that death is universal. She realized the truth, left her child’s body, and attained Stream-entry. After becoming a nun, she meditated on a flickering lamp, seeing the rise and fall of all phenomena, and with the Buddha’s guidance, became an Arahat, earning her title as foremost in wearing coarse robes.

13-Singalakamata.htm.title: 13 Ven. Siṅgālakamātā
13-Singalakamata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ven. Siṅgālakamātā based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
13-Singalakamata.htm.intro: She resolved to be foremost in faith while a nun under Buddha Padumuttara, after hearing a discourse on devotion. Born in Rājagaha, she was the mother of Siṅgālaka, whom the Buddha instructed on worshipping directions. She attained Stream-entry from that discourse and became a nun. Her faith in the Buddha was exceptionally strong, and through conviction she attained Arahatship. The Buddha named her foremost among nuns of strong faith.

Foremost-Laymen.title: The Lives of the Foremost Laymen
Foremost-Laymen.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters depicitng The Lives of the Foremost Laymen together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Foremost-Laymen.intro: These sources detail the lives and spiritual accomplishments of prominent male lay disciples of Buddha Gotama, highlighting how their ancient aspirations were fulfilled in their final existences. Figures like Anāthapiṇḍika and Citta are celebrated for their unparalleled generosity and mastery of the Dhamma, respectively, with Citta reaching the high stage of a Non-returner. The texts describe various foremost titles bestowed by the Buddha, such as Tapussa and Bhallika being the first to take refuge, and Hatthaka Āḷavaka excelling in kindness. Ugga and Uggata are noted for their extraordinary qualities, including the selfless act of relinquishing their wives to new marriages after attaining spiritual milestones. Collectively, the narratives emphasize that steadfast faith, virtuous conduct, and liberal giving lead to profound wisdom and fortunate rebirths. This hagiographic overview serves to illustrate the diverse paths to awakening available to those living outside the monastic order.
Foremost-Laymen.keywords: Buddha, Arahats, Great Disciples, Biography, India, Commentary, Pāḷi

01-Tapussa-and-Bhallika.htm.title: 01 Tapussa and Bhallika
01-Tapussa-and-Bhallika.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Tapussa and Bhallika based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
01-Tapussa-and-Bhallika.htm.intro: Brothers Tapussa and Bhallika aspired across many lifetimes to become the Buddha’s first lay disciples. Guided by a Deva who was once their mother, they encountered Buddha Gotama shortly after his Awakening. They offered him choice preserved food, which he accepted using granite bowls provided by the Four Great Kings. Consequently, they became the first disciples to take refuge, successfully fulfilling their ancient and meritorious vow to serve him faithfully.

02-Anathapindika.htm.title: 02 Anāthapiṇḍika
02-Anathapindika.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Anāthapiṇḍika based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
02-Anathapindika.htm.intro: Anāthapiṇḍika, who aspired under Buddha Padumuttara to be the foremost lay donor, was a wealthy merchant of Sāvatthī. Upon meeting the Buddha in Rājagaha, he became a Stream-enterer and invited him to Sāvatthī. He spent vast sums on transit monasteries and then purchased Prince Jeta's park, covering it with gold coins, to build the famous Jetavana monastery at a total cost of 540 million. His daily generosity to the Saṅgha was unparalleled. On his deathbed, Ven. Sāriputta gave him a profound discourse on non-attachment to the six sense spheres and all phenomena, which moved him to tears. He passed away and was reborn in the Tusita Realm, later visiting the Buddha as a Deva to praise the Jetavana monastery and Ven. Sāriputta.

03-Citta.htm.title: 03 Citta the Householder
03-Citta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Citta the Householder based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
03-Citta.htm.intro: Citta, who aspired in a past life to be a foremost lay exponent of the Dhamma, was born in Macchikāsaṇḍa amidst a shower of flowers. He became a Non-returner after hearing a discourse from Ven. Mahānāma. As a supporter of the Ambāṭaka monastery, he was known for his wisdom, engaging in profound Dhamma discussions with monastics like Ven. Isidatta and witnessing miracles by Ven. Mahaka. He once led a large pilgrimage of 2,000 disciples to see the Buddha in Sāvatthī, receiving divine hospitality. On his deathbed, he admonished relatives to have perfect confidence in the Three Treasures and to be generous. Being a Non-returner, he was reborn in a Brahma realm of the Pure Abodes.

04-Hatthaka-Alavaka.htm.title: 04 Hatthaka Āḷavaka
04-Hatthaka-Alavaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Hatthaka Āḷavaka based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
04-Hatthaka-Alavaka.htm.intro: Reborn as Prince Āḷavaka, Hatthaka was saved from sacrifice after the Buddha converted the Yakkha Āḷavaka. Handed from the Yakkha to the Buddha, he earned the name Hatthaka. He eventually became an intelligent Non-returner and mastered the Tipiṭaka. For his mastery of the four ways of kind treatment—generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—the Buddha declared him the foremost among all lay disciples.

05-Mahanama.htm.title: 05 Mahānāma The Sakyan Prince
05-Mahanama.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mahānāma based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
05-Mahanama.htm.intro: Mahānāma, a Sakyan Prince, once aspired to become a leading lay disciple in providing exquisite offerings. In his final life, he generously supported the Buddha and the Sangha with delicious alms and medicines for a full year following their hardships. Despite facing monastic interference, his unwavering dedication to providing high-quality requisites became legendary. Consequently, the Buddha declared him the foremost lay disciple for offering superior alms food and medicinal requisites.

06-Ugga.htm.title: 06 Ugga the Householder
06-Ugga.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ugga based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
06-Ugga.htm.intro: Ugga of Vesālī was a wealthy householder who aspired to be the foremost giver of delightful things. After attaining Non-returning status through the Buddha’s direct and compassionate teaching, he practiced extraordinary generosity, offering his most cherished possessions to the Saṅgha. Renowned for eight marvellous qualities, including deep faith and profound detachment, Ugga was named the premier lay disciple for giving. He was ultimately reborn in the five Pure Abodes.

07-Uggata.htm.title: 07 Uggata the Householder
07-Uggata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Uggata based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
07-Uggata.htm.intro: Uggata, a wealthy householder, met Buddha Gotama during a drunken spree. Instantly sobered, he became a Non-returner after hearing a discourse. He transformed his life, embracing celibacy and profound generosity. Renowned for eight marvellous qualities, Uggata attended to the Sangha without discrimination, treating all monastics with equal reverence regardless of their morality. The Buddha declared him the foremost lay disciple for his impartial devotion and dedicated service to the Sangha.

08-Surambattha.htm.title: 08 Sūrambaṭṭha the Householder
08-Surambattha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sūrambaṭṭha based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
08-Surambattha.htm.intro: After making an aspiration in a past life, Sūrambaṭṭha attained Stream-entry during his final existence after receiving a discourse from Buddha Gotama. Seeking to shake his newly attained faith, Māra disguised himself as the Buddha and falsely claimed that some aggregates are permanent. Recognising the ruse, Sūrambaṭṭha sternly rebuked Māra, asserting that nothing could shake his conviction. Consequently, the Buddha declared him the foremost lay disciple for unshakeable conviction.

09-Jivaka.htm.title: 09 Jīvaka Komārabhacca
09-Jivaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Jīvaka Komārabhacca based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
09-Jivaka.htm.intro: Born to a courtesan and discarded on a rubbish heap, Jīvaka was rescued by Prince Abhaya. He mastered medicine in Takkasilā, eventually becoming a renowned royal physician. Jīvaka famously cured the Buddha and donated his own Mango Grove monastery to the Saṅgha. Due to his extraordinary faith, the Buddha declared him the foremost lay disciple for personal devotion, fulfilling an ancient aspiration.

10-Nakulapitu.htm.title: 10 Nakulapitu the Householder
10-Nakulapitu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Nakulapitu based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
10-Nakulapitu.htm.intro: Nakulapitu aspired to become the Buddha's closest lay disciple aeons ago. In his final birth, he and his wife Nakulamātu instantly recognized Buddha Gotama as their son, having been his parents or relatives for thousands of past lives. After receiving specific teachings on spiritual harmony and lifelong loyalty, they attained Stream-entry. The Buddha later declared Nakulapitu foremost among lay disciples for his unique intimacy.

Foremost-Laywomen.title: The Lives of the Foremost Laywomen
Foremost-Laywomen.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Lives of the Foremost Laywomen together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Foremost-Laywomen.intro: These posters detail the lives and spiritual milestones of several prominent female lay disciples during the era of Buddha Gotama. The texts recount the histories of women like Sujātā, the first to take refuge, and Visākhā, the foremost donor who constructed the Pubbārāma monastery. Each narrative emphasizes the connection between past-life aspirations and the ripening of merit in their final existence. Highlighting diverse paths to enlightenment, the sources describe Kāḷī’s intuitive devotion, Khujjuttarā’s vast learning, and Sāmāvatī’s mastery of loving-kindness. These accounts illustrate how these women overcame social obstacles and personal tragedies to achieve the status of Stream-entry. Ultimately, the collection serves to document the foremost titles bestowed upon these disciples by the Buddha for their exceptional virtues and contributions to the teaching.
Foremost-Laywomen.keywords: Buddha, Arahats, Great Disciples, Biography, India, Commentary, Pāḷi

toc.label: 01 Sujātā, Wife of the Householder of Bārāṇasī

01-Sujata.htm.title: 01 Sujātā, Wife of the Householder of Bārāṇasī
01-Sujata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sujātā, Wife of the Householder of Bārāṇasīfrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
01-Sujata.htm.intro: Sujātā, daughter of Seniya, aspired under Buddha Padumuttara to become the foremost female lay disciple. Reborn near Uruvelā in her last existence, she offered specially prepared divine milk rice to the Bodhisatta before his Awakening. After her son Yasa became an Arahat, Sujātā successfully attained fruition of Stream-entry knowledge. The Buddha declared her the foremost female lay disciple for being the earliest established in the refuges, fulfilling her ancient aspiration.

02-Visakha.htm.title: 02 Visākhā, Builder of Pubbārāma Monastery
02-Visakha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Visākhā, Builder of Pubbārāma Monasteryfrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
02-Visakha.htm.intro: Visākhā, who aspired under Buddha Padumuttara to be a foremost lay donor, was born into a family of great merit in Bhaddiya. At age seven, she attained Stream-entry after hearing the Buddha teach. She later married Puṇṇavaḍḍhana in Sāvatthī, where her wisdom and virtue were so profound that she converted her father-in-law, Migāra, who then called her "mother." Her life was marked by unparalleled generosity; she famously sold her invaluable bridal gown for 90 million to fund the construction of the Pubbārāma (Eastern Monastery) for the Saṅgha, with Ven. Moggallāna supervising the project. The donation ceremony lasted four months and cost another 90 million. Renowned for her strength, beauty, and 8,000 great-grandchildren, she earned the Buddha's declaration as the foremost female lay disciple in generosity.

03-04-Khujjuttara-Samavati.htm.title: 03-04 Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī
03-04-Khujjuttara-Samavati.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatīfrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
03-04-Khujjuttara-Samavati.htm.intro: Khujjuttarā, who aspired to be foremost in learning, and Sāmāvatī, who aspired to be foremost in loving-kindness, were born as a humpbacked slave and a queen, respectively. Khujjuttarā, while buying flowers for Queen Sāmāvatī, heard the Buddha teach and became a Stream-enterer. She then taught the Dhamma to Sāmāvatī and her 500 ladies-in-waiting, who all attained Stream-entry. Sāmāvatī became renowned for her loving-kindness, which protected her from King Udena's murderous rage, instigated by the jealous Queen Māgaṇḍiyā. Ultimately, Māgaṇḍiyā succeeded in having Sāmāvatī and her retinue burnt alive as a result of their past evil deed. In recognition of their virtues, the Buddha later declared Khujjuttarā as the foremost female lay disciple in learning and Sāmāvatī as the foremost in dwelling in loving-kindness.

05-Uttara-Nandamata.htm.title: 05 Uttarā Nandamātā
05-Uttara-Nandamata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Uttarā Nandamātāfrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
05-Uttara-Nandamata.htm.intro: Uttarā, the daughter of the wealthy treasurer Puṇṇasīha, was a devout Stream-enterer. Married to a non-believer, she hired the courtesan Sirimā to attend to her husband so she could freely practice her Uposatha precepts for fifteen days. Jealous, Sirimā poured boiling oil on Uttarā, but her deep mettā-jhāna protected her from any harm. After Sirimā’s repentance and subsequent Stream-entry, the Buddha declared Uttarā the foremost female lay disciple in jhāna.

06-Suppavasa.htm.title: 06 Princess Suppavāsā the Koliyan
06-Suppavasa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Princess Suppavāsā the Koliyanfrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
06-Suppavasa.htm.intro: During the time of Buddha Padumuttara, a woman aspired to become the foremost female lay disciple in offering superior articles. Reborn later as Princess Suppavāsā in Koliya, she attained Stream-entry and became the mother of Sīvali. She famously offered choicest food to the Buddha and his Saṅgha. For her dedication, the Buddha declared her the foremost among his female lay disciples who make gifts of the choicest quality.

07-Suppiya.htm.title: 07 Suppiyā, Who Attended the Sick
07-Suppiya.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Suppiyā, Who Attended the Sickfrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
07-Suppiya.htm.intro: After aspiring under Buddha Padumuttara, Suppiyā was reborn in Bārāṇasī. As a devoted lay disciple, she promised meat soup to an ailing monk. Finding none for sale, she sacrificed flesh from her own thigh to fulfill her promise. When she met Buddha Gotama, her wound miraculously healed. The Buddha subsequently prohibited monastics from consuming human flesh and named Suppiyā the foremost female lay disciple for looking after the sick monastics.

08-Katiyani.htm.title: 08 Kātiyānī of Unshakable Conviction
08-Katiyani.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Kātiyānī of Unshakable Convictionfrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
08-Katiyani.htm.intro: After aspiring under Buddha Padumuttara, Kātiyānī was reborn during Buddha Gotama’s era. While listening to Ven. Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa’s teaching, she refused to leave even as robbers looted her home, prioritizing the Dhamma over material wealth. This devotion moved the robber chief and five hundred men to seek ordination into the Saṅgha. Kātiyānī attained Stream-entry, and the Buddha declared her the foremost female lay disciple for having unshakable conviction in the teaching.

09-Nakulamata.htm.title: 09 Nakulamātu
09-Nakulamata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Nakulamātufrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
09-Nakulamata.htm.intro: After an ancient aspiration under Buddha Padumuttara, Nakulapitu and Nakulamātu encountered Buddha Gotama in the Bhesakaḷā Forest. Recognizing him as their beloved son from many past lives, they attained Stream-entry knowledge. Desiring to remain together throughout future existences, the Buddha advised they maintain equal conviction, morality, generosity, and intelligence. Consequently, Nakulamātu was declared the foremost among female lay disciples who are close to the Buddha.

10-Kali.htm.title: 10 Kāḷī, the Disciple of Kuraraghara
10-Kali.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Kāḷī, the Disciple of Kuraragharafrom the Great Chronicles together with further information.
10-Kali.htm.intro: Kāḷī of Kuraraghara aspired during Buddha Padumuttara’s era to become the foremost disciple devoted through hearsay. Reborn in Rājagaha under Buddha Gotama, she overheard devas Sātāgiri and Hemavata praising the Triple Gem. Instilled with profound devotion, she attained Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) before even meeting the Buddha. Consequently, Buddha Gotama declared her the foremost female lay disciple among those devoted through hearing, fulfilling her ancient aspiration.

Four-Rich-Men.title: Four Rich Men with Inexhaustible Resources
Four-Rich-Men.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from Rich Men with Inexhaustible Resources together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Four-Rich-Men.intro: These posters provide detailed hagiographies of four exceptionally wealthy householders—Jotika, Meṇḍaka, Jaṭila, and Kāḷavaḷiya—whose lives demonstrate the Buddhist principle of karmic fruition. Each narrative spans multiple incarnations, tracing how extraordinary acts of generosity performed toward Buddhas or Paccekabuddhas in past lives resulted in miraculous prosperity and supernatural abundance in their final existences. The texts describe spectacular phenomena, such as self-arising mansions and inexhaustible resources, while emphasizing that such material wealth is ultimately secondary to spiritual awakening. Most of these figures eventually renounce their immense fortunes to join the monastic order and achieve Arhatship. Collectively, the chronicles serve as moral instructional tools, illustrating that sincere devotion and the abandonment of craving are the true paths to liberation.
Four-Rich-Men.keywords: Buddha, Arahats, Great Disciples, Biography, India, Commentary, Pāḷi

01-Jotika-the-Householder.htm.title: 01 Jotika, the Rich Householder
01-Jotika-the-Householder.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Jotika, the Rich Householder based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
01-Jotika-the-Householder.htm.intro: In a past life during Buddha Vipassī’s era, Aparājita built a grand, jewel-encrusted monastery with a perfumed chamber for the Buddha. Unattached to his immense wealth, he invited visitors to freely collect the scattered gems. In his final life as Jotika, his extraordinary past merit yielded an automatic, miraculous palace that materialized from the earth. He eventually renounced all material splendor to become an Arahat under Gautama Buddha.

02-Mendaka-the-Householder.htm.title: 02 Meṇḍaka, the Householder
02-Mendaka-the-Householder.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Meṇḍaka, the Householder based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
02-Mendaka-the-Householder.htm.intro: In a past life, Meṇḍaka built a magnificent golden-adorned portico with goat statues for Buddha Vipassī. Later, during a severe famine in Bārāṇasī, his family selflessly offered their final meal to a Paccekabuddha, magically refilling their grain stores. Reborn during Gautama Buddha's era, his immense merit manifested as 14 acres of solid-gold goat statues that miraculously produced endless resources, leading him and his household to stream-entry and spiritual realization.

03-Jatila-the-Treasurer.htm.title: 03 Jaṭila, the Treasurer
03-Jatila-the-Treasurer.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Jaṭila, the Treasurer based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhastogether with further information.
03-Jatila-the-Treasurer.htm.intro: After making gold flower offerings to atone for a past insult to the Buddha, Jaṭila was reborn with tremendous merit. Abandoned as a baby in a floating pot, he was raised by a merchant whose unsellable goods he sold in a single day. Upon marrying, an 80-cubit golden hill appeared behind his house. After verifying his youngest son shared his merit to inherit it, Jaṭila ordained and achieved Arahatship within days.

04-Kalavaliya-the-Treasurer.htm.title: 04 Kāḷavaḷiya, a Rich Man
04-Kalavaliya-the-Treasurer.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Kāḷavaḷiya, a Rich Man based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
04-Kalavaliya-the-Treasurer.htm.intro: Living in extreme poverty, Kāḷavaḷiya and his wife offered their only food—a bowl of sour gruel—to Ven. Mahā Kassapa. Recognizing their total sacrifice, the Buddha prophesied rapid wealth. That night, his courageous wife braved dangerous spirits outside the city to deliver the king's meal to a criminal, uncovering two hidden pots of gold along the way. Appointed royal treasurer for his newfound fortune, Kāḷavaḷiya’s story concludes the Great Chronicles.

Dhammapada.title:
Stories from the Dhammapada Commentary
(chapters 1-13 only)
Dhammapada.summary:
Illustrated Stories from the Dhammapada Commentary, which relates many events from the life of the Buddha and his disciples. 
Source of the Stories
Dhammapada.intro: These storybooks illustrate the Dhammapada Commentary, which is a large collection of stories that provide the historical and situational context for each verse in the Dhammapada. Tradition attributes the compilation of the commentary to the 5th-century scholar Buddhaghosa. It explains the specific person, place, and event that prompted the Buddha to speak each verse. It contains over 300 stories detailing the lives, triumphs, and struggles of monks, laypeople, and historical figures during the Buddha’s time. It is a repository of knowledge about the people who were around the Buddha while he was alive; and it also contains a plethora of information about former Buddhas and the previous lives of the Buddha and his disciples.
Dhammapada.keywords: Buddha, Arahats, Great Disciples, Biography, India, Commentary, Pāḷi

01-01.htm.title: 1.1 The Story about the Elder Cakkhupāla
01-01.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about the Elder Cakkhupāla together with further information.
01-01.htm.intro:
The bhikkhu Cakkhupāla determined to fulfil his practice even at the cost of his eyes, and eventually he attained Awakening; the Buddha explained the deed he did in the past which caused his loss of sight in the present, and he summarised the teaching with a verse.
Cast: Mahā Suvaṇṇa, Cakkhupāla (Mahā Pāla, aka Pālita), Culla Pāla, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā
Keywords: Rich Men, Devatās, Determination, Sakka, Amanussa, Doctors, Past Lives

01-02.htm.title: 1.2 The Story about Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī
01-02.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī together with further information.
01-02.htm.intro:
Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, the son of the miser Adinnapubbaka, died after paying his respects to the Buddha and was reborn in heaven; later he came and showed his father the reward of good deeds, and his father was converted; the Buddha explained the matter with a verse.
Keywords: Faith, Merit, Refuge, Precepts, Devaputtas, Past Lives

01-03.htm.title: 1.3 The Story about the Elder Thulla Tissa
01-03.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about the Elder Thulla Tissa together with further information.
01-03.htm.intro:
Tissa, an older relative of the Buddha ordained and was vain and obstinate; the Buddha showed how he was also obstinate in a previous life and almost lost his head, and then he taught the bhikkhus with some verses.
Cast: Thulla Tissa, Devala, Nārada, Bhaggava
Keywords: Vanity, Obstinacy, Past Lives, Bodhisatta, Ascetics

01-04.htm.title: 1.4 The Story about the Yakkhinī Kāḷi
01-04.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about the Yakkhinī Kāḷi together with further information.
01-04.htm.intro:
A barren woman brings home a young woman for her husband, but every time the young wife conceives the barren wife contrives an abortion; through life after life they consume each other’s children, until brought to the Buddha, who taught them with a verse.
Cast: The barren woman, the second wife and their further incarnations are never named, Elder Ānanda, Deva Sumana
Keywords: Revenge, Reconciliation, Marriages, Joint Rebirth, Yakkhinīs

01-05.htm.title: 1.5 The Story about Those from Kosambī
01-05.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about Those from Kosambī together with further information.
01-05.htm.intro:
The followers of two bhikkhus of Kosambī fell into a dispute and despite the Buddha’s admonitions, refused to be reconciled; the Buddha went forth to Pārileyyaka forest and was served by an elephant and a monkey; meanwhile the lay people refused to attend on the bhikkhus till they came to their senses; eventually they asked for forgiveness and the Buddha taught them with a verse.
Cast: Kosambī bhikkhus, Pārileyyaka the elephant, Elder Ānanda, Brahmadatta, Dīghati Kosala, Prince Dīghāvu, Bālaka, Elder Bhagu, Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā
Keywords: Anger, Schism, Concord, Solitariness, Elephants, Monkeys, Past Lives

01-06.htm.title: 1.6 The Story about Culla Kāḷa and Mahā Kāḷa
01-06.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about Culla Kāḷa and Mahā Kāḷatogether with further information.
01-06.htm.intro:
Two brothers, Culla Kāḷa and Mahā Kāḷa, ordained and one went to a cemetery to practice and soon overcame the defilements and attained Awakening; the other, however, did not work at his practice and was soon enticed back to the lay life by his former wives; the Buddha spoke some verses about these two.
Cast: Culla Kāḷa, Majjhima Kāḷa, Mahā Kāḷa
Keywords: Chief Disciples, Listening to Dhamma, Impermanence, Cemeteries, Temptation

01-07.htm.title: 1.7 The Story about Devadatta
01-07.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about Devadatta together with further information.
01-07.htm.intro:
Elder Sāriputta taught on generosity and people decided to give alms; one man gave a robe, which they decided to give to Elder Devadatta; when the Buddha heard about it he related a Birth Story about Devadatta, who, as an elephant hunter, disguised himself as a Paccekabuddha in order to kill his prey, and then spoke some verses about him.
Cast: Elder Sāriputta, Elder Mahā Moggallāna, Devadatta
Keywords: Chief Disciples, Deceit, Offerings, Elephants, Hunters, Past Lives, Bodhisatta

01-08.htm.title: 1.8 The Story about the Chief Disciples
01-08.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about the Chief Disciples together with further information.
01-08.htm.intro:
The future Sāriputta and Moggallāna went forth under Sañjaya, but attained no great distinction; then they heard a summary of the Buddha’s teaching and were converted; they tried to bring Sañjaya to the Buddha but he would not go, his disciples left him and he died unattained; the Buddha spoke some verses showing the difference between them.
Cast: Elder Sāriputta (Upatissa, Sarada), Elder Mahā Moggallāna (Kolita, Sirivaḍḍhana), Elder Assaji, Sañjaya, Buddha Vipassī, Buddha Padumuttara, Aññā Koṇḍañña (Culla Kāḷa), Mahā Kāla, Yasa, Fortunate Group of Thirty, Buddha Tissa, Buddha Phussa, King Mahinda, King Bimbisāra, Uruvelā Kassapa, Nadī Kassapa, Gayā Kassapa, Buddha Anomadassī
Keywords: Chief Disciples, Vanity, Obstinacy, Bodhisatta, Aspirations, Offerings, Repulsion, Petas, Rich Men, Foremost Disciples, Epics, Past Lives, Previous Buddhas

01-09.htm.title: 1.9 The Story about the Elder Nanda
01-09.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about the Elder Nanda together with further information.
01-09.htm.intro:
The Buddha’s half-brother Nanda ordained, but yearned for the lay-life; the Buddha promised him celestial maidens as a reward for his efforts in the spiritual life; Nanda put forth effort and became an Arahat, and the Buddha was released from his promise; these verses were spoken about him.
Cast: Prince Nanda, Janapada Kaḷyāni, Rāhulamātā, Prince Rāhula, Merchant Kappaṭa
Keywords: Desire, Faith, Relatives, Accharās, Animals, Foremost Disciples, Epics, Past Lives

01-10.htm.title: 1.10 The Story about the Pig Butcher Cunda
01-10.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters telling The Story about the Pig Butcher Cunda together with further information.
01-10.htm.intro:
