01-Buddhas-Subjection-of-the-Yakkhas.htm.title: I. Buddha’s Subjection of the Yakkhas
01-Buddhas-Subjection-of-the-Yakkhas.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Buddha’s Subjection of the Yakkhas in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
01-Buddhas-Subjection-of-the-Yakkhas.htm.intro: The first chapter of the Dīpavaṁsa recounts the Buddha’s initial visit to Sri Lanka. After attaining enlightenment, the Buddha perceived the island as a future stronghold for the Dhamma. To prepare it for human habitation and the eventual arrival of Mahinda, he used his spiritual power to subdue and drive out the indigenous Yakkhas, Bhūtas, and Rakkhasas. This event establishes the island’s sanctity and its destiny as a major Buddhist center.

02-The-Conquering-of-the-Nagas.htm.title: II. The Conquering of the Nāgas
02-The-Conquering-of-the-Nagas.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Conquering of the Nāgas in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
02-The-Conquering-of-the-Nagas.htm.intro: In the second chapter of the Dīpavaṁsa, the Buddha travels to Sri Lanka for a second time to settle a violent war between the Nāga kings, Mahodara and Cūḷodara. Using his supernatural powers, he creates a terrifying darkness to subdue their pride, eventually preaching a message of peace and reconciliation. The Nāgas convert to Buddhism, offering him a gem-set throne. The Buddha also visits several sacred sites, including Kalyāṇī and the future Mahāmeghavana.

03-The-Great-Lineage.htm.title: III. The Great Lineage of Kings
03-The-Great-Lineage.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Great Lineage of Kings in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
03-The-Great-Lineage.htm.intro: This chapter traces the Buddha’s royal ancestry, beginning with Mahāsammata, the first king of the world. It enumerates the long succession of dynasties through various eras, highlighting the continuity of the Solar race. The lineage connects the ancient kings of India to the Buddha’s own family, the Sakyas. This genealogical record serves to establish the Buddha’s noble origin and the legitimate royal foundations upon which the Dhamma would eventually spread.

04-The-First-and-Second-Councils.htm.title: IV. [The First Two Councils]
04-The-First-and-Second-Councils.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The First Two Councils in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
04-The-First-and-Second-Councils.htm.intro: Following the Buddha’s Parinibbāna, the First Council was held at Rājagaha to preserve the Dhamma and Vinaya against corruption. Five hundred Arahants, led by Mahākassapa, codified the teachings. One hundred years later, the Second Council convened at Vesālī to suppress the ten unlawful practices of the Vajjian monks. These assemblies ensured the purity of the doctrine and led to the formal establishment of the Theravāda tradition against emerging sectarian schisms.

05-The-Schools-of-the-Teachers.htm.title: V. The Schools of the Teachers
05-The-Schools-of-the-Teachers.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Schools of the Teachers in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
05-The-Schools-of-the-Teachers.htm.intro: After the Second Council, the Buddhist community fractured into various sects. The Mahāsaṅghikas were the first to secede, altering the scriptures and monastic rules. From them and the original Theravāda line, eighteen distinct schools emerged, such as the Gokulikas and Ekavyohārikas. This chapter details the divergence of these groups, contrasting their innovative doctrines with the "True Doctrine" maintained by the elders, which eventually took root in Sri Lanka.

06-Asokas-Conversion.htm.title: VI. [Asoka’s Conversion]
06-Asokas-Conversion.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Asoka’s Conversion in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
06-Asokas-Conversion.htm.intro: This chapter chronicles the rise of King Asoka, who transitioned from a violent conqueror to a pious Buddhist patron. After witnessing the peace of the monk Nigrodha, Asoka embraced the Dhamma and constructed 84,000 monasteries across India. His devotion transformed the Mauryan Empire into a Buddhist state. The text emphasizes his relationship with the Sangha and his role in elevating the religion to unprecedented heights through immense material and spiritual support.

07-The-Council-of-the-True-Faith.htm.title: VII. The Council of the True Faith
07-The-Council-of-the-True-Faith.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Council of the True Faith in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
07-The-Council-of-the-True-Faith.htm.intro: Under Asoka’s patronage, the Sangha became wealthy, attracting heretics who corrupted the doctrine. To purify the religion, the Third Council was held at Pāṭaliputra, led by the elder Moggaliputta Tissa. One thousand Arahants expelled the false monks and compiled the Kathāvatthu to refute heretical views. This council solidified the Vibhajjavāda (Theravāda) school as the orthodox tradition and prepared the way for global Buddhist missions, specifically to Sri Lanka.

08-The-Missions.htm.title: VIII. [The Missions]
08-The-Missions.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Missions in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
08-The-Missions.htm.intro: Following the Third Council, Moggaliputta Tissa dispatched missionaries to nine different regions to spread the Dhamma. Great elders like Majjhantika and Mahādeva traveled to lands including Gandhāra, Mahīsamandala, and Suvaṇṇabhūmi. Each mission successfully converted thousands and established the monastic lineage. This chapter underscores the global expansion of Buddhism, setting the stage for the most significant mission: Mahinda’s journey to the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka).

09-Vijayas-Story.htm.title: IX. [Vijaya’s Story]
09-Vijayas-Story.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Vijaya’s Story in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
09-Vijayas-Story.htm.intro: Coinciding with the Buddha’s Parinibbāna, Prince Vijaya, a reckless prince from India, was exiled by his father. He landed in Sri Lanka with seven hundred followers. The Buddha, foreseeing the island as a future center for his teachings, asked the gods to protect Vijaya. After subduing the local Yakkhas, Vijaya founded the first human kingdom at Tambapaṇṇi. This marks the beginning of the Sinhalese lineage and the island’s organized civilization.

10-Panduvasa.htm.title: X. [Paṇḍuvāsa]
10-Panduvasa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Paṇḍuvāsa in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
10-Panduvasa.htm.intro: Following Vijaya’s death, his nephew Panduvāsudeva arrived from India to take the throne, accompanied by Princess Bhaddakaccānā. Their reign stabilized the monarchy and introduced the Sakya bloodline to the island. The chapter details the subsequent reigns, including the long and prosperous rule of Pandukābhaya, who founded the capital Anurādhapura. These rulers laid the political and infrastructural foundations necessary for the eventual official introduction of Buddhism under King Devānampiyatissa.

11-Devanampiyatissa.htm.title: XI. [Devānampiyatissa]
11-Devanampiyatissa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Devānampiyatissa in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
11-Devanampiyatissa.htm.intro: King Devānampiyatissa, a virtuous ruler, ascended the throne and established a diplomatic friendship with King Asoka. Though they never met, Asoka sent the king royal regalia for a second coronation and a message urging him to take refuge in the Triple Gem. During this reign, miraculous omens appeared across the island. The King’s readiness for the Dhamma set the stage for the arrival of the Great Mahinda from India.

12-The-Coming-of-Mahinda.htm.title: XII. [The Coming of Mahinda]
12-The-Coming-of-Mahinda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Coming of Mahinda in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
12-The-Coming-of-Mahinda.htm.intro: The Elder Mahinda, son of Asoka, traveled through the air and landed on Missaka Mountain (Mihintale). There, he encountered King Devānampiyatissa during a royal hunt. Mahinda tested the King’s wisdom with riddles before preaching the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta. The King and his followers immediately converted. This pivotal moment marks the formal introduction of Buddhism to Sri Lanka, leading to the King’s invitation for the monks to enter the capital.

13-The-Earthquakes.htm.title: XIII. [The Earthquakes]
13-The-Earthquakes.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Earthquakes in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
13-The-Earthquakes.htm.intro: After the King’s conversion, Mahinda entered Anurādhapura. He preached various discourses to the royalty and citizens, leading to thousands attaining enlightenment. The King offered the Mahāmeghavana garden to the Sangha. Mahinda proceeded to mark the boundaries of several sacred sites where future shrines and monasteries would stand. By ritually "fixing" these locations, Mahinda established the spiritual geography of the island, ensuring the Dhamma would remain firmly rooted there.

14-Mahavihara-and-the-Cetiyapabbata.htm.title: XIV. [Mahāvihāra and the Cetiyapabbata]
14-Mahavihara-and-the-Cetiyapabbata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mahāvihāra and the Cetiyapabbata in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
14-Mahavihara-and-the-Cetiyapabbata.htm.intro: King Devānampiyatissa formally donated the Mahāmeghavana park to the Sangha, marking the founding of the Mahāvihāra, the heart of Theravāda Buddhism. Mahinda accepted the donation by scattering jasmine flowers, which triggered miraculous earthquakes signifying the earth’s approval. The chapter describes the establishment of the first residence for monks and the King’s total devotion, ensuring that the monastic community had a permanent, legally consecrated base to teach and preserve the scriptures.

15-The-Relics-the-Buddhas-and-Queen-Anul.title: XV. [The Relics, the Buddhas, and Queen Anulā]
15-The-Relics-the-Buddhas-and-Queen-Anul.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Relics, the Buddhas, and Queen Anulā in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
15-The-Relics-the-Buddhas-and-Queen-Anul.intro: To provide the island with objects of worship, Mahinda requested relics of the Buddha. Through spiritual intervention, the Buddha’s collar-bone relic was brought from India. It was placed atop Missaka Mountain, where it performed miracles, emitting fire and water. The King then constructed the Thūpārāma, the first stupa in Sri Lanka, to enshrine the relic. This gave the island a physical living presence of the Buddha, further sanctifying the land.

16-The-Bodhi-Tree.htm.title: XVI. [The Bodhi Tree]
16-The-Bodhi-Tree.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Bodhi Tree in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
16-The-Bodhi-Tree.htm.intro: Princess Anula desired ordination, but Mahinda explained that only a Bhikkhunī could ordain women. Consequently, King Asoka sent his daughter, Saṅghamittā, to the island. She brought a sapling of the sacred Bodhi Tree from Bodh Gaya. The tree was planted in the Mahāmeghavana garden with great ceremony and miraculous signs. Its arrival established the female monastic order (Bhikkhunī Sasana) and provided a lasting symbol of the Buddha’s enlightenment in Sri Lanka.

17-The-Passing-of-a-Generation.htm.title: XVII. [The Passing of a Generation]
17-The-Passing-of-a-Generation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Passing of a Generation in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
17-The-Passing-of-a-Generation.htm.intro: This chapter records the deaths of King Devānampiyatissa and the great missionaries, including Mahinda and Saṅghamittā. After decades of establishing the Dhamma, they entered Parinibbāna, leaving behind a flourishing religion. The text details the funeral rites and the deep mourning of the islanders. Despite their passing, the monastic lineage and the teachings remained stable, passed down to local disciples who continued the work of the founding generation.

18-The-Bhikkhuni-Lineage.htm.title: XVIII. [The Bhikkhuni Lineage]
18-The-Bhikkhuni-Lineage.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Bhikkhuni Lineage in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
18-The-Bhikkhuni-Lineage.htm.intro: Focusing on the female lineage, this chapter lists the prominent Bhikkhunīs who maintained the Vinaya and taught the Dhamma in Sri Lanka. It traces the succession of teachers from Saṅghamittā down through several generations. These women were renowned for their wisdom, discipline, and ability to recite the scriptures. This record emphasizes that the female order was a vital and scholarly component of the early Buddhist Sangha on the island.

19-Dutthagamani.htm.title: XIX. [Duṭṭhagāmani]
19-Dutthagamani.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Duṭṭhagāmani in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
19-Dutthagamani.htm.intro: After a period of foreign Tamil rule, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi arose to reclaim the island for Buddhism. He led a holy war to liberate Anurādhapura, motivated by the desire to protect the Sasana rather than mere power. After defeating the King Elāra, he unified the country and embarked on massive meritorious works, most notably the construction of the Mahāthūpa (Ruwanwelisaya). His reign represents the heroic restoration and triumph of the Buddhist faith.

20-Tissa-to-Kutikannatissa.htm.title: XX. [Tissa to Kuṭikaṇṇatissa]
20-Tissa-to-Kutikannatissa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Tissa to Kuṭikaṇṇatissa in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
20-Tissa-to-Kutikannatissa.htm.intro:
Duṭṭhagāmaṇi was succeeded by his brother, Saddhātissa, a pious ruler who completed unfinished religious projects and supported the Sangha. The chapter follows the subsequent reigns of several kings, detailing their contributions to the island’s Buddhist infrastructure. It notes a period of instability involving famines and further Tamil invasions, yet highlights the resilience of the monarchy and the clergy in maintaining the religious traditions during times of political and environmental hardship./p>

21-Abhaya-to-Subha.htm.title: XXI. [Abhaya to Subha]
21-Abhaya-to-Subha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Abhaya to Subha in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
21-Abhaya-to-Subha.htm.intro: King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi Abhaya faced a dual threat from a Brahmin rebellion and a Tamil invasion, forcing him into hiding for fourteen years. Upon regaining his throne, he built the Abhayagiri Vihāra, which eventually led to a major schism in the Sangha. Crucially, during his reign, the Buddhist scriptures (Tipiṭaka), which had been preserved orally for centuries, were committed to writing for the first time at Aluvihāra to ensure their survival.

22-Vasabha-to-Mahasena.htm.title: XXII. [Vasabha to Mahāsena]
22-Vasabha-to-Mahasena.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Vasabha to Mahāsena in the Chronicle of the Island together with further information.
22-Vasabha-to-Mahasena.htm.intro: This final chapter details the reign of King Vasabha, who was known for his extensive irrigation works and the construction of numerous stupas and vihāras. He strengthened the island’s prosperity and security. The chronicle continues through various rulers up to King Mahāsena, noting their impacts on the Sangha. The text concludes by affirming the continuity of the island’s Buddhist heritage, linking the ancient past to the enduring presence of the Dhamma.

Thupavamsa.title: Thūpavaṁsa, The Legend of the Thūpas
Thupavamsa.summary: high-definition creative commons posters from Thūpavaṁsa, The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
Thupavamsa.intro: These storybooks are based on an English translation of the Thūpavaṁsa, The Legend of the Thūpas, which begins with the legendary lineages of past Buddhas, detailing their spiritual aspirations and the monuments erected in their honor across India. It specifically traces the life of Gotama Buddha, his enlightenment, and the subsequent distribution of his relics among various nations for veneration. The narrative then shifts to Ceylon, documenting the arrival of sacred relics and the pious efforts of kings like Duṭṭhagāmaṇi to construct magnificent stupas. By combining mythology with genealogical records, the source serves as a comprehensive guide to the architectural and devotional history of the Buddhist faith.
Thupavamsa.keywords: Buddha, Biography, India, Sri Lanka, Dharma, Medieval, Pāḷi

IN-01-The-Aspiration.htm.title: I. The Aspiration
IN-01-The-Aspiration.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Aspiration from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
IN-01-The-Aspiration.htm.intro: This chapter recounts the origin of the Bodhisatta’s journey toward Buddhahood. As the hermit Sumedha, he encounters Buddha Dīpaṅkara and is so inspired that he lays himself in the mire to serve as a bridge for the Buddha and his four hundred thousand Arahats. Recognizing Sumedha’s profound resolve, Dīpaṅkara prophesies his future enlightenment as Buddha Gotama. This sets the spiritual foundation for the eventual creation of sacred Thūpas.

IN-02-The-Existing-Thupas.htm.title: II. The Existing Thūpas
IN-02-The-Existing-Thupas.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Existing Thūpas from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
IN-02-The-Existing-Thupas.htm.intro: This section details the history of ancient Thūpas that existed prior to the current era. It describes the veneration of these shrines by both gods and men, emphasizing their role as focal points for merit-making. The narrative highlights how the physical presence of these Thūpas served as a constant reminder of the Buddhas’ teachings and the spiritual achievements of past Arahats, ensuring the Dhamma remained accessible to all beings.

IN-03-Diadem-and-Garments.htm.title: III. The Diadem and Garments Thūpas
IN-03-Diadem-and-Garments.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Diadem and Garments Thūpas from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
IN-03-Diadem-and-Garments.htm.intro: This chapter focuses on two unique Thūpas erected to honor the Buddha’s personal effects: his royal diadem and his sacred garments. These specific shrines symbolize the transition from the Buddha’s worldly life to his ascetic pursuit of enlightenment. By enshrining these objects, devotees created lasting monuments that allowed the faithful to pay homage to the Master’s renunciation and the high spiritual state attained by him and his Arahats.

IN-04-Ten-Thupas.htm.title: IV. The Ten Thūpas
IN-04-Ten-Thupas.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Ten Thūpas from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
IN-04-Ten-Thupas.htm.intro: Following the Buddha’s Mahāparinibbāna, his bodily remains were divided into eight portions among various tribes and kings. This chapter describes the subsequent construction of ten primary Thūpas—eight over the relics, one over the urn used for distribution, and one over the remaining embers. These original Thūpas became the most sacred sites in India, drawing pilgrims and Arahats who sought to honor the Buddha’s physical legacy.

IN-05-Depositing-the-Relics.htm.title: V. Depositing the Relics
IN-05-Depositing-the-Relics.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Depositing the Relics from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
IN-05-Depositing-the-Relics.htm.intro: King Ajātasattu, realizing the vulnerability of the scattered relics, worked with the elder Arahats to gather them into a single, secure repository at Rājagaha. This chapter details the elaborate precautions taken to protect these sacred remains from theft or decay. This centralized relic deposit was intended to preserve the Buddha’s essence for future generations, eventually allowing King Asoka to distribute them and build thousands of new Thūpas.

IN-06-84000-Relics.htm.title: VI. 84,000 Relics
IN-06-84000-Relics.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting 84,000 Relics from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
IN-06-84000-Relics.htm.intro: Inspired by the Dhamma, King Asoka undertook the monumental task of building 84,000 Thūpas across India. By opening the secret repository created by Ajātasattu, he distributed the Buddha’s relics to every corner of his empire. Guided by wise Arahats, Asoka’s massive construction project transformed the landscape of India into a vast network of shrines, ensuring that the influence of the Buddha’s relics reached a global audience.

SL-01-The-Monasteries.htm.title: 1. The Monastery of the Thūpas
SL-01-The-Monasteries.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Monastery of the Thūpas from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-01-The-Monasteries.htm.intro: The arrival of Thera Mahinda, a powerful Arahat, marked the formal introduction of Buddhism to Ceylon. This chapter describes the establishment of the first monasteries and the initial construction of Thūpas on the island under the patronage of King Devānampiyatissa. These early structures served as the spiritual heart of the new Buddhist community, providing a place for both local converts and visiting Arahats to practice and preserve the Dhamma.

SL-02-04-The-Bodhi-Tree.htm.title: II.–IV. The Arrival of the Bodhi Tree
SL-02-04-The-Bodhi-Tree.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Arrival of the Bodhi Tree from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-02-04-The-Bodhi-Tree.htm.intro: These chapters recount the miraculous arrival of the sacred Bodhi-tree from India, brought by the Arahat Sanghamittā. Following its planting, King Devānampiyatissa ordered the construction of Thūpas at regular one-yojana intervals across the island. This systematic expansion ensured that every citizen could easily access a sacred shrine. These Thūpas acted as spiritual beacons, marking the island as a stronghold for the teachings preserved by the Arahats.

SL-05-Mahiyangana.htm.title: V. The Mayiyaṅgana Thūpa
SL-05-Mahiyangana.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Mayiyaṅgana Thūpa from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-05-Mahiyangana.htm.intro: This chapter details the history of the Mahiyangana Thūpa, traditionally considered the first shrine built in Ceylon. Legend states it was established during the Buddha’s own visit to the island to subdue local supernatural beings. Over centuries, it was enlarged by various kings and maintained by dedicated Arahats. As a primary site of veneration, this Thūpa remains a symbol of the ancient and continuous Buddhist heritage in Sri Lanka.

SL-06-Maricavatti.htm.title: VI. The Maricavaṭṭi Thūpa
SL-06-Maricavatti.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Maricavaṭṭi Thūpa from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-06-Maricavatti.htm.intro: After defeating foreign invaders, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi founded the Maricavaṭṭi monastery and its central Thūpa as an act of merit. The king dedicated the site to the community of Arahats as a gesture of gratitude for their spiritual support during his campaigns. This chapter highlights the king’s devotion, showing how his military success was intrinsically linked to his desire to protect the Dhamma and provide grand residences for the holy Arahats.

SL-07-Obtaining-Materials.htm.title: VII. Obtaining Materials
SL-07-Obtaining-Materials.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting VII. Obtaining Materials from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-07-Obtaining-Materials.htm.intro: King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi sought to build the Mahāthūpa (Great Thūpa) without burdening his subjects with taxes. Miraculously, through the merit of the king and the blessings of the Arahats, all necessary materials—including precious gems, gold, and bricks—appeared spontaneously throughout the land. This chapter describes these divine occurrences, illustrating how the natural world itself cooperated to facilitate the creation of the island’s most magnificent and sacred Thūpa.

SL-08-The-Beginning.htm.title: VIII. The Beginning of the Construction
SL-08-The-Beginning.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Beginning of the Construction from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-08-The-Beginning.htm.intro: This chapter describes the grand ceremony for laying the foundation stone of the Mahāthūpa. King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi invited thousands of Arahats from across the Buddhist world to witness the event. The ritual was performed with extreme precision and immense celebration, marking the start of a project intended to be the ultimate architectural expression of faith. The presence of so many Arahats sanctified the site, ensuring the Thūpa’s enduring spiritual power.

SL-09-The-Relic-Chamber.htm.title: IX. The Description of the Relic Chamber
SL-09-The-Relic-Chamber.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Description of the Relic Chamber from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-09-The-Relic-Chamber.htm.intro: Inside the Great Thūpa, an incredibly elaborate relic chamber was constructed. This chapter provides a vivid description of its interior, which featured a golden Bodhi-tree and detailed depictions of the Buddha’s life and previous births. Designed to be a miniature universe, the chamber was sealed to protect the sacred relics. It served as a hidden, holy center where the essence of the Buddha and his Arahats would reside undisturbed.

SL-10-The-Enshrinement.htm.title: X. The Enshrinement of the Relics
SL-10-The-Enshrinement.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Enshrinement of the Relics from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-10-The-Enshrinement.htm.intro: The climax of the construction was the formal enshrinement of the Buddha’s relics within the Great Thūpa. This chapter details the miraculous events and grand processions that accompanied the ritual. As the relics were placed in the chamber, the earth shook, and the Arahats performed psychic wonders to celebrate the occasion. This act transformed the Great Thūpa into a living monument, forever housing the sacred physical remains of the Enlightened One.

SL-11-The-Great-Shrine.htm.title: XI. The Great Shrine
SL-11-The-Great-Shrine.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Great Shrine from The Legend of the Thūpas together with further information.
SL-11-The-Great-Shrine.htm.intro: As King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi lay dying, his brother Tissa completed the external structure of the Mahāthūpa so the king could see it one last time. This final chapter records the king’s last acts of devotion and his subsequent rebirth in the celestial realms. The Great Shrine stands as his greatest legacy, a massive Thūpa that remains a primary site of pilgrimage, perpetually honored by the faithful and protected by the spiritual influence of the Arahats. The story closes by shwoing how King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi’s great spiritual meritwill earn him a place at the side of Buddha Metteyya in the future. And the author’s own Envoi.

Sasanavamsa.title: Sāsanavaṁsa, The History of the Buddha’s Religion
Sasanavamsa.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Sasanavamsa.intro: The Sāsanavaṁsa, which was composed in 1861 by Ven. Paññasāmi in Myanmar, rewrites the history of the Asokan missions to send most of them to Myanmar (here spelt in Pāḷi as Mramma). Although this is historically unsubstantiated, if we leave that aside, then what we have is a fascinating look at the many times the religion rose and fell away again in Myanmar, and especially its interaction with Sri Lanka over the centuries.
Sasanavamsa.keywords: Buddha, Biography, India, Myanmar, Dharma, Medieval, Pāḷi

01-Nine-Places.htm.title: 01 Nine Places
01-Nine-Places.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Nine Places from The History of the Buddha’s Religion from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
01-Nine-Places.htm.intro: Following the Third Buddhist Council led by Moggaliputta Tissa Mahāthera, nine missions were dispatched to establish the Buddha’s dispensation (sāsana) in different regions. This text details those nine specific destinations, the elder monks who led each mission, and the thousands of locals who converted, laying the groundwork for Buddhism’s global expansion beyond its foundational borders in India.

02-Sri-Lanka.htm.title: 02 Sri Lanka
02-Sri-Lanka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sri Lanka from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
02-Sri-Lanka.htm.intro: This document chronicles the establishment and preservation of Theravāda Buddhism in Sri Lanka (Sīhaladīpa). Led by Mahinda Mahāthera, the mission successfully converted the island’s rulers and populace. It tracks the subsequent historical triumphs, internal schisms, and structural developments of the Sri Lankan Saṅgha, highlighting its critical role as a primary, enduring stronghold of orthodox Buddhist teachings.

03-Suvannabhumi.htm.title: 03 Suvaṇṇabhumi
03-Suvannabhumi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Suvaṇṇabhumi from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
03-Suvannabhumi.htm.intro: Focusing on the mission to Suvaṇṇabhūmi (traditionally identified with regions in Lower Burma), this text details how the elders Soṇa and Uttara subdued local threats to introduce the Dhamma. It records the mass conversions, ordinations, and the subsequent lineage of teachers that successfully preserved the monastic discipline and scriptural traditions in Southeast Asia over generations.

04-Yonaka.htm.title: 04 Yonaka
04-Yonaka.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Yonaka from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
04-Yonaka.htm.intro: This section outlines the Buddhist mission to Yonakaraṭṭha (idetified here as Harinjuñja in Lannā), led by the elder Mahārakkhita. It describes his discourse on the Kālakārāma Sutta, which inspired widespread spiritual awakening, resulting in thousands of ordinations and establishing a robust, distinct monastic presence in what was later Thailand.

05-Vanavasi.htm.title: 05 Vanavāsī
05-Vanavasi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Vanavāsī from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
05-Vanavasi.htm.intro: This document covers the mission to Vanavāsi (here identified with the Pyu kingdom of Sirikhetta), spearheaded by Rakkhita Mahāthera. By preaching the Anamatagga Saṃyutta, he inspired profound devotion among the populace. The text records extensive conversions and ordinations, illustrating how the monastic tradition successfully adapted and integrated into the regional culture of later Myanmar.

06a-Arimaddana-1.htm.title: 06a Arimaddana 1
06a-Arimaddana-1.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Arimaddana 1 from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
06a-Arimaddana-1.htm.intro: This chapter explores the early history of the sāsana in Arimaddana (Pagan or Bagan, Upper Burma). It details the rise of the heterodox Ari monks and the subsequent religious reformation under King Anawrahta, guided by the Mon thera Shin Arahan. This crucial turning point firmly established orthodox Theravāda Buddhism as the state religion, unifying the region under the Dhamma.

06b-Arimaddana-2.htm.title: 6b Arimaddana 2
06b-Arimaddana-2.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Arimaddana 2 from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
06b-Arimaddana-2.htm.intro: Continuing the history of Arimaddana (Pagan or Bagan, Upper Burma), this text focuses on the consolidation of the Buddhist tradition under successive Burmese monarchs. It documents royal patronage, the construction of prominent religious monuments, the arrival of sacred relics, and intellectual developments. These factors solidified Arimaddana’s reputation as a premier international center for Pāli scholarship and monastic discipline.

06c-Vijayapura.htm.title: 06c Vijayapura
06c-Vijayapura.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Vijayapura from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
06c-Vijayapura.htm.intro: This text chronicles the history of Buddhism in Vijayapura (Pinya) and surrounding northern Burmese regions following the shift of political power from Pagan. It highlights how local rulers sustained the sāsana through royal endowments, monastery construction, and active support for scholarly monks, ensuring the continuity of monastic lineages and scriptural learning during political transitions.

06d-Ratanapura.htm.title: 06d Ratanapura
06d-Ratanapura.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ratanapura from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
06d-Ratanapura.htm.intro: This section covers the religious history of Ratanapura (Ava), documenting the vibrant flourishing of Buddhist scholarship and monastic administration. It details royal purification efforts of the Saṅgha, prestigious ecclesiastical appointments, and the prolific literary output of local monks. These achievements cemented Ava’s status as a critical custodian of the Theravāda analytical and textual tradition.

07-Kasmira-Gandhara.htm.title: 07 Kasmīra and Gandhāra
07-Kasmira-Gandhara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Kasmīra and Gandhāra from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
07-Kasmira-Gandhara.htm.intro: This document details the pivotal mission to Kasmīra and Gandhāra (modern-day Kashmir and Swat regions) led by the elder Majjhantika Mahāthera. It describes his dramatic subjugation of a fierce local nāga king, which cleared the way for peaceful teaching. His subsequent discourse on the Āsīvisūpama Sutta inspired mass conversions and thousands of monastic ordinations, securing Buddhism’s northern frontier.

08-10-Three-Countries.htm.title: 08-10 Mahiṁsaka, Mahāraṭṭha and Cīna
08-10-Three-Countries.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mahiṁsaka, Mahāraṭṭha and Cīna from The History of the Buddha’s Religion together with further information.
08-10-Three-Countries.htm.intro: This section chronicles the expansion of the sāsana across three distinct regions: Mahiṁsaka-maṇḍala, Mahāraṭṭha and “Cīna”, the Himalayan regions. Led by the elders Mahādeva, Yonaka Dhammarakkhita, and Mahādhammarakkhita respectively, each mission utilized core discourses like the Devadūta Sutta and Aggikkhandhopama Sutta to prompt profound spiritual awakenings, widespread local conversions, and the establishment of vibrant regional monastic lineages.

Eminent-Monks.title: The Biographies of Eminent Monks
Eminent-Monks.summary: high-definition creative commons posters from The Biographies of Eminent Monks together with further information.
Eminent-Monks.intro: The illustrations are based on some of The Biographies of Eminent Monks, which is a translation by Tianshu Yang of 高僧傳 (Gaoseng Zhuan), compiled by Shi Huijiao in the 6th century. The selection focuses on those who were particularly engaged in bringing the texts to China and translating them, and chronicles the transformative era of Buddhist transmission to China (1st–5th century CE). These monks and pilgrims were the architects of Chinese Buddhism, navigating perilous landscapes—from the Silk Road to maritime routes—to transport sacred Sanskrit manuscripts to the Chinese heartland. By establishing formal ordination lineages, meditation schools, and metaphysical frameworks, these masters integrated Indian philosophy into the Chinese intellectual landscape. Their legacy solidified Buddhism as a permanent, sophisticated component of East Asian civilization, setting the stage for its subsequent flourishing.
Eminent-Monks.keywords: Disciples, India, China, Sanskrit, Chinese, Medieval

A-01-02-Kasyapa-Matanga-and-Gobharana.ht.title:
Section A 01-02
Kāśyapa-Mātaṅga and Gobharaṇa (Central India)
A-01-02-Kasyapa-Matanga-and-Gobharana.ht.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Kāśyapa-Mātaṅga and Gobharaṇa (Central India) together with further information.
A-01-02-Kasyapa-Matanga-and-Gobharana.ht.intro: Kāśyapa-Mātanga and Gobharaṇa were the first monks to bring Buddhism to China during the Eastern Han Dynasty. Following Emperor Ming’s dream of a golden deity, they were invited to Luoyang, where they resided at Baima (White Horse) Temple. They are credited with translating early Buddhist texts, including the sūtra of Forty-two Chapters, establishing the foundation for the religion’s transmission into the Chinese heartland.

A-03-An-Shigao.htm.title:
Section A 03
An Qing (Parthia)
A-03-An-Shigao.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about An Qing (Parthia) together with further information.
A-03-An-Shigao.htm.intro: An Shigao, a former Parthian crown prince, abdicated his throne to become a monk. He arrived in Luoyang during the Han Dynasty and became a prolific translator, focusing on Abhidharma and meditation (Chan) scriptures. Known for his intelligence and supernatural abilities, such as understanding animal languages, he significantly advanced the systematic study of Buddhist philosophy and practice in China through his clear, structured translations.

A-06-Kang-Senghui.htm.title:
Section A 06
Kang Senghui (Sogdiana)
A-06-Kang-Senghui.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Kang Senghui (Sogdiana) together with further information.
A-06-Kang-Senghui.htm.intro: Kang Senghui, of Sogdian descent, introduced Buddhism to the Southern Kingdom of Wu during the Three Kingdoms period. He famously convinced the ruler Sun Quan of the Dharma’s power by successfully invoking a Buddhist relic miracle. He established the Jianchu Monastery, the first in the region, and translated various sūtras, playing a pivotal role in the early expansion of Buddhism in southern China.

A-08-Dharmaraksa.htm.title:
Section A 08
Dharmarakṣa (Yuezhi)
A-08-Dharmaraksa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Dharmarakṣa (Yuezhi) together with further information.
A-08-Dharmaraksa.htm.intro: Known as the Bodhisattva of Dunhuang, Dharmarakṣa (Zhu Fahu) was a tireless translator from the Yuezhi ethnic group. He traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions, mastering thirty-six languages and bringing numerous Sanskrit manuscripts back to China. During the Western Jin Dynasty, he translated over 150 Mahāyāna scriptures, including the Lotus sūtra, making these profound teachings accessible to a wide Chinese audience for the first time.

A-10-Srimitra.htm.title:
Section A 10
Śrīmitra (Western Regions)
A-10-Srimitra.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Śrīmitra (Western Regions) together with further information.
A-10-Srimitra.htm.intro: Śrīmitra, a prince from the Western Regions, renounced his royal status to become a monk and traveled to China during the chaotic Yongjia Period. Settling in Jiankang (modern Nanjing), he became a respected figure among the Southern Jin elite. He is particularly noted for introducing Buddhist mantras and esoteric rituals to China, as well as his expertise in chanting, which deeply influenced Chinese Buddhist liturgical traditions.

A-11-12-14-Samghabhuti-et-al.htm.title:
Section A 11-12-14
Saṁghabhūti (Kashmir), et al
A-11-12-14-Samghabhuti-et-al.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Saṁghabhūti (Kashmir), et al together with further information.
A-11-12-14-Samghabhuti-et-al.htm.intro: This details the stories of several monks in Chang'an, primarily Saṁghabhūti, who specialized in the Abhidharma-vibhāṣā. Under the patronage of officials like Zhao Zheng, he and others like Dharmanandi worked to translate critical Sarvāstivāda texts. Their efforts were central to the flourishing of Buddhist scholasticism in northern China, providing the intellectual framework for deeper doctrinal understanding during the Former Qin period.

A-13-Samghadeva.htm.title:
Section A 13
Saṁghadeva (Kashmir)
A-13-Samghadeva.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Saṁghadeva (Kashmir) together with further information.
A-13-Samghadeva.htm.intro: Saṁghadeva, a master from Kashmir (Jibin), was an expert in the Abhidharma and the Āgamas. After initially working in Chang'an, he traveled south to Mount Lu and later to Jiankang. His primary contribution was the re-translation and refinement of the Madhyama Āgama and various Abhidharma treatises, which helped correct earlier linguistic errors and clarified complex philosophical points for Chinese practitioners

A-15-Dharmayasas.htm.title:
Section A 15
Dharmayaśas (Kashmir)
A-15-Dharmayasas.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Dharmayaśas (Kashmir) together with further information.
A-15-Dharmayasas.htm.intro: Dharmayaśas was a dedicated monk from Kashmir (Jibin) who specialized in the Vinaya (monastic discipline) and the Vibhāṣā. He traveled to southern China, where he translated important texts on meditation and monastic rules. The story also mentions his disciple Zhu Fadu, who controversially attempted to prioritize Hīnayāna teachings and restricted the reading of Mahāyāna doctrines, reflecting early internal doctrinal debates in Chinese Buddhism.

B-01-Kumarajiva.htm.title:
Section B 01
Kumārajīva (India)
B-01-Kumarajiva.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Kumārajīva (India) together with further information.
B-01-Kumarajiva.htm.intro: Kumārajīva is one of the most significant figures in Buddhist history. Captured during a military campaign, he eventually reached Chang'an, where he led a massive translation bureau. He revolutionized Chinese Buddhism by translating foundational Mahāyāna texts—such as the Diamond sūtra and Vimalakirti sūtra—into elegant, accurate Chinese. His work corrected many earlier matching meanings (geyi) misunderstandings, establishing the standard for Buddhist terminology.

B-05-Buddhayasas.htm.title:
Section B 05
Buddhayaśas (Kashmir)
B-05-Buddhayasas.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Buddhayaśas (Kashmir) together with further information.
B-05-Buddhayasas.htm.intro: He was a monk from Kashmir (Jibin) known for his extraordinary memory, and was a close associate and teacher of Kumārajīva. He joined Kumārajīva in Chang'an to assist with complex translations. His most notable contribution was the translation of the Dharmagupta Vinaya (Four-Part Vinaya) and the Dīrghāgama, which he dictated entirely from memory, ensuring the preservation and transmission of essential monastic codes and early discourses.

B-06-Buddhabhadra.htm.title:
Section B 06
Buddhabhadra (Kapilavastu)
B-06-Buddhabhadra.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Buddhabhadra (Kapilavastu) together with further information.
B-06-Buddhabhadra.htm.intro: Buddhabhadra, a descendant of the Shakya clan from Kapilavastu, was a meditation and Vinaya master. After traveling to China, he initially worked in Chang'an but moved south to Mount Lu and Nanjing due to doctrinal friction. He is best known for collaborating with Faxian to translate the Mahāsāṁghika vinaya and producing the first Chinese translation of the vast Avataṁsaka sūtra. His legacy is defined by his expertise in Dhyāna (meditation) and his prolific translation output.

B-07-Dharmaksema.htm.title:
Section B 07
Dharmakṣema (Central India)
B-07-Dharmaksema.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Dharmakṣema (Central India) together with further information.
B-07-Dharmaksema.htm.intro: A Central Indian monk, Dharmakşema was a master of Mahāyāna scriptures and dhāraṇīs. He traveled to the Northern Liang kingdom, where he spent years translating the monumental Mahāparinirvāna-sūtra, which introduced the concept of the universal Buddha-nature to China. Despite his immense contributions to Buddhist philosophy, his life ended tragically; he was assassinated by the ruler Juqu Mengxun while attempting to travel west to find the remaining portions of the Nirvāna scripture.

C-01-Faxian.htm.title:
Section C 01
Shi Faxian (Wuyang)
C-01-Faxian.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Shi Faxian (Wuyang) together with further information.
C-01-Faxian.htm.intro: Driven by a desire to find authentic Vinaya (monastic rules) texts, the Chinese monk Faxian embarked on an epic fifteen-year journey to India and Sri Lanka. He survived treacherous deserts and mountain passes, becoming one of the first Chinese pilgrims to return successfully by sea. His translations of the Mahāsāṁghika-vinaya and his detailed travelogue, Record of Buddhist Kingdoms, provided Chinese Buddhists with essential disciplinary frameworks and a geographical understanding of the Buddhist world.

C-03-Dharmodgata.htm.title:
Section C 02
Dharmodgata (Huanglong)
C-03-Dharmodgata.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Dharmodgata (Huanglong) together with further information.
C-03-Dharmodgata.htm.intro: Inspired by Faxian’s courage, Dharmodgata led a group of twenty-five monks from China toward India. Their journey was marked by extreme physical hardship, including crossing the Pamir Mountains and surviving encounters with wild animals through the invocation of Guanshiyin (Avalokiteśvara). After reaching India and paying homage to sacred relics, he returned to China via the maritime route to Guangzhou. He is primarily remembered for his translation of the Guanshiyin shouji jing.

C-07-Gunavarman.htm.title:
Section C 07
Guṇavarman (Kashmir)
C-07-Gunavarman.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Guṇavarman (Kashmir) together with further information.
C-07-Gunavarman.htm.intro: A prince of Kashmir (Jibin) who abdicated his throne for the monastic life, Guṇavarman became a renowned teacher in Southeast Asia before reaching China. Upon his arrival in Nanjing, he was treated with great imperial favor. He was instrumental in establishing the formal lineage of bhikṣuṇī (nun) ordination in China. Though he died shortly after his arrival, his translation of the Ten-Chant Vinaya and his exemplary asceticism left a lasting impact on Chinese monasticism.

C-09-Dharmamitra.htm.title:
Section C 09
Dharmamitra (Kashmir)
C-09-Dharmamitra.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Dharmamitra (Kashmir) together with further information.
C-09-Dharmamitra.htm.intro: Known as the Chan Master with Connected Eyebrows, Dharmamitra was a native of Kashmir (Jibin) and a specialist in meditation techniques. He traveled extensively through Central Asia before settling in Nanjing during the Liu Song Dynasty. He translated several key meditation sūtras, including the Guan Puxian pusa xingfa jing. His work was pivotal in systematizing Buddhist visualization and repentance practices in Southern China, and he was highly revered by both the royalty and the common people.

C-10-Shi-Zhimeng.htm.title:
Section C 10
Shi Zhimeng (Xi'an)
C-10-Shi-Zhimeng.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Shi Zhimeng (Xi'an) together with further information.
C-10-Shi-Zhimeng.htm.intro: Shi Zhimeng led a large party of fifteen monks from Chang'an to India in search of Mahāyāna scriptures. His travels took him to the birthplace of the Buddha and the capital of King Aśoka. Although many of his companions perished or turned back due to the grueling conditions, Zhimeng reached India and returned with Sanskrit copies of the Nirvāna sūtra and the Mahāsāṁghika-vinaya. He spent his final years in Chengdu translating these precious texts.

C-12-Gunabhadra.htm.title:
Section C 12
Guṇabhadra (Central India)
C-12-Gunabhadra.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Story about Guṇabhadra (Central India) together with further information.
C-12-Gunabhadra.htm.intro: Born into a Brahmin family in Central India, Guṇabhadra was a master of the Five Sciences before converting to Mahāyāna Buddhism. He arrived in China by sea and was warmly welcomed by the Liu Song court. He is most famous for translating the Laṁkāvatāra-sūtra, a foundational text for the later Chan school, and the Saṁyukta Āgama. His scholarly precision and lifelong vegetarianism made him a model of both intellectual and moral excellence in Chinese Buddhism.

Transmission-of-the-Lamp.title: The Transmission of the Lamp
Transmission-of-the-Lamp.summary: high-definition creative commons posters from The Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
Transmission-of-the-Lamp.intro: Storybooks based on an English translation of The Transmission of the Lamp which detail the historical and spiritual lineage of the Indian Patriarchs, tracing the transmission of the True Dharma-eye through successive generations of Buddhist masters. Each account chronicles the unique origins and miraculous deeds of a specific patriarch, from the first leader, Mahākāśyapā, to the twenty-fifth, Vāsasita, and then on to the teachers in China. These narratives emphasize the master-disciple relationship, illustrating how the core essence of the Buddha’s teachings was preserved and passed down through symbolic robes, sacred verses, and profound meditative insights. The texts also describe the supernatural transformations and philosophical debates that defined these figures’ lives as they spread liberation to sentient beings. The collection serves as a chronicle of continuity, documenting how the lineage survived political trials and personal sacrifices to maintain the integrity of the Buddhist tradition.
Transmission-of-the-Lamp.keywords: Buddha, Disciples, India, China, Sanskrit, Chinese, Chan/Zen, Medieval

01-Maha-Kasyapa.htm.title: 1. Mahākaśyapa
01-Maha-Kasyapa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Mahākaśyapa in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
01-Maha-Kasyapa.htm.intro: Mahākaśyapa, the First Patriarch, was a Brahmin from Magadha. He is famous for the Flower Sermon where he alone understood the Buddha’s silent transmission. Known for his asceticism, he presided over the First Council to preserve the Buddha’s teachings. Before his passing, he transmitted the Dharma-eye to Ānanda. He eventually entered the Kukkuṭapada Mountain to wait in samādhi for the future Buddha, Maitreya, still holding the Buddha’s robe as a symbol of the lineage.

02-Ananda.htm.title: 2. Ānanda
02-Ananda.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Ānanda in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
02-Ananda.htm.intro: Ānanda, the Buddha’s cousin and faithful attendant for twenty-five years, was the Second Patriarch. Renowned for his unobstructed wisdom and perfect memory, he recited the sūtras at the First Council. When he approached his parinirvāṇa, he found himself caught between two warring kingdoms seeking his relics. To satisfy both, he rose into the air and divided his body into four parts through samādhi, leaving his remains to various kings and celestial beings to ensure the Dharma’s continued veneration.

03-Sanakavasa.htm.title: 3. Sanakavāsa
03-Sanakavasa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Sanakavāsa in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
03-Sanakavasa.htm.intro: The Third Patriarch, Sanakavāsa, was born in Mathura with a natural robe of auspicious grass, a sign of his high spiritual standing. Following the Buddha’s prophecy, he turned the Wheel of Dharma in the Uruda forest. He famously converted two fiery dragons who then donated land for a monastery. After searching for a worthy successor, he transmitted the Dharma to Upagupta. He passed away after demonstrating the fire-light samādhi, leaving behind sacred relics for his disciples.

04-Upagupta.htm.title: 4. Upagupta
04-Upagupta.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Upagupta in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
04-Upagupta.htm.intro: Upagupta, the Fourth Patriarch, was a powerful teacher who lived in a cave and used bamboo tallies to count those he led to liberation. He is most famous for subduing the demon Māra. When Māra tried to disrupt his teaching, Upagupta transformed three foul corpses into a beautiful garland, trapping Māra until the "Evil One" repented and took refuge in the Three Jewels. Before his death, he transmitted the Heart-Dharma to his disciple Dhritaka through a profound gatha.

12-Asvaghosa.htm.title: 12. Aśvaghoṣa
12-Asvaghosa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Aśvaghoṣa in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
12-Asvaghosa.htm.intro: Aśvaghosa, the Twelfth Patriarch, was a brilliant philosopher and poet from Baranasi. Initially a formidable debater, he was converted to Buddhism and became a Great Bodhisattva. He possessed immense spiritual power, once summoning a golden dragon to defeat a demonic storm. He taught the concept of the Ocean of Innate Nature, explaining that all phenomena depend on this original essence. Before his extinction, he transmitted the awakened understanding to Kapimala and vanished into the form of a sun-disc.

14-Nagarjuna.htm.title: 14. Nāgārjuna
14-Nagarjuna.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Nāgārjuna in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
14-Nagarjuna.htm.intro: Nāgārjuna, the Fourteenth Patriarch, is one of the most influential figures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Born in Western India, he mastered the Dharma and famously authored the Madhyamika Śāstra. He taught that the Buddha-nature is neither born nor dying, transcending all dualities. He was known as the Dragon Conqueror for his deep insight. After converting thousands of heretics and transmitting the True Dharma-eye to his senior disciple Kanadeva, he entered a full moon samādhi and achieved final cessation.

21-Vasubandhu.htm.title: 21. Vasubandhu
21-Vasubandhu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Vasubandhu in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
21-Vasubandhu.htm.intro: Vasubandhu, the Twenty-First Patriarch, was born in Rajagṛha to a merchant family. An Arhat prophesied his birth as a sun of wisdom. He was a prolific scholar who eventually followed the sage’s calling after the King of his region relinquished his own son, Manula, to be Vasubandhu’s disciple. After transmitting the Dharma to Manula and teaching that awakening is unobstructed by the bubbles and shadows of the world, he leapt into the air and passed away in a mountain-like posture.

24-Aryasimha.htm.title: 24. Āryasiṁha
24-Aryasimha.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Āryasiṁha in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
24-Aryasimha.htm.intro: Āryasiṁha, the Twenty-Fourth Patriarch, was a Brahmin from Central India who traveled to Kashmir to unify various meditation sects. His life ended in martyrdom when a local king, testing his indifference to life and death, beheaded him. Miraculously, white milk instead of blood spurted from his neck, and the king’s arm immediately fell off as karmic retribution. Before this, he had already ensured the continuation of the lineage by transmitting the Dharma and the Robe of Faith to Bashyashita.

25-Vasasita.htm.title: 25. Vāsasita
25-Vasasita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Vāsasita in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
25-Vasasita.htm.intro: Vāsasita, the Twenty-fifth Patriarch, was born in Kashmir with a clenched fist, symbolizing a jewel from a past life. He traveled through India, famously defeating a heretic who proposed a silent debate on the nature of No-Heart. He taught that the True Nature is neither a path nor a principle. After serving as a teacher to King Virtuous Conqueror, he transmitted the Dharma-eye to Puṇyamitra. He eventually cremated himself through the power of samādhi fire, leaving behind miraculous relics.

27-Prajnatara.htm.title: 27. Prajñātara
27-Prajnatara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Prajñātara in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
27-Prajnatara.htm.intro: Prajñātara, the Twenty-seventh Patriarch, traveled from Eastern to Southern India. He famously tested the three sons of King Excelling in Fragrance by showing them a priceless jewel. While the older sons praised the physical gem, the youngest son, Bodhitara (the future Bodhidharma), correctly identified the Heart-treasure and Wisdom-lustre as the only true treasures. Recognizing this profound insight, Prajñātara named Bodhitara his heir. Upon his death, Prajñātara ascended into the air and transformed into fire, raining down sacred relics.

28-Bodhidharma.htm.title: 28. Bodhidharma
28-Bodhidharma.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Bodhidharma in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
28-Bodhidharma.htm.intro: Bodhidharma, the Twenty-eighth Patriarch and the First Patriarch of Chinese Chan, was a South Indian prince. Following his master’s advice to wait until the Dharma-medicine was needed in the East, he traveled to China to find men of superior roots. He is the legendary founder of the Shaolin tradition and is famous for his nine years of wall-gazing meditation. His teachings emphasized direct contact with one’s own nature rather than reliance on scriptures, effectively establishing the foundation for all Chan and Zen Buddhism.

29-Huike.htm.title: 29. Huike
29-Huike.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Huike in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
29-Huike.htm.intro: Huike, the Twenty-ninth Patriarch and Second Chinese Patriarch, was a deeply learned scholar who sought Bodhidharma at the Shaolin Monastery. To prove his sincerity and resolve to seek the Dharma, legend says he stood in the snow and severed his own arm. Bodhidharma subsequently pacified Huike’s mind, leading to his enlightenment. Huike spent years living among the common people, teaching the Original Emptiness of karmic obstructions before transmitting the lineage to Sengcan and facing a martyr’s death.

30-Sengcan.htm.title: 30. Sengcan
30-Sengcan.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Sengcan in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
30-Sengcan.htm.intro: Sengcan, the Thirtieth Patriarch and Third Chinese Patriarch, lived during a time of Buddhist persecution and frequently hid in the mountains. He is famously associated with the Hsin Hsin Ming (Verses on the Faith Mind). He enlightened the young novice Daoxin by pointing out that since no one binds you, there is no need to seek liberation. After nine years of training his successor, he transmitted the Dharma and the Robe, ensuring the survival of the Chan lineage through turbulent times.

31-Daoxin.htm.title: 31. Daoxin
31-Daoxin.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Daoxin in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
31-Daoxin.htm.intro: Daoxin, the Thirty-first Patriarch and Fourth Chinese Patriarch, was known for his extreme discipline, never lying down to sleep for sixty years. He established a permanent monastic community, moving Chan toward a more settled lifestyle. He famously saved a city from brigands by teaching the residents to chant the Great Wisdom Sutra, which manifested superhuman warriors that scared the attackers away. He died peacefully at age seventy-two, and his body remained miraculously lifelike after his death.

32-Hongren.htm.title: 32. Hongren
32-Hongren.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Hongren in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
32-Hongren.htm.intro: Hongren, the Thirty-second Patriarch and Fifth Chinese Patriarch, presided over a large community on East Mountain. He is best known for recognizing the spiritual genius of the illiterate layman Huineng. When Huineng wrote a verse demonstrating a perfect understanding of emptiness, Hongren secretly summoned him at night, explained the Diamond Sutra, and transmitted the Patriarchal Robe. To protect Huineng from jealous rivals, Hongren ordered him to flee south and remain in hiding before officially beginning his teaching.

33-Huineng.htm.title: 33. Huineng
33-Huineng.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons about Huineng in the Transmission of the Lamp together with further information.
33-Huineng.htm.intro: Huineng, the Thirty-third Patriarch and Sixth Chinese Patriarch, was a poor firewood seller who achieved enlightenment upon hearing the Diamond Sutra. His Southern School emphasized sudden enlightenment and the idea that Buddha-nature is inherent in everyone, regardless of education or status. His teachings, recorded in the Platform Sutra, revolutionized Chinese Buddhism. Despite his humble origins, he became the most influential figure in Chan history, and his mummified body is still venerated in South China today.

Chinese-Nuns.title: The Lives of Inspiring Chinese Nuns
Chinese-Nuns.summary: high-definition creative commons posters from The Lives of Inspiring Chinese Nuns together with further information.
Chinese-Nuns.intro: Illustrations based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s Lives of the Nuns, which is a translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan (比丘尼傳) which was compiled by Shih Pao-ch’ang. The selection focuses on those who passed on the lineage, some of the discussions surrounding its validity, and the particular sanctity of some of the nuns. It also gives a good idea of 4th and 5th century China, and the society within which these nuns lived and fulfilled their aspirations.
Chinese-Nuns.keywords: Disciples, Nuns, China, India, Sri Lanka, Medieval

Maps.htm.title: Maps and Geography of the Nuns

01-Ching-chien.htm.title: 01 Ching-chien, The First Chinese Nun
01-Ching-chien.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan, entitled Lives of the Nuns.
01-Ching-chien.htm.intro: A historical biography of the first Buddhist nun in China, named Chu Ching-chien, spanning the Chin dynasty. This text details her early life, including her marriage and eventual widowhood, which led her to teach music and calligraphy to support herself. The account tracks her spiritual journey, explaining how she initially encountered Buddhist teachings through the monk Fa-shih and mastered scripture despite a lack of detailed instruction for women. It also recounts the establishment of the Bamboo Grove Convent and the challenges faced by Ching-chien and her twenty-four disciples in receiving the full monastic rules, since the complete texts and a female instructor were initially unavailable in China. Finally, the text describes how, after the required Mahāsaṅghika rules for nuns were translated, Ching-chien formally became a Buddhist nun and concludes with a description of her miraculous departure at the age of seventy.

02-Ling-shou.htm.title: 02 Ling-shou, A Founders Journey
02-Ling-shou.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
02-Ling-shou.htm.intro: The story of the nun An Ling-shou, whose family was originally from Tung-huan, it details her early life, including her decision to devote herself to a spiritual path despite her father’s initial resistance. The account explains that An Ling-shou was exceptionally intelligent and was already immersed in Buddhist teachings, preferring a secluded life to worldly pleasures. A significant part of the narrative focuses on a conversation with her father, Hsü Ch’ung, where she argues that cultivating the Way would free her parents from suffering and benefit all living beings. Hsü Ch’ung eventually consults a monk and allows his daughter to become a nun, with the monk predicting that she would bring her family great honour and guide others to Nirvāṇa. The source concludes by mentioning that An Ling-shou established a convent and was widely respected for her wisdom and piety, even having her father honoured by a later emperor.

05-Ming-kan.htm.title: 05 Ming-kan, Enduring Faith
05-Ming-kan.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
05-Ming-kan.htm.intro: A biographical account of K’ang Ming-kan, a nun whose secular surname was Chu, detailing her life and spiritual journey within the Buddhist tradition. The narrative outlines her family’s connection to Buddhism and recounts a difficult early experience where she was abducted but vowed not to succumb to her captor, instead becoming a shepherdess while maintaining her faith. Her story continues with her eventually becoming a nun and undertaking stringent religious practices like meditation and chanting, eventually starting the Establishing Blessings Convent. The document concludes by noting the respect and authority she commanded as a spiritual teacher and her eventual death.

11-Ling-tsung.htm.title: 11 Ling-tsung, A Founder’s Journey
11-Ling-tsung.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
11-Ling-tsung.htm.intro: A biographical account of the Buddhist nun Ling-tsung from the Ssu Province, detailing her life from a young age when her family was driven from their home by nomadic tribes. The text explains that Ling-tsung had deep, unwavering faith and, after receiving help from the Three Treasures to return home, she dedicated her life to religious practice, becoming known for her sincerity, deep scholarship, and compassion for the suffering. A significant portion of the narrative focuses on her journey home, where she was aided by a white deer in crossing a river after calling upon the Three Treasures, and notes how her exemplary reputation reached Emperor Hsiao-wu. Ultimately, the account describes her peaceful death at age seventy-five, where her companion noted that her spirit had moved to the Western Paradise of Amita Buddha.

14-Hui-kuo.htm.title: 14 Hui-kuo, A Leader
14-Hui-kuo.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
14-Hui-kuo.htm.intro: A biographical account of Hui-kuo, a Buddhist nun active during the Sung Dynasty (420–479), detailing her ascetic and disciplined life and her founding of the Luminous Blessings Convent. The text describes her family origins and the generous gifts she received, which helped establish her monastic residence. A significant portion of the document focuses on a dialogue between Hui-kuo and the Central Asian missionary monk Guṇavarman concerning the validity of the status of Buddhist nuns and the proper training and obligation rules for women entering the monastic life in China. The source concludes by noting Hui-kuo's death at age seventy-seven in 433 and mentioning the strict observance of monastic rules by her disciples.

22-Hui-mu.htm.title: 22 Hui-mu, Her Unfolding Path
22-Hui-mu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
22-Hui-mu.htm.intro: The story of the nun Shih Hui-mu, a figure from the lineage of Shakyamuni, offering multiple versions of her life story and religious experiences. The text focuses on her early adoption of a religious life at age eleven, her dedication to chanting, and her ability to memorise vast amounts of scripture, highlighting her intellectual and spiritual aptitude. A central theme is the challenges Hui-mu faced in fully embracing monastic rules while caring for her elderly, sick mother, which forced her to temporarily live as a householder. The sources recount supernatural visions she experienced, including dreams and sightings of figures in golden robes, and the subsequent scepticism and questioning from her older brother regarding her religious path. The text confirms that Hui-mu later received full monastic admission and continued her spiritual practice, culminating in a vision of the Buddha Amitāyus before her death at age sixty-nine.

27-Seng-kuo.htm.title: 27 Seng-kuo, The Unbroken Lineage
27-Seng-kuo.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
27-Seng-kuo.htm.intro: A biographical account of the Buddhist nun Seng-kuo, who was born in 408 CE in Kuang-ling, detailing her life of exceptional devotion, rigorous asceticism, and meditative practice that led to her body appearing lifeless during deep meditation. A significant portion of the text discusses the challenges and historical precedents for Chinese women seeking full monastic ordination and the establishment of the Assembly of Nuns in China. Seng-kuo questioned the validity of the rituals for Chinese nuns, leading to the arrival of nuns from Sri Lanka who provided the full monastic obligations a second time in 434 CE, fully establishing the official Assembly of Nuns. The biography concludes by describing Seng-kuo’s final death during a period of meditation in 441 CE, where her body was mistaken for being in a profound yogic state.

34-Pao-hsien.htm.title: 34 Pao-hsien, Rector and Rule
34-Pao-hsien.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
34-Pao-hsien.htm.intro: A biographical account of the Buddhist nun Pao-hsien (401–477), focusing on her life, spiritual development, and influence during the Sung dynasty. The text details her decision to enter monastic life at age 16 after a period of extreme austerity during her mother’s mourning and notes her rigorous practice of meditation and monastic observance. A significant portion of the text addresses the controversy surrounding the validity of the full monastic obligation for Chinese nuns, which was debated because the initial transmission of the rules was considered incomplete by some. Pao-hsien played a crucial role when she and other nuns ultimately received the full monastic obligation from a delegation including nuns from Sri Lanka. The text concludes by noting her respected position as an administrator and her ability to settle disputes, confirming her high regard within the Buddhist community until her death at age seventy-seven.

39-Seng-ching.htm.title: 39 Seng-ching, A Path of Reverence
39-Seng-ching.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
39-Seng-ching.htm.intro: Biographical details about Seng-ching, a Buddhist nun whose life spanned the years 402–486, focusing on her origins, her commitment to a religious life, and her impact on the communities she served. The text outlines her early adoption as a disciple to the nun Pai of Establishing Peace Convent and details her remarkable devotion to scripture and ascetic practice, including memorising texts and adopting vegetarianism. Furthermore, the information describes significant events in her life, such as her travels to southern China with an official, her reception of complete monastic obligations, and the establishment of a convent for her and fellow nuns, which was supported by local families and figures like Emperor Ming. Ultimately, the sources record her death at the age of eighty-four and the inscription written to commemorate her virtuous life and lasting spiritual legacy.

42-Chih-sheng.htm.title: 42 Chih-sheng, Victorious Sagacity
42-Chih-sheng.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
42-Chih-sheng.htm.intro: A biographical account of the Buddhist nun Chih-sheng, detailing her life from a young age in the fifth century, when she expressed a profound desire to become a nun despite her grandmother’s initial reluctance. The narrative describes her devotion to monastic life, including her diligent study of scriptures, writing commentaries, and maintaining her purity amidst social and political turmoil. Chih-sheng’s significant interactions with imperial figures, such as the heir apparent Wen-hui, highlight her high standing and influence, with the text mentioning her giving lectures at the palace and earning deep respect from the imperial family. The source also recounts specific events, such as a monastery robbery and her disciplinary response, before concluding with a description of her death at age sixty-six and her honourable burial. Overall, the life presents Chih-sheng as a highly revered, sagacious figure who founded a convent and dedicated her life to Buddhist practice and teaching.

48-Hui-hsu.htm.title: 48 Hui-hsu, An Enlightened Farewell
48-Hui-hsu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
48-Hui-hsu.htm.intro: Hui-hsü was a Buddhist nun during the Sung dynasty, whose life and spiritual dedication are the focus of the historical account. This biographical material details her early life, including her family origins and her resolution to pursue a religious life by maintaining chastity and ascetic practices from a young age. The narrative highlights her significant relationships, particularly with Prince Yü-chang and his wife, who greatly respected her wisdom, sought her religious guidance, and provided her with resources and a place to reside and teach. The text concludes by noting her eventual return to the Collected Goodness Convent and records the date of her death at the age of sixty-nine.

52-Ching-hsiu.htm.title: 52 Ching-hsiu, Pure Refinement
52-Ching-hsiu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters based on Kathryn Ann Tsai’s translation of Pi-chiu-ni chuan entitled, Lives of the Nuns.
52-Ching-hsiu.htm.intro: A biographical account of Ching-hsiu, a nun who lived during the Liang Dynasty (502–557) in ancient China. The text details her early life, including her family background and her early inclination towards Buddhist precepts and compassion, despite her parents’ resistance to her becoming a vegetarian. It further explains her transition into a nun’s life at the age of twenty-nine, her commitment to the monastic rules, and her efforts to promote the Buddhist faith through study and teaching. The narrative recounts various miraculous occurrences and her eventual death at the age of eighty-nine, with the prediction that she would be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

Taoist-Masters.title: Seven Taoist Masters
Taoist-Masters.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Taoist-Masters.intro: Seven Taoist Masters is a folk novel about the founding of the Complete Reality school of Taoism. After years of hidden cultivation, he teaches internal alchemy to Ma Yü and Sun Pu-erh, who sacrifice their wealth. Wang later gathers six more disciples, testing them through harsh trials. Sun Pu-erh endures twelve years of hardship in Loyang, while Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un suffers repeated near-starvation before attaining the Tao. The seven masters overcome obstacles, reunite, and ultimately ascend to heaven, where they are honored by the Jade Emperor and invited to taste the immortal peach. The book closes with Ch’iu’s refusal to take the gift for himself alone.
Taoist-Masters.keywords: China, Taoism, Lao Tzu, Schools, Medieval

01-Mother-Wang.htm.title: 01 Mother Wang
01-Mother-Wang.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mother Wang from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
01-Mother-Wang.htm.intro: On a snowy night Mother Wang turns away two beggars, feeding monks instead; the beggars chide her charity as self-serving. They come to Wang T’ieh-hsin, who shelters them. Calling themselves Gold-Is-Heavy and Empty-Mind Ch’ang, they lead him over a bridge and up a mountain, where Empty-Mind Ch’ang picks seven golden lotus flowers, spirits of his seven future disciples, and gives them to him. He falls from a cliff, losing consciousness.

02-The-Bridge-to-the-Tao.htm.title: 02 The Bridge to the Tao
02-The-Bridge-to-the-Tao.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Bridge to the Tao from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
02-The-Bridge-to-the-Tao.htm.intro: Wang deciphers the beggars’ names as Chung-li Ch’üan and Lü Tung-pin and keeps their three-month appointment at the old bridge, though his wife insists robbers drugged him. The immortals reveal themselves; Lü teaches internal alchemy, eradicating ego and cultivating the true heart, then sends Wang to Shantung to gather his seven disciples, recalling the seven golden lotus flowers. Wang feigns a stroke, and a village doctor confirms a mild one.

03-Divine-Mission.htm.title: 03 The Divine Mission
03-Divine-Mission.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Divine Mission from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
03-Divine-Mission.htm.intro: For twelve years Wang Ch’ung-yang feigns illness in his study until his spirit can leave his body at will. The Lord of T’ai-pa orders him to Shantung Province to find his seven disciples. He vanishes from the locked room, but finds only fame-seekers and fortune-seekers. Rebuked by Lü and Chung-li Ch’üan, who split a mountainside, he hides in a Mount Chung-nan cave, then journeys to Ning-hai disguised as a beggar.

04-Seekers-of-the-Tao.htm.title: 04 Seekers of the Tao
04-Seekers-of-the-Tao.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Seekers of the Tao from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
