04-Seekers-of-the-Tao.htm.intro: Nearing forty and childless, wealthy Ma Yü and his wife Sun Yüan-chen sit in a garden pavilion in Ning-hai County, where she argues that riches and heirs are impermanent and urges him to seek immortality, explaining internal alchemy. They resolve to find a teacher and recognize the radiant beggar near the Ma mansion as Wang Ch’ung-yang, who has waited years for their gesture. Ma posts a servant and hurries out.

05-Taming-the-Heart.htm.title: 05 Taming the Heart
05-Taming-the-Heart.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Taming the Heart from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
05-Taming-the-Heart.htm.intro: The beggar Wang Ch’ung-yang enters Ma Yü’s mansion but refuses offers of comfort. Sun Yüan-chen wins him over by praising his freedom from attachment, and he agrees to teach them in the garden. When Ma Yü asks his name, Wang says he came for Ma’s wealth. Sun calls all riches impermanent; next morning he explains he needs the money to build a retreat for Tao seekers, and Ma is satisfied.

06-The-Inheritance.htm.title: 06 The Inheritance
06-The-Inheritance.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Inheritance from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
06-The-Inheritance.htm.intro: Ma Yü and Sun Yüan-chen ask to become his disciples, and Wang Ch’ung-yang demands they sign over their estate to loosen their attachment. At a clan dinner cousin Ma Ming rages and nephews spit at Wang. In the study Ma Yü bribes granduncle Ma Lung, uncle Ma Wen-fui and cousin Ma Liu with priceless antiques; they agree to witness the transfer, and Ma Liu whispers a scheme to silence dissent.

07-The-Transfer.htm.title: 07 The Transfer
07-The-Transfer.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Transfer from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
07-The-Transfer.htm.intro: Sun Yüan-chen’s plan works: Ma Liu persuades the clan, and Ma Yü’s whole estate is formally signed over to Wang Ch’ung-yang. Wang earns praise by funding widows, orphans, farmers’ debts and public works, and builds retreat huts in the mansion. Ma Yü and Sun Yüan-chen take vows as Ma Tan-yang and Sun Pu-erh, live apart as friends in the Tao, and hear Wang teach that Earlier Heaven cannot be described.

08-Cultivating-the-Tao.htm.title: 08 Cultivating the Tao
08-Cultivating-the-Tao.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Cultivating the Tao from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
08-Cultivating-the-Tao.htm.intro: Wang Ch’ung-yang draws a circle and dot to explain Wu-chi, T’ai-chi and original nature, then teaches Ma Tan-yang and Sun Pu-erh to eradicate liquor, sexual desire, riches and bad temper, with detailed instructions for the hour of tzu. After months of practice they stop seeking guidance. Wang appears separately to each; his talk of yin and yang copulating offends Sun Pu-erh, who flees and summons her husband, interrupting Ma’s lesson.

09-Illusions-of-the-Tao.htm.title: 09 Illusions of the Tao
09-Illusions-of-the-Tao.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Illusions of the Tao from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
09-Illusions-of-the-Tao.htm.intro: Sun Pu-erh tells Ma Tan-yang that Wang Ch’ung-yang entered her bedroom uninvited, though Wang had been with Ma all morning; his spirit had left his body. A month later the spirit returns, saying yin and yang must unite and the Yellow Woman must be go-between. She locks him in her room and finds it empty. Ma explains the teaching means internal energies, that she overused yang, and Sun Pu-erh understands.

10-Path-to-Immortality.htm.title: 10 Path to Immortality
10-Path-to-Immortality.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Path to Immortality from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
10-Path-to-Immortality.htm.intro: Rebuked for pride, Sun Pu-erh begs Wang Ch’ung-yang’s forgiveness. He describes the Great, Middle and Lower Vehicles; she chooses the Great. When Wang refuses to send her to Loyang, warning that her beauty invites rape and suicide, she pours cold water into hot oil, scarring her face. Wang teaches her internal alchemy; she feigns madness, bites a servant’s arm, hides in a haystack, and begs her way safely to Loyang.

11-Beggar-Woman.htm.title: 11 Beggar Woman
11-Beggar-Woman.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Beggar Woman from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
11-Beggar-Woman.htm.intro: In Loyang Sun Pu-erh begs as a madwoman until Chang San and Li Ssu come to molest her; hail and thorns bloody Chang San, and the city leaves her in peace for twelve years. In Shantung villagers test Wang Ch’ung-yang’s prophecy of rain on the twenty-third; it rains. He directs a man to his stolen water buffalo and tells a boy to ask his mother, where his brother’s letter awaits.

12-Path-to-Enlightenment.htm.title: 12 Path to Enlightenment
12-Path-to-Enlightenment.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Path to Enlightenment from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
12-Path-to-Enlightenment.htm.intro: T’an Ch’ang-chen, cured earlier by Wang, arrives at the Ma mansion with Hao T’ai-ku; Liu Ch’ang-sheng and Wang Yü-yang follow. Wang sets training rules and teaches meditation on ch’i and breath. Ch’iu Ch’u-chi, scorning fame, quietly slips from his brothers; Wang refuses him as too sharp-minded, so Ma Tan-yang makes him errand boy. Overhearing Wang on taming the heart, Ch’iu shouts aloud, is reprimanded, and resolves to tame his heart.

13-Eternal-Spring.htm.title: 13 Eternal Spring
13-Eternal-Spring.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Eternal Spring from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
13-Eternal-Spring.htm.intro: Ch’iu Ch’u-chi, eavesdropping again, interrupts Wang Ch’ung-yang’s lecture and is finally accepted, renamed Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un. Wang teaches stillness before the altar, knowing that only six of his students will attain the Tao. When Ch’iu disrupts once more, Wang departs south with Liu Ch’ang-sheng, Wang Yü-yang, T’an Ch’ang-chen and Hao T’ai-ku, leaving Ma Tan-yang behind. Most students scatter by dawn; Ch’iu follows anyway, and Ma quietly outfits him in Taoist robes.

14-Hard-Trials.htm.title: 14 Hard Trials
14-Hard-Trials.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Hard Trials from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
14-Hard-Trials.htm.intro: Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un begs rice and bread for Wang Ch’ung-yang, who repeatedly refuses his food and rebukes him to temper the youngest disciple. When the disciples warm themselves by a fire, Wang bolts them out in the snow; circulating internal energy keeps them warm till dawn. Sentenced to a hundred strokes for taking the blame, Ch’iu is spared when the others plead. Wang abandons the southern journey and returns to Ning-hai.

15-Death-of-Wang.htm.title: 15 Death of Wang
15-Death-of-Wang.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Death of Wang from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
15-Death-of-Wang.htm.intro: Feigning boils and a fatal illness, Wang Ch’ung-yang drives away all but six disciples, then dies after teaching balance of life and original nature, foretelling each one’s obstacles. The six carry his coffin toward Mount Chung-nan while a hidden benefactor in yellow robes supplies food. Ch’iu exposes him, is rebuked for betraying Heaven’s secrets, and provisions stop. At the burial place an old friend, warned in a dream, donates land.

16-Group-Disbands.htm.title: 16 The Group Disbands
16-Group-Disbands.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Group Disbands from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
16-Group-Disbands.htm.intro: At desolate Ta-wei Village, Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un and the disciples find a shrine tended by Wang’s cousin, who recounts the talismans that cured the plague and Wang saving Han-yang from fire with wine. Leaving funds for the shrine, they disband. Hao T’ai-ku, meditating beneath a seven-arched bridge, is mocked by a stone-polishing stranger for ‘dead sitting.’ T’an Ch’ang-chen, refused lodging by Ku Tsu-ting, resolves to lead him back to the Tao.

17-Frauds.htm.title: 17 Fraudulent Masters
17-Frauds.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Fraudulent Masters from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
17-Frauds.htm.intro: T’an Ch’ang-chen endures Ku Tsu-ting’s rebuff, meditating through snowfall until melted snow proves his mastery; Ku becomes his disciple, but T’an escapes the mansion by feigning advances on a servant girl. Meanwhile Wang Yü-yang reaches Fang County’s Immortals’ Meeting Place, where the boasting fraud Hun Yüan, lodged with Yao Chung-kao, denounces Buddhists and Taoists. Wang’s questions about balancing yin and yang and the ten months of pregnancy stump Hun Yüan.

18-Meditation-Duel.htm.title: 18 Meditation Duel
18-Meditation-Duel.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Meditation Duel from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
18-Meditation-Duel.htm.intro: At Yao Chung-kao’s mansion Wang expounds alchemical symbolism, humiliating the impostor Hun Yüan, who challenges him to a three-day meditation contest yet quits on the second day; Wang then vanishes. Liu Ch’ang-sheng, after three years at T’ai Shan, dreams he is driven from the Empress of Heaven’s palace for lingering sexual desire. T’an Ch’ang-chen tells of Hu Hsiang-yang’s plank test, and Liu resolves to train in brothels. Hao T’ai-ku appears.

19-Seventy-Two-Caves.htm.title: 19 Seventy-Two Caves
19-Seventy-Two-Caves.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Seventy-Two Caves from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
19-Seventy-Two-Caves.htm.intro: At Lao-tzu’s birthplace the four disciples, moved by his legend, honor the Ancient One with poems; T’an Ch’ang-chen then exposes Liu Ch’ang-sheng’s dream of the Empress of Heaven and his plan to dissolve lust in brothels. They part ways. Reaching Hua Shan, Hao T’ai-ku digs seventy-two caves over ten years, surrendering each to arriving hermits. His impatient disciple severs his rope; Hao survives, then leaps from the cliff and vanishes.

20-In-a-Brothel.htm.title: 20 In a Brothel
20-In-a-Brothel.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting In a Brothel from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
20-In-a-Brothel.htm.intro: As jeweler Ch’ang Sheng-tzu, Liu Ch’ang-sheng passes a year in a Su-hang brothel, unmoved by Madam Yü, boiling tea and baking cakes on his tan-t’ien. Bodhidharma, seeing a purple cloud, probes his coming and going, then departs. Wang Yü-yang fans candles to flame; Liu sends him south, saying, ‘I shall leave when I leave,’ then ascends after three years in the eastern mountains. Wang Yü-yang and T’an attain the Tao.

21-Sun-Pu-erh-Ascends.htm.title: 21 Sun Pu-erh Ascends
21-Sun-Pu-erh-Ascends.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sun Pu-erh Ascends from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
21-Sun-Pu-erh-Ascends.htm.intro: Sun Pu-erh, twelve years a mad woman in Loyang, transforms two branches into a jesting couple, drawing the mayor’s decree that she be burned. Rising from the flames on clouds, she promises the city prosperity and is enshrined. Returning to Ning-hai, she shames Ma Tan-yang with Lü Tung-pin’s tale and a boiling bath; he abandons his mansion. At Wang Ch’ung-yang’s tomb he teaches Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un nonattachment, then snow traps them.

22-Nine-Day-Fast.htm.title: 22 A Nine Day Fast
22-Nine-Day-Fast.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting A Nine Day Fast from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
22-Nine-Day-Fast.htm.intro: Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un’s wish to feed Ma Tan-yang brings an earth god’s gift of rice, yet Ma angrily splits their cushion and vanishes underground to the Kao mountains, attaining the Tao. A fortune-teller takes Ch’iu’s begged bowl and foretells starvation, citing Po I and Shu Ch’i. Ch’iu fasts nine days and nights in a deep gorge until a flood floats him a red peach; strengthened, he climbs out of the canyon.

23-Converting-Robbers.htm.title: 23 Converting Robbers
23-Converting-Robbers.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Converting Robbers from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
23-Converting-Robbers.htm.intro: Ch’iu fasts nine days in a T’ai Shan shrine until robbers led by Chao Pi arrive. They force food into his mouth and threaten him, but Chao Pi relents; Ch’iu explains karma, refuses their silver, and persuades them to abandon robbery. Later, about to hang himself, he is halted by the herb-gatherer T’ai-pai, who teaches that destiny lies in the heart, not the face; Ch’iu resolves to finish his training.

24-Offering-His-Head.htm.title: 24 Offering His Head
24-Offering-His-Head.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Offering His Head from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
24-Offering-His-Head.htm.intro: The herb gatherer frees Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un, who abandons his fear of death. At a wide stony river he builds a shack and ferries travelers across for six years. Three men dressed as police captains test him; when the bandit’s head is swept away, Ch’iu offers his own. The Heavenly Lords grant him an immortal body. Later he is humbled at the fortune-teller’s, monsters of the mind return, and Heaven calls.

25-Mansion-Destroyed.htm.title: 25 Mansion Destroyed
25-Mansion-Destroyed.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mansion Destroyed from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
25-Mansion-Destroyed.htm.intro: Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un hauls a boulder uphill and rolls it down for three years to dissolve his illusions, then warns the miser Wang Yün, who answers with horse dung. Ch’iu secretly tells the kind servant Ch’un-Hua to hide at the Kuan-Yin shrine when the stone lions’ eyes redden. An earthquake flood destroys the Wang mansion; she survives. At Dragon Gate gorge, Ch’iu prays and three days of rain save the crops.

26-The-Wager.htm.title: 26 The Wager
26-The-Wager.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Wager from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
26-The-Wager.htm.intro: Drought threatens the capital, so the emperor summons Ch’iu, whose three-day prayer to the Jade Emperor brings rain and saves the harvest. Ch’iu then predicts the empress bears a son, but Zen Master Pai-yün of White Cloud Monastery divines a girl and wagers the monastery against Ch’iu’s head. Ch’iu’s fairy swaps the female spirit for a male one. The court sees a prince, and Pai-yün’s elder demands matching Taoist monks.

27-White-Cloud-Monastery.htm.title: 27 White Cloud Monastery
27-White-Cloud-Monastery.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting White Cloud Monastery from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
27-White-Cloud-Monastery.htm.intro: Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un answers Zen Master Pai-yün’s challenge by blowing his whisk: dry leaves become Taoist monks, one ascending for each departing Buddhist. He takes White Cloud Monastery, preaches true renunciation, and welcomes Chao Pi and his reformed bandits as disciples. Meanwhile the empress, guilt-ridden over her changed child, sends for Pai-yün; he recounts Chang Kuo-lao’s poisoned wine and urges the same test. Then she invites Ch’iu to a poisoned dinner.

28-Surviving-Poison.htm.title: 28 Surviving Poison
28-Surviving-Poison.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Surviving Poison from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
28-Surviving-Poison.htm.intro: The empress tests Ch’iu Ch’ang-ch’un at court with three cups of poison. Forewarned, he orders twenty-four tubs of cold water at White Cloud Monastery, drinks, and soaks out the poison, though the shallow last tub leaves him bald. He softens a gold bar with internal energy into a headband. Zen Master Pai-yün repents; the emperor decrees a Buddhist monastery. A hot-tempered monk plots West Wind Monastery, which legend says burned.

29-The-Gift-of-Immortality.htm.title: 29 The Gift of Immortality
29-The-Gift-of-Immortality.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Gift of Immortality from Seven Taoist Masters together with further information.
29-The-Gift-of-Immortality.htm.intro: Ch’iu wrote Journey to the West in solitude at White Cloud Monastery, warning of the mind’s wild horses and mischievous monkey; Pai-yün answered with Legends of the Gods. Ascending to the Palace of Heaven, Ch’iu found the six disciples awaiting the Jade Emperor’s gift. The Lords ranked Sun Pu-erh seventh. Ch’iu refused the gift until the red-bearded Lord of Thunder pledged to guard all seekers; then the immortal peach ripened.

Basho.title: Matsuo Bashō’s Walking Trips
Basho.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from Matsuo Bashō’s Walking Trips together with further information.
inspired by the writings of Matsuo Bashō in 17th century Japan
Basho.intro: These storybooks are based on the travel diaries and poetic logs of the celebrated Japanese writer Matsuo Bashō, chronicling several of his long-distance pilgrimages. Through a blend of lyrical prose and haiku, the texts document his experiences visiting sacred shrines, historical landmarks, and the homes of fellow poets. The narratives illustrate a deep commitment to nature and a rejection of worldly comforts, as the author adopts the persona of a weather-exposed skeleton or a humble wanderer. Throughout his travels in regions such as Ise, Yoshino, and Kashima, Bashō captures moments of profound spiritual reflection, grief over family loss, and the quiet beauty of the changing seasons. By recording these encounters with both the natural landscape and local people, the sources provide an intimate look at the artistic philosophy and solitary lifestyle of a dedicated poet-monk.

toc.label: 01 The Records of a Weather-Exposed Skeleton
02 A Visit to the Kashima Shrine
03 The Records of a Travel-Worn Satchel
05 The Narrow Road to the Deep North

01-Skeleton.htm.title: 01 The Records of a Weather-Exposed Skeleton
01-Skeleton.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Records of a Weather-Exposed Skeleton from Matsuo Bashō’s Walking Trips together with further information.
01-Skeleton.htm.intro: In The Records of a Weather-Exposed Skeleton (Nozarashi Kikō), Matsuo Bashō travels across 17th-century Japan. Departing Edo, he journeys through mist, rain, and mountains—crossing Hakone, Ise, and Yoshino—while reflecting on impermanence, loss, and nature’s quiet power. Reaching his hometown, he mourns his mother’s death over her hair which was preserved. Along the way, Bashō and his companion Chiri compose haiku, interweaving solitude, grief, and beauty.

02-Shrine.htm.title: 02 A Visit to the Kashima Shrine
02-Shrine.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting A Visit to the Kashima Shrine from Matsuo Bashō’s Walking Trips together with further information.
02-Shrine.htm.intro: In A Visit to the Kashima Shrine (Kashima Kikō), Matsuo Bashō travels with two companions to view the mid-autumn moon at the sacred shrine. Journeying past fields, rivers, and Mount Tsukuba, they lodge with a hermit priest. Though rain initially hides the moon, it breaks through at dawn. Together with local friends and hosts, they compose poems reflecting on nature, rural life, and impermanence.

03-Satchel.htm.title: 03 The Records of a Travel-Worn Satchel
03-Satchel.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Records of a Travel-Worn Satchel from Matsuo Bashō’s Walking Trips together with further information.
03-Satchel.htm.intro: In The Records of a Travel-Worn Satchel (Oi no Kobumi), Matsuo Bashō reflects on his lifelong devotion to poetry as an artistic mind seeking alignment with nature. Embarking on a journey across Japan, he travels lightly, composing verses, visiting holy sites, and reflecting on ancient masters. Embracing the uncertainty and freedom of the road, Bashō finds deep spiritual meaning, beauty, and poetic resonance in the landscapes and people he encounters.

04-Village.htm.title: 04 A Visit to Sarashina Village
04-Village.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting A Visit to Sarashina Village from Matsuo Bashō’s Walking Trips together with further information.
04-Village.htm.intro: In A Visit to Sarashina Village (Sarashina Kikō), Matsuo Bashō travels along the treacherous Kiso road with his disciple Etsujin and a servant to view the full moon at Mount Obasute. Navigating dangerous mountain paths, precipices, and comical misadventures, Bashō reflects on human vulnerability and Buddhist providence. Reaching a humble inn, he drinks under the moonlight and composes verses celebrating autumn’s solitude, local life, and Zenkōji Temple.

05-Narrow.htm.title: 05 The Narrow Road to the Deep North
05-Narrow.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Narrow Road to the Deep North from Matsuo Bashō’s Walking Trips together with further information.
05-Narrow.htm.intro: In The Narrow Road to the Deep North (Oku no Hosomichi), Matsuo Bashō embarks on a poetic pilgrimage across northern Japan with his companion Sora. Wandering through holy mountains, historic ruins, and scenic bays like Matsushima, Bashō contemplates transience, nature, and ancient history. Experiencing physical hardships, warm hospitality, and spiritual reflection along the road, he captures timeless moments in linked verse and haiku before concluding his journey at Ōgaki.

Issa.title: Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life
Issa.summary: high-definition creative commons posters from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
Issa.intro: These storybooks are based on The Spring of My Life by Kobayashi Issa, which blend poetic haiku and tanka with prose to chronicle the author’s observations on nature, spirituality, and human suffering. The text features a variety of Buddhist-themed parables, including stories of a priest’s self-induced New Year’s tears and the tragic drowning of a young monk-in-training. Throughout the narrative, the author reflects on his own aging and isolation, drawing poignant parallels between his difficult life and the survival of a stunted chestnut tree. Additional entries explore the fragility of existence through accounts of supernatural vengeance, the innocence of the author’s young daughter, and the mistreatment of stepchildren in regional folklore. Ultimately, these sources serve as a meditative travelogue that seeks spiritual meaning within the fleeting beauty and inherent pain of the changing seasons.

01-The-New-Year.htm.title: 01 The New Year
01-The-New-Year.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The New Year from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
01-The-New-Year.htm.intro: This explores spiritual reflections on the New Year and spring. It recounts a priest’s devotion to Buddhist teachings over worldly greetings, a path the narrator also follows through a life of humble simplicity. The collection features haiku capturing the essence of the changing season, from temple festivals to blooming cherry blossoms. Together, these pieces emphasize a deep connection between nature and spiritual mindfulness.

02-A-Tragic-Death.htm.title: 02 A Tragic Death
02-A-Tragic-Death.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting A Tragic Death from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
02-A-Tragic-Death.htm.intro: On a spring morning, young Takamaru drowned while gathering herbs. His body was recovered with flowers for his parents, whose grief challenged their religious composure. During the cremation, the narrator composed a tanka reflecting on life’s tragic transience. The text contemplates whether flowers, like humans, possess a life force and seek nirvana. The narrative captures the fragile intersection of human emotion and nature’s cycles through poignant prose and evocative poetry.

03-Heavenly-Music.htm.title: 03 Heavenly Music
03-Heavenly-Music.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Heavenly Music from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
03-Heavenly-Music.htm.intro: The text weaves together prose and haiku to explore the intersections of nature and spirituality. The narrator investigates reports of mysterious and beautiful heavenly music, eventually finding profound meaning in a bush warbler’s morning song. Through seasonal poems, the text captures transitions from spring rain to summer moons. It documents travels to Shimabara, observations of cherry blossoms, and personal reflections on illness within a suffering, transient world.

04-Life-Ebbing-Away.htm.title: 04 Life Ebbing Away
04-Life-Ebbing-Away.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Life Ebbing Away from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
04-Life-Ebbing-Away.htm.intro: The narrator embarks on a journey to Japan’s far north to improve his haiku. Approaching sixty, he reflects on his mortality and feels humbled by the legacy of the Zen poet Saigyō. Leaving home with a sense of finality, he crosses the Shirakawa Barrier. The text also includes several poignant poems contemplating idleness, the brevity of life, and nature’s fleeting beauty, ranging from mosquito larvae to dragonflies and radiant fireflies.

05-07-Visions-of-Nature.htm.title: 05-07 Visions of Nature
05-07-Visions-of-Nature.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Visions of Nature from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
05-07-Visions-of-Nature.htm.intro: The text explores nature and artifice through personal anecdotes and poetry. It describes a friend’s witty prank involving paper peonies hidden among real ones, highlighting the contrast between life and imitation. The author also examines the cultural significance of toads, from children’s burial games to their roles in ancient mythology and poetry. Finally, several short verses beautifully capture various fleeting, atmospheric moments found deeply within the quiet, serene, natural landscape.

08-11-Resilience.htm.title: 08-11 Suffering and Resilience
08-11-Resilience.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Suffering and Resilience from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
08-11-Resilience.htm.intro: The sources explore suffering and endurance through nature and Japanese folklore. A narrator compares their unhappy life to a stunted chestnut tree that is constantly crushed by winter snows. Several poems and prose sections further detail the bitter cruelty often endured by stepchildren, including physical abuse and starvation. Finally, a miraculous stone Buddha intervenes to save a starving boy, prompting his cruel stepmother to show kindness.

12-Childhood.htm.title: 12 The Joys of Childhood
12-Childhood.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Joys of Childhood from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
12-Childhood.htm.intro: The narrator reflects on the birth and early years of his young daughter, Sato. He describes her innocent, wandering mind and natural grace, viewing her as closer to Buddhahood than his own aging self. While he struggles with worldly distractions, Sato’s presence brings profound joy to both parents, transcending the exhaustion of daily care. Accompanying poems further highlight the precious, ephemeral nature of childhood innocence within their spiritual and natural world.

13-14-Losing-a-Child.htm.title: 13-14 Losing a Child
13-14-Losing-a-Child.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Losing a Child from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
13-14-Losing-a-Child.htm.intro: This text explores the profound grief and enduring love associated with the loss or separation of children. Through poignant personal narratives and collected poetry, it depicts a divorced mother’s longing, a father’s agonizing witness to his daughter’s fatal smallpox, and the universal fragility of human life. These verses reflect on the “world of dew,” capturing the heartbreaking madness of parental bereavement and the essential oneness of nature.

15-18-Cruelty-and-Seclusion.htm.title: 15-18 Cruelty and Seclusion
15-18-Cruelty-and-Seclusion.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Cruelty and Seclusion from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
15-18-Cruelty-and-Seclusion.htm.intro: This text focuses on poems lamenting cruelty to animals, inspired by a mother crow crying for her caged baby, innocent cranes on hunting grounds, and a nursing doe. It then depicts the author’s cold mountain village on Kurohime Mountain, blending observations of stunted nature with contemplative verses on legend, cuckoos, and the peace of a quiet life.

19-21-Ageing-and-Transition.htm.title: 19-21 Ageing and Transition
19-21-Ageing-and-Transition.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ageing and Transition from Kobayashi Issa’s The Spring of My Life together with further information.
19-21-Ageing-and-Transition.htm.intro: The author reluctantly returns to Edo in winter, reflecting on his aging, poverty, and seasonal transitions. He observes children’s voices, folk practices, and Shinto customs as the New Year approaches. Finally, writing on December 29, 1819, at age fifty-seven, he rejects obsessive anxieties over spiritual salvation. Instead, he advocates surrendering self-obsessions to follow the way of Buddha, finding ultimate peace of mind as he bids farewell to the passing year.

Nalanda-Masters.title: The Nālandā Masters
Nalanda-Masters.summary: high-definition creative commons posters from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
Nalanda-Masters.intro: These storybooks record the legendary biographies and intellectual legacies of influential Buddhist philosophers from Nālandā University, including Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Asaṅga. The texts describe the miraculous origins, rigorous spiritual training, and supernatural feats of these figures as they established the foundations of the Madhyamaka and Yogācāra schools. Detailed accounts emphasize their literary contributions, listing numerous commentaries and treatises written to clarify complex doctrines or defeat theological opponents in debate. Themes of divine prophecy, the pursuit of longevity through magic, and the preservation of the Dharma during times of persecution are central to these narratives. The sources illustrate how these teachers were viewed as enlightened guardians of the faith who secured the survival of the Highest Doctrine for future generations.

01-Nagarjuna.htm.title: 1. Nāgārjuna
01-Nagarjuna.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Nāgārjuna from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
01-Nagarjuna.htm.intro: Born in Vidarbha to a rich Brāhmaņa, Nāgārjuna was prophecied to die young but extended his life by ordaining at Nalanda and reciting Amitāyus magic formulas. As Nalanda's verger, he used alchemy to feed monks during a famine, leading to a temporary exile where he built countless sanctuaries. He later obtained advanced magical powers, defeated heretics, and recovered sacred texts from the Nāgas.

02-Aryadeva.htm.title: 2. Āryādeva
02-Aryadeva.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Āryādeva from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
02-Aryadeva.htm.intro: Miraculously born in a lotus on Simhala island, Aryadeva was adopted by a king before becoming Nāgārjuna's foremost spiritual disciple. Renowned for his vast mastery of orthodox and heterodox philosophies, he famously sacrificed an eye to a tree goddess while traveling to Nalanda. There, he triumphantly vanquished the formidable heretic Matrceta, defending the Buddhist Doctrine and establishing a prolific legacy of Tantric and philosophical treatises.

03-Candragomin.htm.title: 3. Candragomin
03-Candragomin.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Candragomin from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
03-Candragomin.htm.intro: Born in Bengal, the scholar Candragomin abandoned his marriage to Princess Tārā because she shared her name with his tutelary deity. Condemned by the king to be drowned in the Ganges, he was miraculously saved when the goddess Tārā formed the island of Candra. He later entered Nalanda, famously mastering Pāṇini's grammar and engaging in historic intellectual debates with the Madhyamika master Candrakīrti.

04-Candrakirti.htm.title: 4. Candrakirti
04-Candrakirti.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Candrakirti from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
04-Candrakirti.htm.intro: Born in Samana, Candrakīrti became a sublime Pandit by mastering the Sūtras and Tantras under the lineage of Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva. He possessed extraordinary miraculous powers, such as milking a painting of a cow and telekinetically moving stone columns. He authored foundational Madhyamika texts, including the Madhyamika-avatāra, alongside his famous "sun and moon" commentaries: the Prasannapadā and the Pradīpa-uddyotana.

05-Aryasanga.htm.title: 5. Āryāsaṅga
05-Aryasanga.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Āryāsaṅga from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
05-Aryasanga.htm.intro: After heretics repeatedly burned Buddhist temples and texts, a devout Brāhmaṇa woman named Prasannaçila vowed to give birth to sons who would propagate and preserve the endangered Abhidharma. Her union with a Kṣatriya produced Asanga, whom she fiercely dedicated to spiritual practice. Asanga became a celebrated Saint, spreading Mahāyāna doctrines widely and obtaining the profound Dharmasrotah-samādhi after years of intensive forest meditation.

06-Vasubandhu.htm.title: 6. Vasubandhu
06-Vasubandhu.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Vasubandhu from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
06-Vasubandhu.htm.intro: Born as the younger son of Prasannaçila, Vasubandhu was educated in Kashmir, where he effortlessly mastered the Mahāvibhāṣā and the seven fundamental Abhidharma treatises. Initially criticizing the Mahāyāna teachings of his elder brother Asanga, he was eventually converted by him. Vasubandhu went on to write highly celebrated commentaries, establishing an immense renown for his skill in discriminating reality and expanding Buddhist philosophy.

07-Sthiramati.htm.title: 7. Sthiramati
07-Sthiramati.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sthiramati from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
07-Sthiramati.htm.intro: Sthiramati was a brilliant student of Vasubandhu who surpassed his master in the specific study of the Abhidharma. Tradition holds that in his past life, he was a dove that gained spiritual merit simply by listening to Vasubandhu recite sacred texts. Reborn as a human, he quickly mastered the five sciences, studied at Nalanda, authored numerous scholarly commentaries, and trained eminent pupils like Pūrṇavardhana.

08-Dignaga.htm.title: 8. Dignāga
08-Dignaga.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Dignāga from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
08-Dignaga.htm.intro: Initially ordained in the Vātsiputrīya sect, Dignāga was expelled by his preceptor after using rigorous logic to reject their literal concept of an "Ego". He subsequently sought out Vasubandhu, becoming a master of Logic and Vijñānavāda. Guided directly by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, he composed the seminal Pramāṇa-samuccaya, systematically refuting heretical philosophers and firmly establishing the golden age of Buddhist epistemology and dialectics.

09-Dharmakirti.htm.title: 9. Dharmakīrti
09-Dharmakirti.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Dharmakīrti from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
09-Dharmakirti.htm.intro: Born into a heretical Brāhmaṇic family, Dharmakīrti turned to Buddhism and vowed to vanquish all heretics after being driven away by his uncle Kumārila. He studied Dignāga's Pramāṇa-samuccaya three times under Īśvarasena, ultimately correcting his teacher’s own misunderstandings of the text. Dharmakīrti composed the monumental Pramāṇa-vārtika, predicting that his profound logic would match the deep, vast nature of the ocean.

10-Haribhadra.htm.title: 10. Haribhadra
10-Haribhadra.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Haribhadra from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
10-Haribhadra.htm.intro: Born into a heretical Brāhmaṇic family, Dharmakīrti turned to Buddhism and vowed to vanquish all heretics after being driven away by his uncle Kumārila. He studied Dignāga's Pramāṇa-samuccaya three times under Īśvarasena, ultimately correcting his teacher’s own misunderstandings of the text. Dharmakīrti composed the monumental Pramāṇa-vārtika, predicting that his profound logic would match the deep, vast nature of the ocean.

11-Santideva.htm.title: 11. Śāntideva
11-Santideva.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Śāntideva from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
11-Santideva.htm.intro: Prince Śāntivarman fled his impending coronation after the deity Mañjuśrī claimed the throne in a dream. Ordained as Śāntideva at Nālandā, he secretly received deep teachings from Mañjuśrī while other monks mocked his external routine of eating, sleeping, and walking. Labeled ‘Bhu-Su-Ku’ and deemed lazy, he surprised his detractors by masterfully reciting profound treatises, proving his immense sanctity and internal realization.

12-Grammar.htm.title: The Grammatical Lineage
12-Grammar.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Grammatical Lineage from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
12-Grammar.htm.intro: Prophesied to achieve Enlightenment, Pāṇini authored foundational grammatical treatises. The text recounts that early divine grammars like Sarvajñāna's perished, while Indra composed the Indravyākaraṇa. When the sage Bṛhaspati mastered Indra's work and grew proud, Indra humbled him by demonstrating that total grammatical science resembles a vast ocean, while Bṛhaspati's complete knowledge equals merely a single drop extracted with a blade of grass.

13-The-Loss-of-the-Doctrine.htm.title: The Loss of the Doctrine
13-The-Loss-of-the-Doctrine.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Loss of the Doctrine from Buston’s History of Buddhism together with further information.
13-The-Loss-of-the-Doctrine.htm.intro: In the Candragarbha-paripṛcchā, the Buddha predicts the gradual decay of his Doctrine across successive 500-year epochs. Spiritual practice weakens as kings, citizens, and monks abandon genuine internal realization for hypocritical outward show and worldly wealth. As protective deities depart, famine, plagues, and relentless warfare consume the land, punctuated only briefly by fleeting periods of temporal relief brought by surviving righteous practitioners.

Buddhism-in-Tibet.title: Buddhism in Tibet
Buddhism-in-Tibet.summary: high-definition creative commons posters from Buddhism in Tibet together with further information.
Buddhism-in-Tibet.intro: These stroybooks provide a comprehensive look at the foundational figures and evolutionary history of Tibetan Buddhism through a series of illustrated biographical summaries. The collection highlights the three great Dharma Kings who utilized political power and strategic alliances to establish the faith, alongside Indian mahāsiddhas like Padmasambhava who introduced esoteric tantric practices. It details the emergence of major spiritual lineages, such as the Sakya, Kagyu, Nyingma, and Gelug schools, through the dedicated work of prolific translators and monastic reformers. The texts also honor prominent female masters like Yeshe Tsogyal and Machig Labdron, who shaped the tradition’s meditative and philosophical depth. Collectively, these sources illustrate how Tibet transformed from a fragmented warrior society into a sophisticated center of Buddhist scholarship and practice over several centuries. Through the lives of these saints and scholars, the archives document the systematic preservation and translation of sacred teachings that define the region’s unique religious identity.

01-Songsten-Gampo.htm.title: 1. Songsten Gampo (1st Dharma King)
01-Songsten-Gampo.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Songsten Gampo (1st Dharma King) together with further information.
01-Songsten-Gampo.htm.intro: Songsten Gampo (c. 605–650) was the 33rd Tibetan king and the primary founder of the Tibetan Empire. Credited with introducing Buddhism to Tibet, he strategically married Princess Wencheng of China and Princess Bhrikuti of Nepal, who brought sacred Buddha images to Lhasa. He established the first Tibetan script and a code of laws based on Buddhist principles. His reign transformed a fragmented warrior culture into a centralized, literate state, earning him recognition as an emanation of Avalokiteśvara.

02-Sadmarkar.htm.title: 2. Sadmarkar (Songsten’s Sister)
02-Sadmarkar.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sadmarkar (Songsten’s Sister) together with further information.
02-Sadmarkar.htm.intro: Princess Sadmarkar (7th Century) played a pivotal role in the expansion of the Tibetan Empire through strategic diplomacy. Sent by her brother, Songsten Gampo, to marry the King of Zhangzhung, she found herself isolated in a loveless political alliance. According to legend, she sent a cryptic message hidden in a song and a gift of silk to her brother, signaling the King of Zhangzhung’s betrayal. This intelligence allowed Songsten Gampo to conquer Zhangzhung, unifying the Tibetan plateau.

03-Trisong-Detsen.htm.title: 3. Trisong Detsen (2nd Dharma King)
03-Trisong-Detsen.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Trisong Detsen (2nd Dharma King) together with further information.
03-Trisong-Detsen.htm.intro: As the 38th King of Tibet, Trisong Detsen (742–797) was the principal architect of the First Diffusion of Buddhism. Rejecting the influence of the indigenous Bön priests, he invited the scholar Śāntarakṣita and the master Padmasambhava to establish the first monastery at Samye. He presided over the Great Debate at Samye, where Indian gradualism was chosen over Chinese sudden enlightenment. His patronage ensured that Buddhism became the official state religion, cementing Tibet’s spiritual identity.

04-Santaraksita.htm.title: 4. Śāntarakṣita (Monastic Founder)
04-Santaraksita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Śāntarakṣita (Monastic Founder) together with further information.
04-Santaraksita.htm.intro: A renowned Indian scholar and abbot of Nālandā, Śāntarakṣita (725–788) was invited to Tibet to establish a formal monastic lineage. Known as the Bodhisattva Abbot, he integrated Madhyamaka philosophy with Yogācāra logic. Facing local resistance and natural disasters, he advised the King to invite Padmasambhava to subdue the local spirits. Together, they founded Samye Monastery, where Śāntarakṣita ordained the first seven Tibetan monks, ensuring the survival of the Vinaya in the snowy land.

05-Padmasambhava.htm.title: 5. Padmasambhava (Tantric Master)
05-Padmasambhava.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Padmasambhava (Tantric Master) together with further information.
05-Padmasambhava.htm.intro: The Lotus-Born Guru Rinpoche (8th Century) is revered as the second Buddha in Tibet. A powerful tantric mahāsiddha from Oḍḍiyana, he was invited by King Trisong Detsen to subdue the demonic forces obstructing the construction of Samye Monastery. Through his mastery of ritual and meditation, he converted local deities into protectors of the Dharma. He hid Terma (hidden treasures) across the landscape to be discovered by future masters, ensuring the vitality of the Nyingma lineage.

06-Yeshe-Tsogyal.htm.title: 6. Yeshe Tsogyal (Mother of Tibetan Buddhism)
06-Yeshe-Tsogyal.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Yeshe Tsogyal (Mother of Tibetan Buddhism) together with further information.
06-Yeshe-Tsogyal.htm.intro: Yeshe Tsogyal (757–817) is the preeminent female figure in Tibetan Buddhism. As the primary consort and disciple of Padmasambhava, she possessed a photographic memory, allowing her to record and codify his vast tantric teachings. Through her intense ascetic practice in caves, she achieved full enlightenment. She is responsible for concealing the Terma treasures and remains the ultimate role model for practitioners seeking realization in a female form.

07-Vimalamitra.htm.title: 7. Vimalamitra (Dzogchen Master)
07-Vimalamitra.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Vimalamitra (Dzogchen Master) together with further information.
07-Vimalamitra.htm.intro: Vimalamitra was an 8th-century Indian master who played a crucial role in bringing the Deepest Essence of the Great Perfection (Dzogchen) to Tibet. Invited by King Trisong Detsen, he worked alongside Padmasambhava and Vairocana to translate essential tantric texts. His legacy, the Vima Nyingtig, remains one of the most profound instruction sets in the Nyingma tradition. He is said to have achieved the rainbow body and promised to reappear in Tibet every century.

08-Ralpachen.htm.title: 8. Ralpachen (3rd Dharma King)
08-Ralpachen.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ralpachen (3rd Dharma King) together with further information.
08-Ralpachen.htm.intro: King Ralpachen (806–838) was the most devout of the three Dharma Kings, legendary for his extreme piety—he reportedly tied ribbons to his long hair so monks could sit on them. He standardized Tibetan translations through the Mahāvyutpatti dictionary, ensuring consistency across all Buddhist texts. However, his heavy taxation to support the clergy led to a political backlash. He was eventually assassinated by his brother, Langdarma, marking a temporary end to the Tibetan Empire.

09-Atisa-Dipankara.htm.title: 9. Atiśa Dīpaṅkara (Lamrim Master)
09-Atisa-Dipankara.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Atiśa Dīpaṅkara (Lamrim Master) together with further information.
09-Atisa-Dipankara.htm.intro: The arrival of the Bengali master Atiśa (982–1054) in 1042 sparked the Second Diffusion of Buddhism in Tibet. He revitalized the Dharma by emphasizing ethical discipline and the integration of Sūtra and Tantra. His seminal work, A Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment, introduced the Lamrim (Graduated Path) framework. This systematic approach corrected many tantric abuses of the era and laid the foundational structure for the Kadam, and later, the Gelug schools.

10-Drokmi.htm.title: 10. Drokmi Śākya Yeshe (Sakya Master
10-Drokmi.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting 10. Drokmi Śākya Yeshe (Sakya Master together with further information.
10-Drokmi.htm.intro: Drokmi Śākya Yeshe (992–1072) was a prolific translator and the foundational figure of the Sakya tradition’s Path and Result (Lamdré) teachings. He spent many years in India studying under great mahāsiddhas like Virūpa. Upon returning to Tibet, he transmitted these esoteric instructions to Khön Könchok Gyalpo. His focus on strict translation and the synthesis of tantric practice with scholastic study defined the intellectual and meditative rigor that became the hallmark of the Sakya lineage.

11-Marpa.htm.title: 11. Marpa Lotsāwa (The Great Translator)
11-Marpa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Marpa Lotsāwa (The Great Translator) together with further information.
11-Marpa.htm.intro: Marpa (1012–1097) was a rugged, householder lama who made three perilous journeys to India to bring the Kagyu teachings to Tibet. Studying under Naropa and Maitripa, he mastered the Six Dharmas and Mahāmudra. Known for his fierce personality, he tested his main disciple, Milarepa, through grueling trials. By translating key Sanskrit texts into Tibetan and establishing a lineage based on direct experience, Marpa became the forefather of the Kagyu school’s oral transmission.

12-Khon-Konchok-Gyelpo.htm.title: 12. Khön Könchok Gyalpo (Sakya Trizin)
12-Khon-Konchok-Gyelpo.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Khön Könchok Gyalpo (Sakya Trizin) together with further information.
12-Khon-Konchok-Gyelpo.htm.intro: A member of the noble Khön family, Könchok Gyalpo (1034–1102) founded the Sakya Monastery in 1073. Witnessing the corruption of the Old Nyingma practices in his region, he sought out the New translations from Drokmi Śākya Yeshe. By establishing a permanent seat for his family’s spiritual lineage, he transitioned the Khön clan from ancient rituals to the systematic New Translation (Sarma) schools. This act laid the institutional foundation for the powerful Sakya sect.

13-Machig-Labdron.htm.title: 13. Machig Labdron (Chöd Master)
13-Machig-Labdron.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Machig Labdron (Chöd Master) together with further information.
13-Machig-Labdron.htm.intro: Machig Labdron (1055–1149) was a 11th-century female master who developed the unique practice of Chöd (Cutting Through). Combining Prajñāpāramitā philosophy with tantric methods, her practice involves offering one’s own body as a feast to gods and demons to sever the root of ego-clinging. Remarkably, Chöd is one of the few lineages that originated in Tibet and was subsequently exported back to India. She remains an iconic symbol of fearless compassion and female wisdom.

14-Milarepa.htm.title: 14. Jetsun Milarepa (Great Yogi)
14-Milarepa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Jetsun Milarepa (Great Yogi) together with further information.
14-Milarepa.htm.intro: Milarepa (1040–1123) is perhaps Tibet’s most beloved saint. After using black magic to avenge his family, he sought out Marpa to purify his karma. Following years of grueling labor and solitary meditation in high mountain caves, he achieved enlightenment in a single lifetime. Dressed only in a thin cotton robe despite the Himalayan cold, he taught through spontaneous songs of realization. His life story serves as the ultimate proof of the potential for total transformation.

15-Gampopa.htm.title: 15. Gampopa Sönam Rinchen (Dagpo Kagyu)
15-Gampopa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Gampopa Sönam Rinchen (Dagpo Kagyu) together with further information.
15-Gampopa.htm.intro: Gampopa (1079–1153) was the physician-monk who merged the Kadam monastic discipline with Milarepa’s Mahāmudra instructions. Following the tragic death of his family, he entered the monastery and later became Milarepa’s heart disciple. By organizing the Kagyu teachings into a systematic monastic framework, he founded the Dagpo Kagyu lineage. His masterpiece, The Jewel Ornament of Liberation, remains the primary textbook for students of the Kagyu school, bridging the gap between monkhood and yogic practice.

16-Rechungpa.htm.title: 16. Rechungpa Dorje Drakpa (Kagyu Master)
16-Rechungpa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Rechungpa Dorje Drakpa (Kagyu Master) together with further information.
16-Rechungpa.htm.intro: Rechungpa (1083–1161) was one of Milarepa’s two moon-like disciples, representing the yogic, non-monastic side of the Kagyu lineage. Unlike Gampopa, Rechungpa traveled to India several times, bringing back esoteric teachings that Milarepa himself had not mastered. His pride often led to clashes with his teacher, providing classic lessons on the student-teacher relationship. Rechungpa’s lineage emphasizes the hidden, tantric aspects of the oral transmission, preserving the raw, wild spirit of the mahāsiddhas.

17-Sakya-Pandita.htm.title: 17. Śākya Paṇḍita (Mañjuśrī Emanation)
17-Sakya-Pandita.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Śākya Paṇḍita (Mañjuśrī Emanation) together with further information.
17-Sakya-Pandita.htm.intro: The fourth of the Five Sakya Patriarchs, Śākya Paṇḍita (1182–1251) was a peerless scholar who mastered the five sciences. He is credited with establishing the rigorous standard of logic and debate in Tibet. His diplomatic skills saved Tibet from Mongol invasion when he befriended Godan Khan, leading to the Sakya family’s political regency over Tibet. Regarded as an emanation of the Buddha of Wisdom, Mañjuśrī, his works remain the gold standard for Tibetan scholasticism.

18-Longchenpa.htm.title: 18. Longchenpa (Great Perfection)
18-Longchenpa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Longchenpa (Great Perfection) together with further information.
18-Longchenpa.htm.intro: Longchen Rabjam (1308–1364) was a master of the Nyingma school and arguably the greatest philosopher of the Dzogchen tradition. He systematically organized the disparate Nyingma teachings into the Seven Treasuries, which remain the most profound expositions of the Great Perfection view. His writings bridge the gap between the intellectual mind and the primordial nature of reality. For Nyingmapas, Longchenpa is the omniscient guide who clarified the deepest mysteries of the mind’s natural state.

19-Buton-Rinchen-Drub.htm.title: 19. Butön Rinchen Drub (Scholar and Historian)
19-Buton-Rinchen-Drub.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Butön Rinchen Drub (Scholar and Historian) together with further information.
19-Buton-Rinchen-Drub.htm.intro: Butön () was a monumental figure, famous for organizing the Tibetan Buddhist Canon. He compiled and cataloged the Kangyur (The Words of the Buddha) and the Tengyur (The Commentaries), providing the definitive structure for Tibetan scripture. As the abbot of Shalu Monastery, he was a master of the Kālachakra Tantra and a prolific writer. His historical work, History of Buddhism in India and Tibet, is an essential primary source.

20-Tsongkhapa.htm.title: 20. Tsongkhapa (Gelug Master)
20-Tsongkhapa.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Tsongkhapa (Gelug Master) together with further information.
20-Tsongkhapa.htm.intro: Lobsang Drakpa, known as Je Tsongkhapa (1357–1419), was the great reformer who founded the Gelug school. Deeply influenced by Atiśa’s Kadam lineage, he emphasized strict Vinaya discipline, intensive study, and a precise understanding of the Madhyamaka view of emptiness. He founded Ganden Monastery and established the Great Prayer Festival in Lhasa. His magnum opus, the Lamrim Chenmo, provides a comprehensive map of the spiritual path, earning him a reputation as the Second Atiśa.

Marpa.title: The Life of Marpa the Translator
Marpa.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Marpa.intro: The Life of Marpa the Translator recounts the eleventh-century Tibetan master’s journey to India three times, seeking dharma from Nāropa, Maitrīpa, and other siddhas. He endured great hardships, received tantric teachings, and returned to Tibet to translate scriptures and teach. Marpa married Dagmema, raised a family, and trained disciples including Milarepa, Ngoktön, and Metön. His son Tarma Dode died young but transferred his consciousness to a brahmin boy in India. Marpa displayed miracles, established the Kagyü lineage, and dissolved into dharmadhātu at eighty-eight amid rainbows and flowers.

00-Prologue.htm.title: 00 The Prologue
00-Prologue.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Prologue from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
00-Prologue.htm.intro: The text praises Marpa the Translator, describing how he fulfilled his vows, crossed to India, received the jewel of dharma from Nāropa, and brought it to Tibet. It offers prostrations to his body, speech, and mind, confesses faults, rejoices in his deeds, and requests the turning of the dharma wheel. The author announces his intention to briefly recount Marpa’s wondrous life story for the benefit of beings.

01-Early-Years.htm.title: 01 The Early Years
01-Early-Years.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Early Years from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
01-Early-Years.htm.intro: Marpa was born in Pesar, in Lhotrak Chukhver, to Marpa Wangchuk Öser and Lady Gyamo Sa Dode. He was the youngest of three children, short-tempered and stubborn from youth. His father, foreseeing potential for great benefit or harm, decided to entrust him to dharma. At twelve, Marpa was sent to a local teacher, studied reading and writing, and then, due to his aggressive nature, was sent far away. He went to Drogmi Lotsāwa, offering provisions, and studied Sanskrit and Indian languages for three years.

02-First-Journey.htm.title: 02 The First Journey to India
02-First-Journey.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The First Journey to India from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
02-First-Journey.htm.intro: Marpa, inspired by Vajrayoginī, travels to India seeking Nāropa. He receives Hevajra, Guhyasamāja, and other tantras from Nāropa, Jñānagarbha, and the mahāsiddha Kukkuripa on an island in a poison lake. He then meets Maitrīpa, who grants him full abhiṣekas and mahāmudrā instructions. Marpa also receives the Catuhpīṭha from a ḍākinī. After twelve years in India and Nepal, he returns to Tibet, having become a treasury of oral instruction

03-First-Return.htm.title: 03 The First Return from India
03-First-Return.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The First Return from India from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
03-First-Return.htm.intro: On his return voyage, the jealous translator Nyö has Marpa’s books thrown into the Ganges. Marpa responds without anger, singing a song of shame, and later teaches the view to Nepalese disciples. At a border town, he dreams of Saraha, who blesses his body, speech, and mind and teaches mahāmudrā. Marpa then sings a profound song at Kyerphu. He visits Nyö to copy texts but is refused. Returning to Lhotrak, he finds his parents dead, then begins gathering gold for a second journey to India.

04-Second-Journey.htm.title: 04 The Second Journey to India
04-Second-Journey.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Second Journey to India from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
04-Second-Journey.htm.intro: He meets his first chief disciple, Ngokton Chödor of Shung, teaches Hevajra, and heals nine women. In Phen, he gives abhiṣekas, then meets the merchant Marpa Golek, who invites him north. Golek tests Marpa’s apparent miserliness, realizes it is devotion to dharma, and becomes his disciple. Marpa gathers much gold, returns to Lhotrak, gives teachings to Ngokpa, Tsurtön, and others, and sings a song recounting his Indian gurus and journeys. His wealth and fame increase, and he marries Dagmema.

05-Third-Journey.htm.title: 05 The Third Journey to India
05-Third-Journey.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Third Journey to India from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
05-Third-Journey.htm.intro: Marpa, urged by a ḍākinī’s coded verse and Milarepa’s dream, resolves to return to India despite his disciples’ pleas. He travels alone, meeting Atiśa on the way. In India, he learns Nāropa has entered the action. Guided by Maitrīpa, Kukkuripa, and others, Marpa searches for eight months through visions and hardships. Finally he meets Nāropa at Phullahari, receives the hearing lineage and Cakrasaṁvara abhiṣekas, survives obstacles, and is established as Nāropa’s regent.

06-Third-Return.htm.title: 06 The Third Return from India
06-Third-Return.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Third Return from India from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
06-Third-Return.htm.intro: Marpa receives Nāropa’s final command-prophecy, establishing him as regent for Tibet. He bids farewell to Nāropa and visits Maitrīpa, receiving further abhiṣekas and witnessing miraculous signs. Returning through Nepal, he meets Paiṇḍapa and other disciples, singing songs of his eight wondrous signs of meeting Nāropa, his realization of Maitrīpa’s mahāmudrā, and the hardships he endured. He finally returns to Lhotrak, where Marpa Golek and other disciples welcome him. This was his last journey to India.

07-Transference.htm.title: 07 The Transference of Consciousness
07-Transference.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Transference of Consciousness from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
07-Transference.htm.intro: Marpa demonstrates his mastery of transference of consciousness by entering the bodies of a dead pigeon, a lamb, a deer, and a yak. These miracles inspire faith in many, including his skeptical brother Chowo and the slanderer Marpa Cha-se. Marpa sings songs explaining that secret mantra practitioners bring sense pleasures to the path rather than abandoning them. He attains renown as an undisputed siddha and transmits the profound instructions on transference to his son Tarma Dode.

08-Tarma-Dode.htm.title: 08 Marpa’s Son, Tarma Dode
08-Tarma-Dode.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Marpa’s Son, Tarma Dode from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
08-Tarma-Dode.htm.intro: Marpa’s son Tarma Dode, in strict retreat, is lured to a fair by Māra’s illusions. Despite his mother’s seven vows and Milarepa’s warnings, he rides a horse, falls, and suffers a fatal head injury. Marpa and Dagmema each sing songs clarifying the ejection of consciousness. Tarma Dode transfers his consciousness into a pigeon, then into a dead brahmin boy in India, becoming Tiphupa. Marpa clears Dagmema’s grief with a song, and the Kagyu lineage flourishes through his disciples.

09-Prophecy.htm.title: 09 The Prophecy
09-Prophecy.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Prophecy from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
09-Prophecy.htm.intro: Marpa’s disciples request a prophecy about the Kagyu teachings. He asks them to await dreams. Milarepa dreams of a great snow mountain with four pillars—a lion, tigress, garuḍa, and vulture. Marpa interprets this as the future spread of the teachings through his four chief disciples: Tsurtön, Ngoktön, Metön, and Milarepa. The vulture’s chick and the flock of birds signify Milarepa’s unique disciple and the flourishing of the Kagyu lineage.

10-Transmission.htm.title: 10 The Transmission
10-Transmission.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Transmission from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
10-Transmission.htm.intro: Marpa opens the treasury of teachings to his heart-sons. He gives each disciple the transmission suited to them: Ngokpa the method of explaining tantras, Tsurtön the ejection of consciousness, Metön luminosity, and Milarepa yogic heat. Marpa tells Metön not to restrict the dharma. He then gives Milarepa the dakini hearing lineage, the special teaching no one else possesses, and prophesies its spread. Marpa displays miracles, and Dagmema dissolves into light.

11-Passing.htm.title: 11 Marpa’s Passing
11-Passing.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Marpa’s Passing from The Life of Marpa the Translator together with further information.
11-Passing.htm.intro: At eighty-eight, Marpa declares that Nāropa and hosts of ḍākas and ḍākiṇīs have come to escort him. After offering the sevenfold service, he passes into dharmadhātu amid rainbows, flowers, and music. His body remains unburned as a wish-fulfilling relic. Ngokpa later takes the body to Shung and enshrines it in a stūpa. The biography concludes with a colophon by Trakthung Gyalpo and a translator’s colophon by Chökyi Gyatso.

Milarepa.title: The Life of Milarepa
Milarepa.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Milarepa.intro: The Life of Milarepa recounts the eleventh-century Tibetan yogin’s journey from sinner to Buddha based on the 11th Century Biography by Tsangnyön Heruka. Born Töpaga, he suffers poverty after his father’s death, then commits murder and casts hailstorms through black magic. Tormented by remorse, he seeks dharma and meets Marpa Lotsawa, who subjects him to years of abuse and tower-building to purify his karma. Finally receiving initiations, Milarepa meditates in mountain caves for years, living on nettles, attaining realisation and miracles. He gathers disciples like Rechungpa and Gampopa, and dies at eighty-four after accepting poisoned curds. His relics are carried to a pure land by ḍākinīs. The text portrays him as a Tibetan Buddha.

00-Prologue.htm.title: The Prologue
00-Prologue.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Prologue from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
00-Prologue.htm.intro: The Prologue introduces the extraordinary life story of Jetsün Milarepa, a supreme Tibetan saint. Born into a family that faced tragedy after his father’s death, Milarepa initially carried out wrathful magic against hostile relatives. However, filled with renunciation, he surrendered life and limb to the dharma under an authentic lama. Through intensive solitary meditation, he overcame all afflictions, mastered miraculous powers, and ultimately achieved full buddhahood, liberating countless sentient beings.

01-Birth.htm.title: 01 The Birth of Milarepa
01-Birth.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Birth of Milarepa from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
01-Birth.htm.intro: Inspired by a prophetic dream about his master’s greatness, the disciple Rechungpa requests Milarepa to share his life story. Milarepa agrees, recounting his family lineage. He explains how an ancestor subdued a demon, earning the name Mila. Despite losing their fortune in a dice game, the family rebuilt their wealth, leading to the birth of Milarepa, named Töpaga. Indeed, he spent his early childhood years raised in great material luxury.

02-Suffering.htm.title: 02 Milarepa’s Suffering
02-Suffering.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Milarepa’s Suffering from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
02-Suffering.htm.intro: Following the death of Milarepa’s father, his greedy paternal uncle and aunt seized his family’s immense wealth instead of preserving it. They forced Milarepa, his mother, and sister into brutal, dog-like servitude. When Milarepa turned fifteen, his mother formally demanded their inheritance back. The relatives aggressively denied the claim, beat them, and evicted them. Consequently, Milarepa was sent to study Nyingmapa traditions while his family endured extreme poverty.

03-Enemies.htm.title: 03 The Destruction of Enemies
03-Enemies.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Destruction of Enemies from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
03-Enemies.htm.intro: To avenge his family’s mistreatment by cruel relatives, Milarepa trains in black magic at his mother’s desperate request. He summons powerful dharma protectors who collapse his uncle’s house, killing thirty-five enemies during a wedding feast. Funded by seven ounces of gold secretly hidden inside a messenger’s cloak, he later learns how to cast a devastating hailstorm that destroys the hostile villagers’ entire harvest, completing his worldly deeds of vengeance.

04-Meeting.htm.title: 04 Meeting with the Lama
04-Meeting.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Meeting with the Lama from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
04-Meeting.htm.intro: Regretful of his past sins using harmful black magic, Milarepa seeks the genuine dharma. After failing to practice diligently under lama Rongtön Lhaga, he is directed to the legendary translator Marpa Lotsāwa. Upon arriving, Milarepa unknowingly meets Marpa disguised as a plowing cleric. After testing Milarepa with hard field labor, Marpa reveals his true identity and accepts him as a devoted disciple, offering him authentic dharma instead of material comforts.

05-Purification.htm.title: 05 Purification
05-Purification.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Purification from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
05-Purification.htm.intro: Seeking sacred dharma instructions, the Great Magician (Milarepa) submits to Lama Marpa to purify his past evil deeds. Marpa subjects him to relentless trials, repeatedly forcing him to build and tear down massive stone towers while refusing to grant him secret initiations. Despite festering sores, harsh beatings, and a failed attempt to receive teachings elsewhere through forged permission, he faithfully endures this profound suffering to purify his negative karma.

06-Initiation.htm.title: 06 Initiation Under Lama Marpa
06-Initiation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Initiation Under Lama Marpa from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
06-Initiation.htm.intro: Lama Marpa invites Milarepa as the chief guest of honour after testing him through severe trials. Marpa explains that his harsh discipline was designed to purify negative deeds, wear down self-importance, and lead him toward enlightenment. Filled with joy, Milarepa receives lay vows, secret names, and the Cakrasaṃvara mandala initiation. Marpa interprets auspicious omens, bestows essential oral instructions, and predicts that Milarepa’s spiritual lineage will expand like the waxing moon.

07-Realisations.htm.title: 07 Realisations
07-Realisations.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Realisations from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
07-Realisations.htm.intro: Milarepa completes eleven months of solitary meditation before presenting his spiritual realisations in song to his master, Marpa, and Dakmema. Prompted by a ḍākinī’s vision, Marpa travels to India to obtain special Transference instructions from Nāropa. Afterwards, Milarepa recounts a dream of four pillars, which Marpa interprets as the future spread of Kagyu teachings through his four main disciples. Marpa then assigns specific lineage instructions and gifts to each disciple.

08-Departure.htm.title: 08 Departure
08-Departure.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Departure from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
08-Departure.htm.intro: Troubled by a distressing dream revealing his home in ruins and his elderly mother dead, Milarepa breaks his strict retreat to ask Lama Marpa for permission to return to his homeland. Observing auspicious signs, Marpa consents and bestows the complete tantric initiations and secret oral instructions. After tearful farewells, prayers, and ritual feasts with Marpa and Dakmema, Milarepa departs to briefly visit his family before entering a solitary mountain retreat.

09-Determination.htm.title: 09 Determination
09-Determination.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Determination from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
09-Determination.htm.intro: Returning to his homeland, Milarepa discovers his home in ruins, his sister missing, and sacred texts damaged by vermin. Overcome with grief upon finding his mother’s bleached bones, he applies his lama’s instructions to liberate her consciousness. With help, he crafts sacred figurines from her bones to place inside a stupa. Moved by the impermanence of worldly life, Milarepa vows to dedicate himself entirely to dharma meditation at Drakar Taso.

10-Perseverance.htm.title: 10 Perseverance
10-Perseverance.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Perseverance from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
10-Perseverance.htm.intro: Moved by remorse and renunciation, Milarepa endures extreme austerity in mountain retreats, surviving on nettles. Despite poverty, abuse, and family conflict, he perseveres in meditation. Through the lama’s guidance, his practice deepens, yielding profound realization. He teaches his sister Peta and aunt, emphasizing conviction in cause and effect, renunciation of worldly concerns, and unwavering perseverance as essential for attaining buddhahood in one lifetime.

11-Benefiting.htm.title: 11 Benefiting the Teachings
11-Benefiting.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Benefiting the Teachings from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
11-Benefiting.htm.intro: Rechungpa asks Milarepa about the episodes of his life that inspire laughter. The Jetsün explains these are the times he established fortunate disciples—human and non-human—on the path of ripening and liberation, thereby benefiting the Buddha’s teachings. He names his many retreat places and recounts meeting his heart-disciples, including Rechungpa, Gampopa, and Tseringma.

12-Activities.htm.title: 12 Activities
12-Activities.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Activities from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
12-Activities.htm.intro: Geshe Tsakpuwa, jealous of Milarepa, sends a woman with poisoned curds. Knowing his time has come, Milarepa accepts the poison. He teaches his disciples, transfers his illness to demonstrate his power, and forgives the Geshe. Before passing, he gives final instructions, distributing his few possessions. At cremation, dakinis carry his relics to a pure land.

13-Colophon.htm.title: 13 Disciples and Colophon
13-Colophon.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Disciples and Colophon from The Life of Milarepa together with further information.
13-Colophon.htm.intro: This closing section lists Milarepa’s disciples—eight heart-sons including Gampopa and Rechungpa, thirteen close-sons, four female disciples, and countless human and non-human followers. After the funeral rites, the disciples departed to mountain retreats. The text describes Milarepa’s life as twelve marvelous deeds—three worldly and nine supreme—and concludes with verses praising the biography’s power to inspire faith, renunciation, and liberation.

Ramayana.title:
The Ramayana
The Epic of Rama, Prince of India
Ramayana.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from the Ramayana together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Ramayana.intro: Storybooks based on a condensed English verse translation of the ancient Indian epic, the Ramayana, by the scholar Romesh C. Dutt. The text chronicles the virtuous life of Prince Rama, beginning with his miraculous marriage to Sita after he successfully proves his strength by breaking a divine bow. The narrative shifts to the tragic intrigue of the royal court, where Queen Kaikeyi’s demands lead to Rama’s fourteen-year banishment and the subsequent death of King Dasa-ratha from a broken heart. Throughout the journey, the sources emphasize the unwavering loyalty of Sita and Lakshman, who follow Rama into the wilderness of the Dandak forest. The provided sections also highlight the moral conflict faced by Rama’s brother, Bharat, who seeks out the exiled prince to beg for his return to the throne of Ayodhya. The work serves as a spiritual and cultural revelation, illustrating the timeless ideals of duty, honor, and sacrifice inherent in Indian tradition, that were so influential not only in India, but throughout SE Asia.
