GW-1-01-Introduction-to-Meditation.htm.title: 1: Why We Should Meditate
GW-1-01-Introduction-to-Meditation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Why We Should Meditate from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-1-01-Introduction-to-Meditation.htm.intro: Godwin introduces meditation as a way of living rather than just a sitting practice. He emphasizes understanding the mind and its reactions to daily challenges. Instead of controlling thoughts, we should observe them with a friendly, non-judgmental attitude. This gentle way transforms suffering into learning, helping us find peace within ourselves amidst the chaos of worldly life.

GW-1-02-The-Importance-of-Awareness.htm.title: 2: The Importance of Awareness
GW-1-02-The-Importance-of-Awareness.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Importance of Awareness from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-1-02-The-Importance-of-Awareness.htm.intro: This talk focuses on the role of awareness in daily activities. Godwin explains how mindfulness acts as a mirror, reflecting our thoughts and emotions without bias. By staying present, we break the habit of reacting mechanically to unpleasant situations. Awareness allows us to make conscious choices, leading to a life of freedom, clarity, and reduced internal conflict or stress.

GW-1-03-The-Importance-of-the-Dhamma.htm.title: 3: The Importance of the Dhamma
GW-1-03-The-Importance-of-the-Dhamma.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting The Importance of the Dhamma from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-1-03-The-Importance-of-the-Dhamma.htm.intro: Godwin discusses how material consumerism and the pursuit of toys fail to provide lasting happiness. He suggests that through Dhamma, we become our own toy, finding joy within. He encourages learning from mistakes without self-criticism and viewing life as the ultimate teacher. Being an island unto oneself means developing self-reliance and befriending one’s own mind and loneliness.

GW-1-04-Mindfulness-of-Breathing.htm.title: 4: Mindfulness of Breathing
GW-1-04-Mindfulness-of-Breathing.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mindfulness of Breathing from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-1-04-Mindfulness-of-Breathing.htm.intro: The breath is presented as a constant friend that grounds us in the present moment. Godwin explains that focusing on breathing helps manage emotions and provides relief from stress. He advises against making meditation a battle or a search for concentration. Instead, by simply knowing the breath, we drop social identifications and discover a natural state of inner calm.

GW-1-05-Meditation-on-Loving-kindness.ht.title: 5: Meditation on Loving-kindness
GW-1-05-Meditation-on-Loving-kindness.ht.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Meditation on Loving-kindness from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-1-05-Meditation-on-Loving-kindness.ht.intro: Godwin explores the healing power of Loving-Kindness, beginning with oneself. He explains that self-forgiveness and accepting our human-ness are essential precursors to being kind to others. Metta is not just a formal meditation but an attitude that dissolves anger and fear. By cultivating a soft heart, we change our relationship with ourselves and the world around us.

GW-1-06-Meditation-and-Emotions.htm.title: 6: Meditation and Emotions
GW-1-06-Meditation-and-Emotions.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Meditation and Emotions from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-1-06-Meditation-and-Emotions.htm.intro: The final talk serves as a practical guide for integrating spiritual practice into a busy urban environment. Godwin emphasizes that every situation—even an argument or a traffic jam—is an opportunity for meditation. He encourages maintaining a don't-know mind, staying open to learning, and prioritizing a peaceful state of mind over external achievements or the need for perfection.

GW-2-01-Integrating-Meditation.htm.title: 1: Meditation in Daily Life
GW-2-01-Integrating-Meditation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Meditation in Daily Life from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-2-01-Integrating-Meditation.htm.intro: During this retreat, Godwin guides participants through periods of silence and sitting. He emphasizes the importance of bodily relaxation as a foundation for mental stillness. Participants are encouraged to observe the rise and fall of thoughts without interference. The session focuses on recognizing the difference between thinking and knowing, helping practitioners cultivate a steady, unshakeable center within themselves.

GW-2-02-Meditation-in-Daily-Life.htm.title: 2: How to Integrate Meditation with Daily Life
GW-2-02-Meditation-in-Daily-Life.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting How to Integrate Meditation with Daily Life from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-2-02-Meditation-in-Daily-Life.htm.intro: This session provides tools for handling difficult emotions like anxiety and grief. Godwin teaches participants to "make friends" with their pain rather than pushing it away. By observing the physical sensations of an emotion, its power to overwhelm the mind is diminished. The retreat highlights that through acceptance and gentle investigation, even the most painful emotions can become paths to wisdom.

GW-3-01-What-We-Can-Try-To-Do.htm.title: 1: What We Can Try To Do During the Retreat
GW-3-01-What-We-Can-Try-To-Do.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting What We Can Try To Do During the Retreat from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-3-01-What-We-Can-Try-To-Do.htm.intro: The retreat begins with the transition from worldly noise to noble silence. Godwin explains that silence is not just the absence of speech, but an inner quietude. He introduces basic breath awareness and encourages students to let go of expectations. The goal is to settle into the present moment and begin the journey of self-discovery with a gentle heart.

GW-3-02-What-Happened-on-That-Day.htm.title: 2: Sharing on What Happened on That Day
GW-3-02-What-Happened-on-That-Day.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sharing on What Happened on That Day from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-3-02-What-Happened-on-That-Day.htm.intro: Participants focus on mindfulness of the body and its movements. Godwin teaches that by deeply feeling physical sensations, we ground ourselves in reality. Whether walking, eating, or sitting, every movement is a chance to be awake. This practice helps bridge the gap between formal meditation and the simple, physical realities of life, reducing the habit of mental wandering.

GW-3-03-Benefits-of-Loving-kindness-Medi.title: 3: Benefits of Loving-kindness Meditation
GW-3-03-Benefits-of-Loving-kindness-Medi.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Benefits of Loving-kindness Meditation from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-3-03-Benefits-of-Loving-kindness-Medi.intro: Godwin addresses the hindrances of meditation, such as restlessness and boredom. He suggests that distractions are not enemies but reflections of the mind’s habits. Instead of struggling to focus, students learn to note distractions and return gently to their object of meditation. This teaches patience and helps practitioners stay equanimous when things do not go as planned.

GW-3-04-Emotions-and-Meditation.htm.title: 4: Emotions and Meditation
GW-3-04-Emotions-and-Meditation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Emotions and Meditation from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-3-04-Emotions-and-Meditation.htm.intro: The focus shifts to Vipassanā or insight. Participants are encouraged to see the changing nature (impermanence) of their thoughts and sensations. By seeing that everything arises and passes away, the tendency to cling or resist is weakened. This realization brings a sense of lightness and freedom, as the meditator stops taking their mental dramas so personally and seriously.

GW-3-05-Thoughts-and-Meditation.htm.title: 5: Thoughts and Meditation
GW-3-05-Thoughts-and-Meditation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Thoughts and Meditation from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-3-05-Thoughts-and-Meditation.htm.intro: The retreat emphasizes the practice of Metta. After days of quiet observation, participants turn their attention to cultivating goodwill. Starting with themselves, they extend thoughts of peace to friends, strangers, and even enemies. This practice softens the ego and builds a sense of interconnectedness, ensuring that the wisdom gained is balanced with compassion for all living beings.

GW-3-06-Meditation-in-Daily-Life.htm.title: 6: Integrating Meditation with Daily Life
GW-3-06-Meditation-in-Daily-Life.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Integrating Meditation with Daily Life from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-3-06-Meditation-in-Daily-Life.htm.intro: Godwin addresses the inner judge that often hampers spiritual progress. He warns against the perfectionist model of meditation and encourages a playful, experimental approach. By letting go of plus and minus ratings of their practice, students learn to accept themselves as they are. This radical self-acceptance is presented as a key to true liberation and mental health.

GW-3-07-Summary-and-Conclusion.htm.title: 7: Summary and Conclusion
GW-3-07-Summary-and-Conclusion.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Summary and Conclusion from the Gentle Way together with further information.
GW-3-07-Summary-and-Conclusion.htm.intro: On the final day, the focus is on taking the retreat experience back into the world. Godwin emphasizes that the real retreat begins when they leave. He provides advice on maintaining awareness in the face of family and work pressures. The session ends with a message of encouragement: to continue being a light unto oneself and living the Dhamma daily.

Perfections.title: The Ten Perfections (Pāramī)
Perfections.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from The Ten Perfections (Pāramī) together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Perfections.intro: This collection of storybooks outlines the ten perfections found in Buddhist teachings, serving as a comprehensive guide to moral and spiritual development. Each section explores a specific virtue—such as generosity, morality, renunciation, and wisdom—by defining its core characteristics and the mental discipline required for its mastery. The texts further examine the practical application of energy, forbearance, truthfulness, and resolution, illustrating how these qualities protect and strengthen the practitioner. Additionally, the final chapters focus on the cultivation of loving-kindness and equanimity, emphasizing a balanced, compassionate attitude toward all living beings. Together, these sources utilize poster art and scriptural stories to provide a clear roadmap for achieving ethical excellence and ultimate enlightenment.

01-Generosity.htm.title: 01 Generosity (Dāna)
01-Generosity.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Generosity (Dāna)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
01-Generosity.htm.intro: Generosity (dāna) involves volition to give suitable things. Distinguished from charity (pariccāga)—giving to noble persons versus lower status, personal distribution versus abandoning possessions. True giving requires supporter, objects, recipient, and volition. Great charities include relinquishing limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, family. Volitional and material generosity both contribute to merit. Four conditions must be fulfilled for an act to qualify as true generosity.

02-Morality.htm.title: 02 Morality (Sīla)
02-Morality.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Morality (Sīla)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
02-Morality.htm.intro: Morality (sīla) controls physical/verbal actions and upholds meritorious deeds. Includes volition, abstention from wrong actions, and right mental states. Restraints include monastic rules, mindfulness, knowledge, forbearance, and energy. Morality serves as foundation for consciousness in sensuous, material, immaterial, and supermundane realms. Like a yak sacrificing life to protect its tail-hair, one should preserve morality even at life’s risk.

03-Renunication.htm.title: 03 Renunication (Nekkhamma)
03-Renunication.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Renunication (Nekkhamma)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
03-Renunication.htm.intro: Renunciation means emancipation from sense-desires and Saṁsāra. Three wrong thoughts (sensuous, hateful, cruel) versus right thoughts (renunciation, hatelessness, non-violence). Renunciation can precede or follow monastic life. Forest dwelling has five types; only those praised by Buddhas or with few wishes are commendable. Renunciation by old married people is more difficult than by youths. Supreme renunciation is exemplified by King Cūḷa Sutasoma who went to the Himālayas despite pleas.

04-Wisdom.htm.title: 04 Wisdom (Paññā)
04-Wisdom.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Wisdom (Paññā)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
04-Wisdom.htm.intro: Wisdom arises from thinking, hearing, or meditation. Basic wisdom comes from learning from the wise. Four kinds of wise persons: original thinkers, learned, interpreters of meaning, and those with ready speech. Wisdom perceives with discrimination, penetrates reality, and overcomes ignorance. The story of Sulasā shows wisdom can involve knowing about evil without committing it. True wisdom understands four noble truths and three characteristics of existence.

05-Energy.htm.title: 05 Energy (Viriya)
05-Energy.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Energy (Viriya)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
05-Energy.htm.intro: Energy should be applied uniformly to all tasks, like a lion hunting small or large prey. Right effort involves preventing evil, abandoning arisen evil, generating good, and maintaining good. Eleven factors develop energy including reflecting on the dangers of the lower realms, the benefits of effort, honoring alms, and associating with industrious people. Spiritual urgency from knowledge serves as the main foundation. Proper mental attitude determines whether energy becomes wholesome or unwholesome.

06-Forbearance.htm.title: 06 Forbearance (Khanti)
06-Forbearance.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Forbearance (Khanti)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
06-Forbearance.htm.intro: Forbearance means enduring praise without greed and insults without hate. It is non-hate specifically when provoked. Ven. Puṇṇa exemplified tolerance even to physical assault. Nine causes of anger relate to self, friends, or enemies regarding past, present, or future actions. Forbearance is strength of ascetics and Brahmins. Supreme patience tolerates rudeness from inferiors without special reason. Sakka’s forbearance demonstrated enduring insults while remaining calm.

07-Truthfulness.htm.title: 07 Truthfulness (Sacca)
07-Truthfulness.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Truthfulness (Sacca)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
07-Truthfulness.htm.intro: Truth has two kinds: conventional (names based on perception) and ultimate (reality discerned through wisdom). Conventional truth aids generosity, morality, and prevents evil. Ultimate truth reveals mind, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna. Buddha taught both—discourses use conventional terms to guide beings to happy states, Abhidhamma reveals ultimate reality. Noble truth sees all worldly happiness as suffering due to impermanence. Wisdom alone can discern Nibbāna’s peace.

08-Resolution.htm.title: 08 Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna)
08-Resolution.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Resolution (Adhiṭṭhāna)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
08-Resolution.htm.intro: Resolution means unwavering determination like a rocky mountain. Vinaya uses resolution for Observance Day, robes, and bowls. Absorption mastery involves five skills including resolution (determining duration in jhāna). Ten supernormal powers include power of resolution—projecting copies of oneself. Stories of Ven. Bākula and novice Saṅkicca show miraculous protection from imminent wisdom. Noble ones can contemplate objects as loathsome or unloathsome at will.

09-Loving-Kindness.htm.title: 09 Loving-Kindness (Mettā)
09-Loving-Kindness.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Loving-Kindness (Mettā)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
09-Loving-Kindness.htm.intro: True loving-kindness (mettā) is pure goodwill, unlike craving or affection. It is hatelessness directed toward beings’ welfare. 528 ways to develop: five unlimited categories (all beings, breathing, creatures, persons, individuals) and seven limited (female, male, noble, ignoble, devas, humans, petas), each with four wishes. Fifteen virtues precede development. The Metta-sutta teaches all-inclusive and group-divided loving-kindness. Its object is always living beings.

10-Equanimity.htm.title: 10 Equanimity (Upekkhā)
10-Equanimity.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting 10 Equanimity (Upekkhā)based on the Great Chronicles of the Buddhas together with further information.
10-Equanimity.htm.intro: Equanimity means balanced neutrality between sorrow and happiness—not negligence. Development uses one mode: all beings have their deeds as their own property (kammassakā), totaling 132 methods. Equanimity is more difficult than loving-kindness because it requires impartiality toward friends, foes, and neutrals alike. It belongs to the highest absorption, indicating superiority. The Bodhisatta’s story of enduring ill-treatment while remaining unshaken exemplifies supreme equanimity perfection.

Basic-Concepts.title: Basic Buddhist Concepts
Basic-Concepts.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from Basic Buddhist Concepts by Henri van Zeyst together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Basic-Concepts.intro: These storybooks provide a comprehensive overview of fundamental Buddhist principles through a series of instructional posters and analytical texts. The collection explores the interconnected nature of reality, emphasizing how the illusion of a permanent self leads to internal conflict and suffering. Key concepts such as impermanence, karma, and rebirth are examined to show how intentional actions and psychological attachments drive the cycle of existence. The materials further detail the process of dependent origination, illustrating how ignorance fuels mental formations and sensory cravings. The sources advocate for the cultivation of direct insight and wisdom to dissolve false identities. By moving beyond temporary mental concentration to genuine understanding, a practitioner can achieve liberation and live authentically in the present.
Basic-Concepts.keywords: Lay Teacher, Sri Lanka, Dharma, Meditation, Modern

01-Impermanence.htm.title: 01 Impermanence
01-Impermanence.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Impermanence from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
01-Impermanence.htm.intro: Impermanence (anicca) reveals that all composed things (saṅkhāra) inevitably decompose. This process encompasses negative change, positive becoming, and the general aspect of conditionality. While memory and instinct serve biological functions, they psychologically construct a false I (ahaṁkāra) by seeking permanence in the ephemeral. Recognizing anicca through dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda) dissolves this delusion. Understanding that existence is naturally impermanent finally resolves conflict (dukkha).

02-Conflict.htm.title: 02 Conflict
02-Conflict.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Conflict from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
02-Conflict.htm.intro: The concept of dukkha represents an internal conflict arising from a distorted mind’s active resistance to impermanence (anicca). This profound suffering—including sorrow (soka), lamentation, and physical decay (jarā)—stems from a fragile ego desperately clinging to memories and possessions for security. Conflict persists because the mind fears self-dissolution. Freedom is achieved through liberating direct insight, dissolving the false self to embrace life’s constant change without fear or attachment.

03-Non-Self.htm.title: 03 Non-Self
03-Non-Self.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Non-Self from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
03-Non-Self.htm.intro: The text explores anatta (non-self), asserting that the self is a psychological construct created by memory and sustained craving for permanence. This delusion fuels choice and conflict (dukkha) within an impermanent world (anicca). By dismantling various logical and theological arguments for an eternal soul, the author emphasizes that direct insight into the voidness of self (anatta saññā) is essential to the achievement of liberation and ending all unnecessary suffering and conflict.

04-Karma.htm.title: 04 Karma
04-Karma.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Karma from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
04-Karma.htm.intro: Karma, defined by the Buddha as volition (cetanā), denotes intentional action. It functions as a principle of action and reaction, rather than fatalistic destiny. This force drives rebirth, shaping individuality without an abiding soul (anatta). While karma accumulates, it can be modified or even obliterated through conscious awareness. Ultimately, the doctrine aims to regularize the mind, seeking freedom from all forms of bondage.

05-Rebirth.htm.title: 05 Rebirth
05-Rebirth.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Rebirth from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
05-Rebirth.htm.intro: Karma corresponds to four planes of existence (bhūmi). Unskilful actions lead to sub-human spheres (apāya), while skilful ones reach fortunate realms (kāma loka) or mental absorptions (jhāna). Rebirth is not soul transmigration but a reaction to volitional activity. The “I” is a delusion seeking continuity. True rebirth occurs every moment by letting go of the past, eventually reaching formless spheres (arūpaloka) where the cycle of ego and conflict finally ceases.

06-Ignorance.htm.title: 06 Ignorance
06-Ignorance.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Ignorance from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
06-Ignorance.htm.intro: Ignorance (avijjā) drives the desire for becoming and purposeful formations (saṅkhāra) through dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda). Enlightenment reveals the non-self (anatta), allowing one to live as a Tathāgata, experiencing reality’s “thus-ness” and ultimate reality without conflict. When ignorance is recognized as ignorance, the search for goals ends. This insight stops the reactive mind from creating artificial compositions, effectively dissolving the illusory “searcher” and ending all purposeful reactions.

07-Formations.htm.title: 07 Formations
07-Formations.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Formations from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
07-Formations.htm.intro: Saṅkhāra, meaning formations, is the second term in dependent origination (paṭicca-samuppāda). Originally equated with volition (cetanā) and ideation, it encompasses all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata) except Nibbāna. These formations arise in dependence on ignorance (avijjā), manifesting as karmic volitions or psychological complexes. Because ignorance conditions these reactive mental states, understanding this relationship is vital to seeing how saṅkhāra determines the specific character and nature of every arising thought within the mind.

08-Relinking.htm.title: 08 Relinking
08-Relinking.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Relinking from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
08-Relinking.htm.intro: Relinking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) arises from past conditions, shaping matter into recognizable experience known as nāma-rūpa. This psycho-physical relationship activates the six senses (saḷāyatana), resulting in contact (phassa) and sensation (vedanā). This sequence constitutes the cycle of birth (jāti) and death (maraṇa), occurring within each intentional thought as the “I” seeks continuity through memory and mental formations.

09-Experience.htm.title: 09 Experience
09-Experience.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Experience from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
09-Experience.htm.intro: Complexes arise from ignorance (avijjā), defined as a non-understanding of the present moment. This ignorance fuels conditioning complexes (saṅkhāra), producing a relinking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) that creates the illusion of a persisting self or soul. Theravāda Buddhism emphasizes anatta (no-soul), viewing rebirth not as an entity’s continuation but as a conditioned process of dependent origination across the past, present, and future.

10-Sensation.htm.title: 10 Sensation
10-Sensation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Sensation from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
10-Sensation.htm.intro: The text examines the crucial link between sensation (vedanā) and craving (taṇhā) within the wheel of Saṁsāra. While sensations are necessary conditions for desire, they do not inevitably cause it; for instance, the Buddha experienced physical needs without them becoming greed. True liberation requires understanding how the “I”-concept drives clinging (upādāna) and becoming (bhava) to maintain the false illusion of permanent self-continuance and sensory gratification.

11-Meditation.htm.title: 11 Meditation
11-Meditation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Meditation from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
11-Meditation.htm.intro: Bhāvanā signifies the methodical cultivation of the mind, focusing on developing mental power to achieve specific transcendental or mundane goals. Though often driven by an ego seeking to overcome perceived weakness and inner vacuums, its spiritual value is defined by its ultimate scope and application. This practice frequently utilizes sīla (virtue) as a foundation to discipline the uncontrolled mind and strive toward a perfected “self”.

12-Concentration.htm.title: 12 Concentration
12-Concentration.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Concentration from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
12-Concentration.htm.intro: Meditation consists of concentration (samādhi) and insight (vipassanā). Concentration employs various subjects to achieve one-pointedness (ekaggatā) and mental absorption (jhāna), leading to temporary tranquility (samatha). While samādhi suppresses the five mental hindrances (nīvaraṇa), it is often an escape from conflict rather than a permanent solution. Ultimately, one must move beyond concentration to insight (vipassanā) to gain the understanding required for true deliverance and lasting peace.

13-Insight.htm.title: 13 Insight
13-Insight.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Insight from Basic Buddhist Concepts, together with further information.
13-Insight.htm.intro: Concentration (samādhi) seeks peace through methods, yet wisdom (paññā) understands things as they truly are (yathā bhūtaṁ pajānāti). While knowledge explains “how,” wisdom investigates “why”. Conflict (dukkha) stems from the “self” (anattā) craving permanence in an impermanent (anicca) world. True insight (vipassanā) reveals the emptiness of this artificial “self,” enabling immediate, spontaneous liberation by discarding the false to live fully in the present moment.

Bojjhanga.title: Henri van Zeyst, The Seven Facets of Insight
Bojjhanga.summary:
high-definition creative commons posters from Henri van Zeyst, The Seven Facets of Insight together with further information.
Source of the Stories
Bojjhanga.intro: These storybooks describe the seven factors of awakening, which serve as the essential elements for achieving spiritual enlightenment and inner freedom. This journey begins with mindfulness, a grounded awareness that leads to the active investigation of reality and the cultivation of resilient energy. As these qualities mature, they spark spiritual delight and a deep sense of physical and mental tranquillity. This calm state enables unwavering concentration, allowing the practitioner to perceive truth with laser-like clarity. The process culminates in equanimity, a state of perfect balance and liberation that remains undisturbed by life's fluctuations. Together, these facets function not just as a sequence, but as a harmonious system for transforming the mind.
Bojjhanga.keywords: Lay Teacher, Sri Lanka, Dharma, Meditation, Modern

00-Seven-Facets-of-Insight.htm.title: Seven Facets of Insight
00-Seven-Facets-of-Insight.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Seven Facets of Insight together with further information.
00-Seven-Facets-of-Insight.htm.intro: The seven factors of awakening are not progressive steps toward enlightenment, but the very components that constitute it. True enlightenment requires a pure, unprejudiced mind free from attachment and bias. This allows for a total revolution in living—seeing reality exactly as it is. While individual factors can dynamically balance a sluggish or over-active mind, it is the harmony of all seven, anchored by mindfulness, that realizes complete inner freedom.

01-Mindfulness.htm.title: 1. Mindfulness
01-Mindfulness.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Mindfulness from The Seven facets of Insight together with further information.
01-Mindfulness.htm.intro: Mindfulness (sati) is the foundational anchor of the entire process. It is the practice of maintaining a clear, non-judgmental awareness of the present moment. By simply observing thoughts, physical sensations, and emotions as they arise and pass away without getting swept up in them, mindfulness creates the necessary mental space and stability required to see things exactly as they are, rather than how we wish they were.

02-Investigation.htm.title: 2. Investigation
02-Investigation.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Investigation from The Seven facets of Insight together with further information.
02-Investigation.htm.intro: Once mindfulness stabilizes the mind, investigation (dhamma vicaya) actively explores what has been revealed. This facet is an energetic, analytical quality that scrutinizes reality. It investigates mental states to distinguish between what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, uncovering the core truths of impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, and the lack of a permanent self. It turns passive awareness into deep, liberating wisdom through active, insightful inspection.

03-Energy.htm.title: 3. Energy
03-Energy.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Energy from The Seven facets of Insight together with further information.
03-Energy.htm.intro: Investigation naturally ignites energy (viriya), a courageous and sustained mental effort. This is not a forced, aggressive strain, but a joyful, resilient determination to abandon harmful mental habits and cultivate beneficial ones. Energy provides the vital momentum needed to overcome mental sluggishness, doubt, and complacency, ensuring the mind remains bright, active, and fully committed to the deep, transformative work of insight practice.

04-Delight.htm.title: 4. Delight
04-Delight.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Delight from The Seven facets of Insight together with further information.
04-Delight.htm.intro: Sustained energy awakens a sense of delight (piti), often described as spiritual rapture or zest. It is a profound, non-sensual joy that arises when the mind becomes deeply absorbed in wholesome practice. Delight acts as a natural emotional lubricant, uplifting the spirit, filling the body with pleasant vitality, and making the meditative process deeply rewarding. It proves that the path inward is one of profound happiness.

05-Tranquillity.htm.title: 5. Tranquillity
05-Tranquillity.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Tranquillity from The Seven facets of Insight together with further information.
05-Tranquillity.htm.intro: As the intensity of delight matures, it naturally cools into tranquillity (passaddhi). This facet represents a profound physical and mental calmness. The turbulent waves of excitement, anxiety, and restlessness subside, leaving both the body and mind deeply relaxed yet fully awake. Tranquillity brings a soothing, effortless peace, smoothing out any remaining mental friction and preparing the consciousness for the deepest states of unified focus.

06-Concentration.htm.title: 6. Concentration
06-Concentration.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Concentration from The Seven facets of Insight together with further information.
06-Concentration.htm.intro: Tranquillity allows the mind to gather itself into concentration (samadhi). This is the unwavering, single-pointed unification of consciousness. Free from distractions and inner noise, the mind becomes like a laser beam—steady, still, and exceptionally powerful. Concentration absorbs the mind entirely into the object of meditation, providing the absolute stillness and pristine clarity required to finally see through long-held psychological illusions.

07-Equanimity.htm.title: 7. Equanimity
07-Equanimity.htm.summary: high-definition creative commons posters depicting Equanimity from The Seven facets of Insight together with further information.
07-Equanimity.htm.intro: The culmination of the journey is equanimity (upekkha). This is a profound, spacious mental balance that looks upon all experiences—pleasure or pain, success or failure—with complete neutrality and lack of attachment. Equanimity is not cold indifference; it is a radiant, unshakeable freedom that remains undisturbed by the changing tides of life. It allows the mind to rest in absolute, liberated peace.
